statement: Bash is the only shell scripting language permitted for executables.
exception: legacy or constrained execution environments may force plain Bourne shell for certain scripts

statement: Executables must begin with `#!/bin/bash` and minimal flags, and use `set` to configure shell options so that invoking the script as `bash script_name` does not break its functionality.
Use shell only for small utilities or simple wrapper scripts; it is a recognized utility language, not a development language for widespread deployment.
If performance matters, use a language other than shell.
condition: performance matters for the task

statement: Rewrite a script in a more structured language once it exceeds roughly 100 lines or uses non-straightforward control flow, and do so early because scripts tend to grow.
condition: a script exceeds about 100 lines or uses non-straightforward control flow

statement: An executable should have a `.sh` extension or no extension: prefer `.sh` when a build rule renames the source file, and prefer no extension when the file is added directly to the user's PATH.
Libraries must have a `.sh` extension and must not be executable.
SUID and SGID are forbidden on shell scripts because shell cannot be secured sufficiently.
exception: use `sudo` to provide elevated access instead

statement: Send all error messages to STDERR so normal status is separated from actual errors; a shared error function that timestamps the message and writes to STDERR is recommended.
Begin every file with a top-level comment describing its contents; a copyright notice and author information are optional.
Any function that is not both obvious and short must have a header comment, and any function in a library must have one regardless of its length or complexity.
condition: a function is not both obvious and short, or the function is in a library

statement: A function header comment should document the intended API: a description plus the Globals used and modified, Arguments taken, Outputs to STDOUT/STDERR, and Returns beyond the default exit status.
Comment tricky, non-obvious, or important parts of the code, but do not comment everything.
Use TODO comments for code that is temporary, a short-term solution, or good-enough but not perfect.
A TODO must contain the literal all-caps string TODO followed by the identifier (name or e-mail) of the person with the best context, so TODOs can be searched consistently.
Apply the required formatting rules to all new code, but when modifying an existing file stay faithful to that file's existing style.
condition: the code is new; when modifying existing files, match the existing style instead

statement: Indent with 2 spaces and never tabs, and use blank lines between blocks to improve readability.
exception: the body of a `<<-` tab-indented here-document may use tabs

statement: Maximum line length is 80 characters.
Write literal strings longer than 80 characters using a here-document or an embedded newline.
exception: words longer than 80 chars that cannot sensibly be split (e.g. file paths or URLs) may exceed the limit, ideally on their own line or factored into a variable

statement: Keep a pipeline on one line if it fits; otherwise split it one segment per line with the `|`, `||`, or `&&` at the start of each continued line, indented 2 spaces, using `\` for line continuation.
condition: the pipeline does not all fit on one line

statement: Put `; then` and `; do` on the same line as the `if`, `for`, `while`, `until`, or `select`, and place `else`, `fi`, and `done` on their own lines vertically aligned with the opening statement.
Consistently include `in "$@"` in for loops for clarity, even though it may be omitted.

In a case statement, indent alternatives 2 spaces, put a space after the pattern's `)` and before `;;` on a one-line alternative, split long alternatives with pattern/actions/`;;` on separate lines, do not quote match expressions or precede patterns with an open parenthesis, and avoid the `;&` and `;;&` notations.
As strongly recommended but non-mandatory guidelines, in order of precedence: stay consistent with existing code, quote your variables, and prefer `"${var}"` over `"$var"`.
Do not brace-delimit single-character shell specials or positional parameters, but prefer brace-delimiting all other variables.
exception: unless strictly necessary or to avoid deep confusion

statement: Braces in `${var}` are not a form of quoting; double quotes must be used as well.
Always quote strings that contain variables, command substitutions, spaces, or shell metacharacters.
exception: unless careful unquoted expansion is required or the value is a shell-internal integer

statement: Use arrays for safe quoting of lists of elements, especially command-line flags, and use `"$@"` rather than `$*` when passing arguments on.
exception: use `$*` only for a specific reason, such as joining arguments into one message or log string

statement: ShellCheck is recommended for all scripts, large or small.
Use `$(command)` instead of backticks for command substitution, because it does not change when nested and is easier to read.
Prefer `[[ ... ]]` over `[ ... ]`, `test`, and `/usr/bin/[`, because no pathname expansion or word splitting occurs inside `[[ ... ]]` and it supports pattern and regular-expression matching.
When testing strings, use quotes rather than filler characters, prefer explicit `-z` and `-n` for empty/non-empty tests, and use `==` rather than `=` for equality.
Inside `[[ ... ]]`, `<` and `>` perform a lexicographical comparison, so use `(( ... ))` or `-lt`/`-gt` for numeric comparison.
Expand filename wildcards with an explicit path such as `./*` rather than `*`, because filenames can begin with a `-`.
Avoid `eval`, which munges input on assignment and makes it impossible to check what variables were set.

Use Bash arrays to store lists of elements (especially argument lists) to avoid quoting complications, access them with quoted `"${array[@]}"`, and avoid unquoted command-substitution expansion in array assignments.
exception: if more advanced data manipulation is required, avoid shell altogether rather than using arrays for complex data structures

statement: Prefer process substitution or the `readarray` builtin over piping to `while`, because a pipe runs in a subshell so variables modified there do not propagate to the parent; likewise be cautious with `for var in $(...)`, which splits on whitespace rather than lines.
Do all arithmetic with `(( ... ))` or `$(( ... ))` and never with `let`, `$[ ... ]`, or `expr`, and do not use `[[ ... ]]` at all for numeric comparison.
exception: avoid a bare `(( ... ))` statement, especially under `set -e`, since an expression evaluating to zero causes the shell to exit

statement: Avoid aliases in scripts and use functions instead, which provide a superset of alias functionality.

Name functions and variables in lower-case with underscores separating words, separate package names with `::`, require parentheses after a function name with the optional `function` keyword used consistently project-wide, keep the brace on the same line with no space before `()`, and name a loop variable to match the collection it iterates over.
Constants and anything exported to the environment should be capitalized with underscores separating words and declared at the top of the file.
For clarity, prefer `readonly` or `export` over the equivalent `declare` commands when defining constants or exported variables.
It is acceptable to set a constant at runtime or conditionally, but it must be made `readonly` immediately afterwards.
condition: a constant is set at runtime or inside a conditional

statement: Source filenames should be lowercase, with underscores to separate words if desired (e.g. `make_template`, not `make-template`).
Declare function-specific variables with `local` so they and their children's scope stay inside the function, avoiding pollution of the global namespace.

Declaration and assignment must be separate statements when the value comes from a command substitution, because `local` does not propagate the command substitution's exit code (so `$?` would reflect `local`, not the command).
condition: the assignment value is provided by a command substitution

statement: Put all functions together in the file just below the constants and do not hide executable code between functions, which makes code hard to follow and debug.
Only includes, `set` statements, and constant declarations may appear before the function declarations.
Scripts long enough to contain at least one other function require a `main` function placed as the bottom-most function, with the last non-comment line of the file being a call to `main "$@"`.
condition: the script is long enough to contain at least one other function
exception: short scripts with a simple linear flow do not require a main function

statement: Always check return values and give informative return values.
For unpiped commands, check the return value with `$?` or directly via an `if` statement to keep it simple.

Use the `PIPESTATUS` variable to check the return codes of a pipe, and assign it to another variable immediately after the pipe, because any subsequent command (including `[`) overwrites `PIPESTATUS`.
condition: you need to distinguish which segment of a pipe failed

statement: Given a choice between invoking a shell builtin and invoking a separate process, choose the builtin (e.g. parameter expansion over `sed`), because it is more efficient, robust, and portable.
When in doubt, be consistent: using one style consistently lets the team focus on more important issues and enables automation.
Consistency is a good tie-breaker only when there is no clear technical argument or long-term direction, and should not be used to justify an old style over the benefits of a newer one.
condition: there is no clear technical argument or long-term direction

statement: Never iterate over the output of `ls` or `find` via command substitution (e.g. `for f in $(ls *.mp3)`); the approach is fundamentally broken and no quoting trick fixes it — use a glob or `find` instead.

An unquoted command substitution or parameter expansion undergoes both word splitting (on the characters in `$IFS`) and filename expansion (globbing), so a value containing whitespace or glob characters (`*`, `?`, `[`) is split or replaced by matching filenames.
Command substitution gives no reliable way to delimit multiple filenames (a pathname may contain any byte except NUL, including newlines) and it also strips all trailing newlines from its output.
Never parse the output of `ls`; it is formatted for human reading and may mangle filenames (e.g. replace characters with `?`) depending on platform, arguments, and whether its stdout is a terminal.
Quoting an entire command substitution (`for f in "$(ls)"`) makes the loop run once over one concatenated string rather than once per filename.
Setting `IFS` to a newline still cannot safely iterate filenames, because a filename can itself contain a newline.
To iterate files non-recursively, expand a glob (`for file in ./*.mp3`) and always double-quote the loop variable (`"$file"`).
A glob that matches nothing expands to the literal pattern text, so guard each iteration with `[ -e "$file" ] || continue` or enable `shopt -s nullglob`.
condition: when no file matches the glob

statement: For portable recursive iteration over files, use `find ... -exec cmd {} \;`, or `find ... -exec cmd {} +` when the command accepts multiple filenames.
In bash, iterate `find` results safely with `find ... -print0` piped to `while IFS= read -r -d '' file`; this also runs the loop body in the current shell so variables assigned inside it persist.
Bash 4.0+ `globstar` (`shopt -s globstar`) lets `**` expand a glob recursively.
Always double-quote parameter expansions that hold filenames (`cp -- "$file" "$target"`), because unquoted expansions undergo word splitting and pathname expansion.
Filenames with a leading dash can be misinterpreted as command options; insert `--` after the command to mark the end of options.
The `--` end-of-options marker must be repeated at every use site and relies on the program honoring it: standard utilities should, but some (notably `echo`) and poorly-written option parsers do not.
exception: echo and programs that do not recognize end-of-options

statement: Alternatively prefix expanded filenames with `./` so a leading-dash name becomes `./-foo`, which commands treat as a safe path rather than an option.
Quote variables inside a `[ ]` test (`[ "$foo" = bar ]`); otherwise a blank or word-split value yields a `unary operator expected` or syntax error.
Prefer `[[ ]]` over `[ ]` in bash/ksh: expansions inside `[[ ]]` are not word-split or globbed, so even a blank variable is handled correctly.
Inside `[[ ]]`, the right-hand side of `=`/`==` is treated as a pattern, not a literal string; quote it to force a literal match.
condition: when the right-hand side contains pattern metacharacters

statement: Quote command substitutions used as arguments (`"$(dirname -- "$f")"`) because their result undergoes word splitting and pathname expansion.
Double quotes nest across a command-substitution boundary: the quotes inside `$(...)` form a separate pair from the quotes outside it.
`&&` and `||` cannot be used inside `[ ]` — the parser splits the line into two commands; use `[ ... ] && [ ... ]` or `[[ ... && ... ]]`.
Avoid the `-a`, `-o`, and `( )` operators of `[ ]`: they are obsolescent XSI extensions, and POSIX leaves the result of `[ ]` with more than four arguments unspecified.
Use `(( ))` for numeric comparison, not `[[ ]]`; `[[ ]]` is meant for test operators, not pure arithmetic.
Inside `[[ ]]`, `>` and `<` compare by string collation order rather than as integers; inside `[ ]`, `>` is an output redirection that creates a file.

Untrusted input evaluated in any arithmetic context (`(( ))`, `let`, an array index, or a `[[ ]]` numeric comparison) is an arbitrary-command-injection vector (e.g. `a[$(reboot)]`); validate that the input is decimal digits before evaluating it.
condition: when the value is untrusted or externally sourced

statement: `[ "$foo" -gt 7 ]` resists arithmetic injection because `[` requires decimal-integer operands, but `$foo` must still be quoted to avoid injection through `[`'s own argument parsing.
`[`/`test` interpret numeric operands as decimal, so `010` means 10, whereas `(( ))` and `[[ ]]` treat `010` as octal (8).
Each command in a pipeline runs in a separate subshell, so variables modified inside a `... | while` loop do not persist after the pipeline ends.

POSIX does not specify whether the last element of a pipeline runs in a subshell; ksh93 and bash >= 4.2 with `shopt -s lastpipe` run it in the current shell, so portable scripts must not depend on either behavior.

`if` takes a command, not a bracket condition: `[` is an ordinary command equivalent to `test`, so branch on a command directly (e.g. `if grep -q re file`) instead of wrapping it in `[ ]`, parentheses, or backticks.
`[` and `[[` require whitespace around every operand; `[bar="$foo"]` is wrong — write `[ bar = "$foo" ]`.
Do not wrap a compound conditional in an outer `[ ]`; join separate test commands with `&&`/`||`, e.g. `if [ a = b ] && [ c = d ]`.
Do not prefix the target variable with `$` in `read`; use `read foo` (or `IFS= read -r foo` to preserve backslashes and leading/trailing whitespace).
You cannot read from and write to the same file in one pipeline (`cat file | sed ... > file`); it clobbers the file — stage a temporary file plus `mv`, use `sed -i`, or use an editor.

Redirect-to-temp-then-`mv` and `sed -i` both stage a temporary file, whereas a soak-up-then-write tool like `sponge` keeps no on-disk original during the write and so risks data loss on a crash; add `sync` before `mv` for power-loss safety.
Quote the argument to `echo` (`echo "$foo"`); unquoted, the value is word-split and globbed, distorting the output.
`echo` cannot safely print arbitrary data (a leading `-n`/`-e` is taken as an option); use `printf '%s\n' "$foo"` to print a variable's value reliably.
Assign variables as `foo=bar` — do not put a `$` before the name and do not put spaces around `=`, or the shell parses the line as a command with arguments.
`echo` does not read standard input, so a here-document redirected into `echo` prints nothing; use `cat <<EOF` to emit a here-document block.
To run a command via `su`, supply a username before `-c` (`su root -c 'cmd'`); bare `su -c 'cmd'` can bind `-c` to su's own login-class option on some platforms.

Always check the exit status of `cd` before running commands that depend on the new directory: use `cd /foo && bar`, or `cd /foo || exit 1` before a block — an unchecked failed `cd` can run later commands (e.g. `rm -f *`) in the wrong place.
`set -e` (abort on any non-zero exit) is tricky to use correctly because many commands return non-zero for a non-fatal warning, which it would treat as fatal.
When changing directory per loop iteration, run the work in a subshell (`(CDPATH= cd -P -- "$subdir" || exit; cmds)`) so the `cd` is scoped to that iteration and you need not change back manually.
`==` is not valid for the POSIX `[` command; use `=` in `[ ]` (or use `[[ ]]`). Bash accepts `[ x == y ]` only as a non-portable extension.
exception: Bash accepts == in [ ] as a non-portable Bashism

statement: You cannot place a `;` immediately after `&`; `&` already terminates the command, so remove the extra `;` (e.g. `for i in ...; do ./x & done`).
`cmd1 && cmd2 || cmd3` is not a safe substitute for if/then/else: if `cmd2` returns non-zero, `cmd3` also runs — use `if cmd1; then cmd2; else cmd3; fi` whenever `cmd2` can fail.
condition: when the command after && can return non-zero

statement: In an interactive bash before 4.3, a `!` inside double quotes triggers csh-style history expansion (`event not found`); disable it with `set +H` / `set +o histexpand`, or use single quotes. This affects only interactive shells, not scripts.
condition: in an interactive shell (bash < 4.3)

statement: Iterate positional parameters with `"$@"` (or the bare `for arg`, which defaults to `for arg in "$@"`), not `$*` or unquoted `$@`, which word-split the parameters into the wrong number of words.
Do not combine the `function` keyword with `()` when defining a function; for portability use `foo() { ...; }`.
Tilde expansion happens only when `~` is unquoted; write home-relative paths with `"$HOME/..."` rather than a quoted `~`, especially when the path contains spaces.

Declare and assign a local on separate lines (`local var; var=$(cmd); rc=$?`): combined, `local`'s own exit status masks the command's, and in some shells the right-hand side is not treated as an assignment so it undergoes word splitting. The same applies to `export` and `readonly`.

Tilde expansion after `=` is only guaranteed in a real assignment, and `export`/`local` are not always assignments — so write `foo=~/bar; export foo` or `export foo="$HOME/bar"` rather than `export foo=~/bar`.
Prefer `"${HOME%/}/bar"` over `"$HOME/bar"` to avoid a leading double slash when `$HOME` is `/`, since some systems give a path beginning with `//` a special meaning.
Single quotes prevent parameter expansion, so `$foo` is not expanded inside `sed 's/$foo/.../'`; use double quotes when you need the variable expanded (and escape as needed).

`tr [A-Z] [a-z]` is wrong: the unquoted brackets are shell globs, tr does not use bracket notation (so the brackets are translated literally), and it should be `tr A-Z a-z` or the quoted `tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]'`.
Character ranges like `A-Z`/`a-z` are locale-dependent (in some locales `z` sits mid-alphabet), so force `LC_COLLATE=C` for the 26 ASCII letters or use the `[:upper:]`/`[:lower:]` character classes.
A running process's name is inherently unreliable for identifying it (there may be several, or one spoofing the name), so prefer `pgrep`/`pkill` or `ps -C name -o pid=` over scraping `ps ax | grep`.
`ps ax | grep foo` frequently matches the grep process itself (a race); avoid it with `grep '[f]oo'` (a glob-safe bracket) or `grep -v grep`.
`pgrep`/`pkill name` match by substring and so also hit related names (e.g. `ssh` matches `sshd`); confirm the target before killing.
exception: processes whose names merely contain the search string

statement: Never pass untrusted data as printf's format string (`printf "$foo"`): `\` and `%` in it cause a format-string exploit — always supply your own format, e.g. `printf '%s\n' "$foo"`.
condition: when the value is not strictly under your control

statement: Brace expansion runs before variable expansion, so `{1..$n}` never expands with a runtime variable; use an arithmetic for loop `for ((i=1; i<=n; i++))` instead.
Prefer an arithmetic for loop over brace expansion for integer iteration: brace expansion pre-expands every element, which can be slower and consume memory unnecessarily.

For the `=~` operator, an unquoted right-hand side is a regular expression while a quoted one is a literal string; put a long regex in a variable (`re='...'; [[ $foo =~ $re ]]`) to avoid escaping and cross-version `=~` differences.
`test`/`[ -e ]` follows symlinks, so it returns false for a broken symlink even though the link exists; test both existence and link-ness: `[ -e "$l" ] || [ -L "$l" ]`.
Avoid `expr` for string operations (it also fails when the operand is an expr keyword such as `match`); use parameter expansion instead (`${word#?}`, `${word:1}`), which is in-process and faster.
Do not put a UTF-8 byte-order mark (BOM) in files interpreted by machines (scripts, source, config): a BOM breaks the leading `#!` shebang and any format expecting specific ASCII bytes at the start.
All command-substitution forms (`` `...` ``, `$(...)`, `$(<file)`) strip trailing newlines; to preserve them, append a sentinel inside and strip it outside, e.g. `x=$(cmd; printf x); result=${x%x}`.

When filtering `./*` glob results with a pattern, the `./` prefix is part of the string, so `[[ $file != *.* ]]` misbehaves; strip the directory first (`${path##*/}`) before matching, or include the prefix in the pattern.

Redirections are applied left-to-right before the command runs, so to send both stdout and stderr to a file the order matters: use `cmd >>logfile 2>&1`, not `cmd 2>&1 >>logfile` (which leaves stderr on the tty).

To test only a command's success or failure, test the command directly (`if cmd; then ...`); capture `$?` only when you need the exact status, and save it immediately (`status=$?`) before other commands overwrite it.

An arithmetic context expands the array name and index text (including command substitution) before evaluating it, so an index such as `array[$x]` can execute code even quoted; inside arithmetic use bare variable names (no `$`), validate inputs to numeric literals, and escape any needed expansion.
condition: when the array index or operand is untrusted

statement: POSIX treats IFS as a field terminator, not a separator, so `read` silently drops a trailing empty field (and `read -r f1 rest` drops a single trailing separator); append an extra IFS character to the input and strip it afterward to preserve it.
condition: when the input ends in an empty field or trailing separator

statement: Do not export CDPATH: an inherited CDPATH can send `cd` in any script to an unexpected directory and can leak a resolved path onto stdout when the output is captured (`out=$(cd dir && cmd)`). Setting it unexported in `.bashrc` is fine.

Copying a variable to a temporary (`OIFS=$IFS`) does not preserve the unset-versus-empty distinction; because an empty IFS differs from an unset IFS, scope a temporary IFS with a `local IFS` in a function or a subshell `( IFS=/; ... )` instead.

Do not populate an array with an unquoted command substitution (`arr=( $(cmd) )`): the output is word-split on all whitespace and globbed; use `read -ra arr < <(cmd)` for a single line or `readarray -t arr < <(cmd)` (bash 4.0+) for multiple lines.

With `xargs -P` (parallel), a single write larger than ~8192 bytes, or multiple echo/printf calls per job, is not atomic, so parallel outputs can interleave; use a tool that serializes output (such as GNU Parallel) when the output must stay unmixed.
condition: when jobs run in parallel and output must not interleave

statement: Never interpolate `{}` into the shell code of `find -exec sh -c '... {} ...'` — the filename is parsed as shell code (a code-injection vector); pass it as a positional argument instead: `find . -exec sh -c 'echo "$1"' x {} \;`.
condition: when filenames are untrusted

statement: Redirections and globbing are performed by the invoking user before `sudo` runs the command, so `sudo cmd > /file` and `sudo ls /foo/*` do not use elevated privileges for the redirect or glob; wrap them in `sudo sh -c '...'` (or use `cmd | sudo tee /file`) when they need the privileges.
Do not close stdin/stdout/stderr (`2>&-`) as a shorthand for redirecting to `/dev/null`: a program that writes to a closed descriptor may fail unpredictably. Redirect explicitly with `2>/dev/null`.

`xargs` splits on whitespace and treats quotes specially, so it mangles filenames containing spaces or quotes; feed it NUL-delimited input with `-0` (`find -print0 | xargs -0`, `printf '%s\0'`) or use `find -exec ... +`. Comment any deliberate use of `xargs` without `-0`.

Quote an indexed array element when unsetting it (`unset -v 'a[0]'`): unquoted it may be glob-expanded against the current directory, and the `-v` guards against a bare name being taken as a function.

Call `date` once and extract all fields in a single invocation, because separate calls (`month=$(date +%m); day=$(date +%d)`) can straddle a midnight or month boundary and mix fields; capturing epoch seconds once and deriving fields avoids this.

Forced base-10 conversion `$(( 10#$i ))` only works for signless digits; a possibly-negative value breaks it (noisily or, worse, silently), so strip and reapply the sign for input that might be negative.
condition: when the value may carry a leading + or -

statement: `set -e` (errexit) is unreliable: it can only read exit status (which many commands like `[`/`grep` use as a boolean), it is ignored for commands inside a function invoked in a tested context, and command substitution disables it — so explicitly check critical commands (`cd -- "$1" || return`) regardless of errexit.

With `pipefail` a pipeline fails if any element does, but it is normal for an earlier element to exit non-zero (e.g. SIGPIPE when `grep -q` closes the pipe early), so enable pipefail only for the specific pipelines where it makes sense, not globally.
`set -u` (nounset) is the least harmful of `set -euo pipefail` but still has gotchas; a linter such as shellcheck detects typoed variable names more reliably.

Testing associative-array membership with `[[ -v hash[$key] ]]` is broken (and injectable) before bash 5.2 because `$key` is expanded before subscript evaluation; single-quote the whole argument (`[[ -v 'hash[$key]' ]]`, bash 4.3+) or test a non-empty value with `[[ ${hash[$key]} ]]`.
condition: on bash versions before 5.2

statement: Modifying an associative-array element inside a math context (`(( hash[$key]++ ))`) is unsafe with arbitrary keys across bash versions (single-quoting fails in 5.2+); copy the value to a plain string variable, modify it, and assign back (`tmp=${hash[$key]}; ((tmp++)); hash[$key]=$tmp`).
condition: when keys are arbitrary / not simple identifiers

statement: A portable, readable way to safely modify an associative-array element in an arithmetic calculation is `let 'hash[$key]++'` with the whole expression single-quoted, or a temp-variable round-trip; the `(( ... ))` single-quote trick is not portable across bash 5.2.
condition: when keys may contain quotes/brackets/command-substitution syntax

statement: Prefer process substitution `while ...; done < <(foo)` over the here-string `while ...; done <<< "$(foo)"`: the here-string collects all of foo's output first (no concurrency) and, because of `$(...)`, discards NUL bytes, strips trailing newlines, appends a newline, and stages a temporary file.

Redirections on a simple command may be performed in a subshell (an optimisation), so a side effect inside the redirect target — e.g. `cmd > "file$((i++))"` — may not persist in the main shell (it does not in bash or ksh); compute the target into a variable first, or wrap the command in a `{ ...; }` group to force the redirect in the current shell.
condition: in bash and ksh (dash does update the variable)

statement: `IFS= read -r -d ''` can still read past the delimiter in a multibyte locale on bash 5.0 through 5.2 (a decoding bug on truncated multibyte sequences), so read arbitrary bytes with a single-byte locale: `IFS= LC_ALL=C read -r -d '' var`.
condition: in a multibyte (e.g. UTF-8) locale on bash 5.0-5.2

statement: A bash variable cannot store a NUL byte, so truly binary data containing NULs cannot be read intact with `read`.
Bash splits each command line into words on whitespace; the first word is the command name and the rest become separate arguments.
The amount of whitespace between arguments does not matter; extra spaces are collapsed unless the text is quoted.
exception: when the whitespace is inside quotes it is preserved

statement: Quote any filename or string that contains whitespace or special characters, otherwise Bash word-splits it and passes each word to the command as a separate argument.
condition: the value contains whitespace or special characters

statement: Quotes group everything inside them into a single argument, and Bash removes the quotes before handing the argument to the command.
As a habit, always quote sentences or strings that belong together even when not strictly necessary, to reduce the risk of human error in scripts.
[ is an ordinary command whose final argument must be ]; its operands must be separated from it by whitespace, so [-f file] fails while [ -f file ] works.
In Bash almost everything is a string, and strings have no intrinsic meaning; their meaning is defined only by how and where they are used.
Aliases are only used in interactive shells and not in scripts, and the replacement happens only on the first word of a command.

Prefer a function over an alias when more than a simple textual shortcut is needed, because functions work in scripts, take arguments, and create local variables while aliases only substitute the first word.
condition: more flexibility than a first-word text substitution is required

statement: Builtins are handled directly by the Bash executable and do not create new processes.
Keywords are part of Bash syntax and may be parsed by special rules; [ is a builtin whereas [[ is a keyword.
Inside single-bracket [ ] test, Bash treats < as a file-redirection operator, whereas inside [[ ]] it is parsed as a lexicographic string comparison, so use [[ ]] to compare strings.
condition: comparing strings with < or >

statement: For a command given without a path, Bash searches the colon-separated directories in PATH left to right and runs the first matching executable found.
condition: the name is not an alias, function, builtin, or keyword

statement: To run an executable that is not in PATH you must give its path, e.g. ./myprogram for one in the current directory.
condition: the executable is outside any PATH directory

statement: A script's shebang (#!) must be the very first line of the file with no spaces or blank lines before it, so the kernel can read it to choose the interpreter.
#!/usr/bin/env bash makes env search $PATH for the bash executable, an alternative to hardcoding #!/bin/bash.
sh is not bash: do not use /bin/sh as the interpreter for a bash script, because some Bash features break or behave unexpectedly under sh.
condition: the script relies on Bash-specific features

statement: Do not give bash scripts a .sh extension, because it serves no purpose and is misleading since it is a bash script rather than an sh script.
Bash expects Line-Feed-only line endings; DOS-style Carriage-Return+Line-Feed endings (e.g. from Notepad) cause strange error messages, so remove carriage returns before running such scripts.
condition: the script file has DOS-style CRLF line endings

statement: Running 'bash myscript' treats the #! line as a mere comment, whereas running the script directly (after chmod +x) makes the OS use the #! line to choose the interpreter.
Edits to .bashrc do not take effect immediately; the file must be re-read with source, exec bash, or a new terminal before the changes apply.

Single quotes protect their contents literally so no interpretation occurs, while double quotes prevent word splitting yet still allow substitutions such as parameter expansion and command substitution.
A backslash escapes the next character so it is not interpreted specially; it works outside quotes and inside double quotes but is generally ignored inside single quotes.
Use $( ) for command substitution instead of the deprecated backticks, and $(( )) for arithmetic instead of the deprecated $[ ]; these older forms are retained only for backwards compatibility.
In a variable assignment no whitespace is allowed around the = sign; writing 'var = data' makes the parser treat var as a command name and = and data as its arguments.
A valid variable name (identifier) consists only of letters, digits, and underscores and must begin with a letter or underscore.

Parameter expansion replaces $parameter with the variable's contents and then Bash may perform further manipulation such as word splitting on the result, unlike variable handling in most other languages.
Put double quotes around every parameter expansion; an unquoted expansion like rm $song is subjected to word splitting and can operate on the wrong files.
Parameters themselves do not start with a $ sign; the $ triggers expansion, replacing the parameter that follows it with its content.

Double-quoted "$@" expands to each positional parameter as a separate word, whereas double-quoted "$*" expands to a single string joining all of them with the first character of IFS; prefer "$@" to preserve arguments individually.
condition: iterating over or forwarding the script's or function's positional parameters

statement: $? holds the exit code of the most recently completed foreground command, $# the number of positional parameters, $$ the PID of the current shell, and $! the PID of the most recent background command.
$0 (the script name or path) is not always reliable, and UID is not reliable for security or authentication purposes.
Variable names in Bash are case-sensitive.
A variable marked for export (declare -x) is inherited by any child process and is then called an environment variable, while a read-only variable (declare -r) can no longer be modified or unset.

Prefer explicit arithmetic commands (( ... )) or let over declaring integer variables with declare -i, because the -i behavior can surprise a maintainer who misses the declaration; declare -i is rare in practice.
condition: performing arithmetic on a variable

statement: An ordinary indexed array does not need an explicit declare -a because array=(...) tells Bash the variable is an array, but an associative array must be declared explicitly with declare -A.
exception: associative arrays require explicit declare -A

statement: Arrays store multiple strings together without relying on a delimiter to split them apart, which is tedious to do correctly and error-prone when done wrong.
Use curly braces ${name} to mark the beginning and end of a parameter name when it is immediately followed by characters that would otherwise be read as part of the name, e.g. ${USER}s versus $USERs.
condition: the expansion is directly followed by characters valid in a variable name

statement: ${parameter#pattern} and ${parameter%pattern} delete the shortest match from the beginning or end respectively, and doubling the character (## or %%) deletes the longest (greedy) match instead.

${parameter:-word} substitutes a default value when the parameter is unset or null, ${parameter:=word} also assigns that default to the parameter, and ${parameter:+word} substitutes an alternate value only when the parameter is set.
You cannot combine multiple parameter expansions in one expression; apply them in separate statements when several transformations are needed on one parameter.
condition: more than one PE transformation is required on a parameter

statement: Prefer parameter expansion over external tools such as sed, awk, cut, or perl for string manipulation, because each external tool starts an extra process which can cause slowdowns.
condition: the string operation can be expressed as a parameter expansion

statement: Globs are implicitly anchored at both ends, so a glob must match the whole string; a* will not match 'cat' but ca* will.
When a glob matches filenames, * and ? cannot match a slash (/); when a glob is used to match arbitrary strings (patterns) that slash restriction is removed.
Filename expansion happens after word splitting, so filenames generated by a glob are never subject to word splitting and are always handled correctly even when they contain spaces.

Always use globs instead of ls (or parsing ls output) to enumerate files, because a glob expands each filename as a single safe argument whereas iterating over ls output word-splits filenames that contain spaces.
condition: enumerating files programmatically

statement: Extended globs (?(list), *(list), +(list), @(list), !(list)) are turned off by default and must be enabled with shopt -s extglob.
condition: extended-glob syntax is used

statement: The =~ regex operator is available only inside [[ ]] since Bash 3.0; it returns exit code 0 when the string matches the ERE pattern, 1 when it does not, and 2 when the pattern syntax is invalid.
Since Bash 3.2 do not quote the regex on the right side of =~; store the regex in a variable and expand it unquoted in [[ ]] (escaping special characters) so it works across all 3.x Bash versions.
condition: using the =~ regex match operator

statement: A regex with capturing groups (parentheses) assigns its captured substrings to the BASH_REMATCH array for later retrieval.
Brace expansion expands to every permutation of its contents (which need not be filenames), produces an unsorted list, happens before filename expansion, and cannot be used for pattern matching.

Character ranges in brace expansion always use ASCII ordering and ignore locale variables like LANG and LC_COLLATE and can count backward (e.g. {5..1}, {b..Y}), whereas globbing character ranges are affected by locale settings.
Every command terminates with an integer exit code between 0 and 255; by convention 0 denotes success and any non-zero value denotes some failure, with the specific number being application-specific.
Make your scripts return a non-zero exit code whenever something unexpected happens, for example using 'rm file || { echo error >&2; exit 1; }'.
The control operator && runs the next command only if the first succeeded (exit code 0), and || runs the next command only if the first failed (non-zero exit).
Avoid stringing together multiple different control operators in one command; they are useful for simple error checks but make complex logic hard to understand and hard to maintain.
condition: the logic is more than a simple two-command success/failure check

statement: A cmd1 && cmd2 || cmd3 chain is not a safe if/then/else, because the exit status carries through skipped commands left to right, so a failure early in the chain can trigger the trailing || even though its associated command never ran; group the commands that belong together with { ...; } instead.
condition: mixing && and || in a single command line where later commands must belong together

statement: Curly-brace grouping { ...; } makes the enclosed commands act as a single statement, and a semicolon or newline is required before the closing brace.

Command grouping lets you redirect input or output to a whole group of statements at once; the redirected file is opened when the group starts, stays open for its duration, and is closed when the group finishes.
A leading ! negates a command's exit status: a success becomes a failure and a failure becomes a success.
A common safe error-handling idiom is 'cd "$dir" || { echo "error" >&2; exit 1; }', which reports to standard error and exits when the guarded command fails.
The if keyword runs a command and branches on its exit code, executing the then block on success and the else block on failure; no separate test command is required.

Inside single-bracket [ ] test an unquoted parameter expansion that contains whitespace or is empty splits into extra arguments and causes errors like 'too many arguments', so always quote parameter expansions used with [ ].
condition: using [ ] (test) with a parameter expansion

statement: [[ is a shell keyword that parses its arguments before Bash expands them and does not word-split the expansions, so parameter expansions inside [[ ]] need not be quoted to prevent splitting; however literal strings that contain spaces still must be quoted.
exception: literal whitespace outside quotes is still treated as an argument separator

statement: Inside [[ ]] the = and == operators perform glob pattern matching when the right-hand side is unquoted, but literal string comparison when the right-hand side is quoted.
condition: using = or == inside [[ ]]

statement: Inside single-bracket [ ] the < and > characters are still interpreted as redirection operators, so [ apple < banana ] tries to read a file named banana; escape them (\<) or use [[ ]] for string ordering comparisons.
condition: comparing string order with [ ]

statement: The operators =, !=, <, and > treat their operands as strings, so to compare operands as numbers you must use -eq, -ne, -lt, -gt, -le, or -ge; for example [ 314 < 9 ] is true lexicographically while [ 314 -lt 9 ] is false numerically.
condition: comparing values that should be treated as numbers

statement: File test operators for [ and [[ include -e (exists), -f (regular file), -d (directory), -h (symlink), -r/-w/-x (readable/writable/executable by you), -s (exists and non-empty), plus -z (empty string) and -n (non-empty string), and FILE -nt/-ot FILE compares modification times.

Always use [[ rather than [ in a Bash script, and use [ only when writing a portable POSIX shell script that may run where Bash is unavailable, since [ is far more portable and also exists as an external command usable with find -exec and xargs.
condition: the script targets Bash specifically
exception: prefer [ when portability to non-Bash shells is required

statement: Never use the -a or -o operators of the [ command; use multiple separate [ commands joined by && / || (or use [[), because POSIX does not define the behavior of [ with complex sets of tests.
condition: combining several conditions with the [ command

statement: Make quoting a habit because it usually gives the behavior you want; quoting bugs are hard to find since code is often valid both with and without quotes but means different things, and Bash cannot detect the mistake.
exception: omit quotes only when the specific situation requires unquoted behavior

statement: while repeats its body as long as its command succeeds, until repeats as long as its command fails, for..in iterates a variable over each word in a list, and C-style for (( init; test; update )) evaluates arithmetic expressions.

Choose the for..in loop when you have a known list of things to iterate over, and choose the while loop when you do not know in advance how many repetitions are needed; picking the right loop keeps scripts readable and maintainable.

In 'for i in WORDS', Bash splits the words between 'in' and the end of the line on spaces and tabs, and any unquoted substitutions there are further word-split using IFS, with each resulting word becoming one iteration element.

Never loop over the output of ls (for file in $(ls *.mp3)): unquoted, the output is word-split and breaks on filenames containing spaces, and quoting it protects all the whitespace as one string; loop over a glob (for file in *.mp3) instead so Bash splits real filenames correctly.
condition: iterating over a set of files in a loop

statement: The continue builtin skips to the next iteration of a loop without running the rest of the body, and the break builtin exits the loop entirely; both work in for and while loops.
The until loop is rarely used because it is essentially equivalent to 'while !'; most people simply write 'while !' instead.

A case statement matches a parameter against an enumerated list of glob patterns, runs the block of the first pattern that matches, and stops matching; a final *) pattern therefore catches anything not matched earlier.
In a case statement ;; ends a block, ;& falls through and unconditionally runs the next choice's block, and ;;& continues testing and runs the next matching choice.

The select construct generates a numbered menu, sets a variable to the user's chosen word (empty if the choice was invalid), repeats until a break is executed, and uses the PS3 variable as its prompt.
Use select for a simple menu, but for anything more elaborate write your own menu with a while loop plus echo/printf and read, because select offers little flexibility.
condition: the menu needs more than a basic fixed list of choices

statement: A subshell (commands wrapped in parentheses) runs like a temporary child shell: cd and variable changes made inside it do not persist after it ends, and each command in a pipeline runs in an implicit subshell.
An exit inside a subshell terminates only the subshell and not the parent or interactive shell, which is useful in patterns like (cd dir || exit 1; ...).

A curly-brace command group runs in the same shell as everything else, unlike a subshell, so it is faster and its variable assignments remain visible afterward; use a command group rather than a subshell when you need exit to terminate the whole script.
condition: you need the grouped commands' side effects (variables, exit) to affect the current shell

statement: Redirections applied to a command group apply to every command within it, and the redirected file is opened once and stays open until the whole group completes rather than being reopened for each command.

The ((...)) arithmetic evaluation can be used as a test command: it exits with status 0 when the expression is true or non-zero and status 1 when the expression is false or zero, which is the reverse of the usual convention and a common source of confusion.
$((...)) is arithmetic substitution that expands to the numeric result and is portable to the POSIX shell, whereas the ((...)) compound command is not portable to POSIX sh.

Inside an arithmetic context (( )) or $(( )) you do arithmetic rather than string operations, can reference variables without a $ prefix, and can use C-like features such as the ternary operator and treating a non-zero integer as true.
A function is a named block of commands that runs in the same process (creating no new process), takes its own positional arguments $1, $2, ..., and can modify variables in the calling script.
A function's positional parameters are separate from the script's positional parameters, so to give a function the script's arguments you must pass them explicitly, e.g. func "$1" "$2".
condition: a function is embedded in a script and should act on the script's arguments

statement: Use functions to isolate a task so it does not clutter other code and to reuse a block of code with different arguments, but only in moderation, since scattering many functions that must be tracked down hurts readability.
exception: too many scattered functions reduce readability

statement: Declare a function's internal variables with local (or declare) so the function can do work without overwriting variables of the same name in the caller's namespace.
condition: a function uses temporary variables that might collide with the caller's

statement: A for loop written as 'for var' with no 'in' list is equivalent to 'for var in "$@"' and iterates over all of the positional parameters.

Aliases do not work in scripts (interactive shells only), cannot take arguments, cannot recurse, cannot have local variables, and are only first-word text replacements; use a function whenever more complex behavior is needed.
Inside a wrapper function named the same as a command, use the command builtin to call the real command (e.g. ls() { command ls --color=auto "$@"; }) to prevent infinite recursion.
condition: a function shadows a command of the same name

statement: Remove a function or variable with unset, being explicit with -f (function) or -v (variable) because variables take precedence over functions when unspecified; remove an alias with unalias.
Quote the argument when unsetting an array element (unset -v 'myArray[2]') to prevent the subscript from being interpreted as a glob.
condition: unsetting a specific array element

statement: A string holds exactly one element; capturing command output into a string yields a single string no matter how many items it represents, and there is no reliable delimiter to split it back because any separator character could itself appear inside a filename.

The only safe way to hold multiple string elements in Bash is an array, which maps integers to strings so each element can safely contain any character including whitespace; whenever you have a list of things, keep it in an array.
condition: you need to store or process more than one string value

statement: Never build a file list with files=$(ls) or files=($(ls)): the first is an unsplittable string and the second still splits filenames on whitespace; use a glob such as files=(*) so each filename becomes a separate array element.
condition: collecting filenames into an array

statement: Create an array with arr=(...), optionally giving explicit indexes; Bash permits sparse arrays that have gaps in their indices.

When globbing filenames into an array, quote only the literal parts that contain spaces (e.g. (~/"My Photos"/*.jpg)); do not quote ~ or *, because quoting them makes them literal and Bash stops treating them as special.
condition: a glob path contains a directory name with spaces

statement: Split a string into an array on a delimiter with IFS=<delim> read -ra arr <<< "$string" (for example IFS=. to split an IP address into its octets).
condition: splitting a known in-memory string on a single-character delimiter

statement: Do not delimit filenames by newline when parsing a command's output because filenames can contain newlines; use the NUL byte instead (e.g. find -print0 read into a loop with read -r -d ''), since filenames cannot contain a NUL byte.
condition: parsing a stream of filenames from an external command into elements

statement: Append one or more elements to the end of an array with the arr+=(...) syntax.
Keep a list of things in array (list) form for as long as possible and do not flatten it into a single string or file until you absolutely must, to avoid the delimiter problem.

"${array[@]}" expands to a list of words with each array element preserved as exactly one word regardless of its content (spaces, tabs, newlines, quotes), just like "$@"; always quote it, or unquoted expansion word-splits the elements and loses the benefit of using an array.
condition: expanding all elements of an array

statement: declare -p prints one or more variables' contents plus Bash's inferred type, formatted as code you could paste into a script.

printf implicitly loops over all its arguments, so printf '%s\n' "${arr[@]}" prints each element on its own line, and printf '%s\0' "${arr[@]}" can produce a NUL-delimited stream for safe later retrieval.
Bash arrays are zero-based by default, so the first element has index 0, and a single element is referenced with ${arr[index]}.

"${array[*]}" joins all elements into a single string and is only useful for producing such a string (e.g. human-readable output); it too must be quoted or word-splitting cuts it apart, and it loses the boundaries between elements.
condition: you deliberately want one joined string rather than separate elements

statement: "${array[*]}" joins elements using only the first character of IFS, so joining with a multi-character separator such as comma-plus-space requires a different technique like a for loop.

When temporarily changing IFS to join an array via "${array[*]}", do it inside a subshell (IFS=,; ...) so the main shell's IFS is not permanently altered, because IFS is used for many things and a non-default value causes surprising behavior elsewhere.
condition: changing IFS for a join operation

statement: Get the number of elements in an array with ${#array[@]}.

"${!array[@]}" expands to the array's indices in order; loop over the indices rather than the values when you must use the same index across parallel arrays or when the index values themselves matter.
condition: matching elements across parallel arrays or when indices carry meaning

statement: The [...] subscript of an indexed array is an arithmetic context, so you can perform arithmetic directly inside it (e.g. ${a[i+1]}) without wrapping it in $((...)).

Sparse arrays with gaps in their indices arise from assigning past the current end or from unsetting an element; do not assume indices are sequential or that the first loop iteration is index 0, and iterate over the indices whenever the index values matter.
condition: an array may be sparse

statement: Re-index a sparse array to remove all gaps by reassigning it to its own quoted @-expansion: array=("${array[@]}").
condition: you need contiguous indices from a sparse array

statement: Associative arrays (declare -A, Bash 4 and later) map arbitrary string keys to string values, removing any need for variable indirection or eval to translate one string to another.
condition: you need to map arbitrary string keys to values

statement: The order of keys or values returned from an associative array via "${!arr[@]}" or "${arr[@]}" is unpredictable (neither insertion nor sorted order), so associative arrays are not suited to lists that must be processed in a specific order.

You cannot omit the $ on a parameter used as an associative-array key (use ${assoc[$key]}), unlike an indexed array whose subscript is an arithmetic context where a bare Name is taken as a variable's value.
condition: using a variable as an associative-array key

statement: The positional parameters are the shell's simple numerically indexed string array (in POSIX sh the only array), referred to as $1, $2, and so on, and beyond $9 you must use braces such as ${10}, ${11}.

The shift builtin discards $1 and renumbers each remaining positional parameter down by one; a common option-processing pattern loops on $1 while it begins with a dash, shifting each away, then treats whatever remains in "$@" as filenames.
condition: processing command-line options

statement: Passing filenames to a program as command-line arguments is an excellent approach because each filename is encapsulated as a single word, ready to use without further splitting.
condition: you control how data flows into the script

statement: Environment variables behave like ordinary shell variables except that they are already set when the script starts, inherited from the process that started it.

Do not use all-capital variable names in your scripts unless they are environment variables; use lower-case or mixed-case names so you never accidentally collide with environment variables or Bash's special variables, which are all capitalized.
condition: naming your own script variables
exception: all-caps is appropriate for actual environment variables

statement: Prefix a command with VAR=value to apply a temporary environment change that affects only that single command, for example LANG=C ls.

Use export to place a variable into the environment for child processes; environment changes are inherited only by descendants, so you cannot change the environment of an already-running process or one you did not start.

Every new process starts with three open file descriptors: standard input (FD 0), standard output (FD 1), and standard error (FD 2); error messages go to stderr by convention so they stay separate from normal output.
Send your script's error messages to standard error with >&2 (e.g. echo "..." >&2), following the convention so that downstream tools can separate errors from the program's normal output.
condition: your script emits an error or diagnostic message

statement: Redirection changes the source or destination of a program's file descriptors, and the shell performs the redirections before it runs the command they apply to.

The > operator redirects a command's stdout to a file, applies only to that one command, is performed before the command runs, and by default truncates an existing file (destroying its contents) or creates it if it does not exist.
The < operator redirects a command's stdin so it reads from a file instead of from the keyboard.
A redirection operator may be preceded by an FD number to choose which descriptor is changed; > defaults to FD 1 (stdout) and < to FD 0 (stdin), and 2> redirects stderr.

Do not use cat to feed a single file to a command inside a script; use a redirection (< file) instead, because a useless use of cat spawns an extra process and piping instead of redirecting removes the command's ability to seek within its input file.
condition: a command can read the file directly via stdin redirection

statement: A redirection placed on a compound command such as a loop's done applies to the whole construct: Bash opens the file before the loop, every command inside inherits the open FD, and the file is closed when the loop ends.
Silence a file descriptor by redirecting it to /dev/null (the bit bucket), a virtual device that discards everything written to it and is always empty.
condition: you want to discard a command's output

statement: The >> operator appends to a file instead of truncating it, unlike > which empties the file first.

Design an application to read from stdin so users can feed it data from any source via redirection; a program that reads standard input in a generalized way is called a filter and is more flexible than one hardcoded to open a file.
condition: the application could receive data from a variety of sources

statement: Never point two independent redirections at the same file (e.g. >file 2>file), because they open two independent FDs to that file whose writes clobber each other with results that are not well-defined.
condition: sending more than one FD to the same destination file

statement: To send both stdout and stderr to one file, first redirect stdout to the file and then duplicate it into stderr with >file 2>&1; a duplicated FD shares the same file position so the two streams do not clobber each other.
condition: combining stdout and stderr into a single file

statement: Read file redirections left to right in the order Bash processes them: 2>&1 >file duplicates the current stdout (still the terminal) into stderr and only then points stdout at the file, so error messages still go to the terminal; the order of 2>&1 relative to >file is significant.
condition: combining a duplication (2>&1) with a file redirection

statement: The &>file operator is a Bash shorthand for >file 2>&1 that redirects both stdout and stderr, but it is not portable to the Bourne shell and is not recommended, though you should recognize it in others' scripts.
A heredoc (<<WORD ... WORD) feeds the enclosed lines to the command as stdin, and the closing sentinel word must appear on a line by itself at the start of the line.
Bash performs parameter and other substitutions on a heredoc's contents by default; quote the delimiter word (<<'WORD') to suppress all substitution and pass the content literally.
condition: the heredoc content should be treated literally

statement: Use the <<-WORD heredoc operator to strip leading tab characters (but not spaces) from each content line, so heredoc content can be indented with tabs to match the surrounding code without those tabs reaching the command.
condition: you want to indent heredoc content along with the code

statement: Avoid long heredocs: scripts should contain logic, not data, so ship a large document in a separate file alongside the script rather than embedding it.
condition: the embedded data set is large
exception: a small data set embedded inline is acceptable

statement: Prefer a herestring (<<<"string") over echo "string" | cmd for sending variable content to a filter such as grep or sed, because a herestring creates no subshell and is lighter on both the shell and the script's style.
condition: feeding the contents of a variable or short string to a command's stdin
exception: herestrings are not portable to the Bourne shell

statement: The pipe operator | connects the stdout of one command to the stdin of the next, and the whole set of piped commands is called a pipeline.

Each command in a pipeline runs in its own subshell, so variables assigned inside a piped command are lost when the pipeline ends; for example 'echo x | read var' leaves var unchanged in the parent shell.
condition: a piped command sets or modifies a variable you need afterward

statement: Do not over-use pipes: a pipeline of three or more commands is a sign you should instead use a feature of one of the tools already in the pipe, because each extra stage spawns another subshell and process and makes the script's logic harder to follow.
condition: a pipeline grows to three or more commands

statement: A FIFO (named pipe, created with mkfifo) never stores data: a read blocks until another process writes, and a write blocks until another process reads.

Process substitution <(cmd) runs cmd and substitutes a temporary filename (a bash-created FIFO such as /dev/fd/63) that yields the command's output, letting you pass a command's output where a command expects a filename (e.g. diff <(sort a) <(sort b)), with the temporary file cleaned up automatically.
condition: a command needs a filename argument but you want to supply another command's output

statement: Running a script as a child process cannot change your current shell's working directory or variables, because the child's environment is discarded when it finishes.

Source a script with the . (dot) command (. ./script) to run its commands in the current shell so they can change the current shell's variables, working directory, file descriptors, and functions; the . command is more portable than its source alias.
condition: a script must alter the calling shell's state

statement: On POSIX systems jobs are process groups; each terminal has a single foreground process group allowed to interact with the terminal, and all other process groups sharing that terminal are background jobs that may be running or suspended.

A background job that tries to read from or write to the terminal is automatically suspended by SIGTTIN or SIGTTOU, which is why a command like 'cat &' is immediately suspended rather than running in the background.
At the terminal, Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP to suspend the foreground job, Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to terminate it, and Ctrl-\ sends SIGQUIT to make it dump core and abort.
Job control is on by default in interactive shells and is not typically used in scripts, but it can be enabled in a script with set -m (set -o monitor).

fg brings a background or suspended job to the foreground, bg resumes a suspended job in the background, jobs lists background and suspended jobs, and disown makes bash forget a job so it will not send it SIGHUP (but the job can then no longer be referenced by jobspec).

Before writing a script, enumerate its requirements and goal and pick the best tool; Bash is not always the best choice, since awk, perl, or ruby suit complex text processing and XPath/XSLT suit reliable HTML/XML extraction.
Limit a script to POSIX sh syntax only if it may need to run where Bash is not available by default; otherwise use the Bash features you require and record the minimum Bash version the script needs.
condition: the script may run in an environment without Bash

statement: Bash feature availability varies across operating systems: macOS ships Bash 3.2 permanently because of GPL 2.0, and long-lifespan systems keep an old Bash for years, so account for the target's Bash version rather than assuming the latest.
condition: the script must support multiple operating systems

statement: Use the correct shebang: write #!/usr/bin/env bash for a Bash script; omitting the shebang or using #!/bin/sh is incorrect because sh restricts the script to POSIX shell features even when /bin/sh is really a symlink to Bash.
condition: the script uses Bash-specific features

statement: First and foremost, use more quotes: quoting strings and parameter expansions protects them from word splitting and globbing, which otherwise cause major problems on unquoted expansions.

Word splitting applies only to expansions (parameter expansion, arithmetic expansion, and command substitution) and splits on the characters of $IFS (space, tab, newline by default) rather than on arbitrary whitespace, and unquoted expansions are additionally subject to globbing; because it is hidden it is easy to overlook.

In the shell, quotes do not create string literals as in other languages; they remove the special syntactic meaning of characters such as space, semicolon, newline, &, |, <, and > so those characters are treated as ordinary parts of a string.

Use built-in parameter expansion and POSIX arithmetic for simple operations instead of external tools: prefer ${filename%.*} over piping to sed or cut, and x=$((x + 1)) over x=`expr $x + 1`, which is faster and portable.
condition: the string or arithmetic operation is simple enough for a builtin

statement: In the rare case you deliberately need word splitting, set IFS explicitly to the value you want and add set -o noglob to prevent globbing before the unquoted expansion; but for nearly all such cases use an array instead, since arrays separate strings without a delimiter and so each element can contain any non-NUL character.
condition: you intentionally rely on word splitting of an unquoted expansion

statement: Treat code readability as almost as important as correctness: indent consistently, separate logic blocks with blank lines, avoid overusing backslash-escaping (quotes read more clearly), comment your reasoning, and be consistent in naming, capitalization, and feature use, because you will maintain the script later.

With [ ], an empty unquoted variable disappears before test sees it, so [ $var = '' ] on an empty $var expands to [ = '' ] and errors with 'unary operator expected'; quoting it ([ "$var" = '' ]) fixes it, and [[ ]] sees the variable before expansion so it is safer and needs no quotes there.
condition: testing a variable that may be empty with [ ]

statement: Inside [ ] the > operator triggers output redirection and silently creates a file, so [ "$var" > b ] gives a wrong result with no error message and can overwrite an important file; [[ ]] treats > as a comparison operator, so trust [[ ]] more than [.
condition: comparing string order inside a test

statement: Because [[ ]] and (( )) evaluate arbitrary arithmetic expressions, using them with an arithmetic operator on untrusted data (e.g. [[ $external_data -gt 0 ]]) introduces an arbitrary-command-execution vulnerability; use [ "$external_data" -gt 0 ] for untrusted numeric input, whose worst case is only a syntax error.
condition: performing a numeric comparison on externally-supplied or untrusted data

statement: test's arithmetic operators (-eq, -ne, -lt, -gt, -le, -ge) accept only decimal integer literals, which makes them safer for arbitrary values, whereas [[ ]] and (( )) evaluate full arithmetic expressions and can misinterpret numbers with leading zeros as octal.

A common [[ ]] pitfall is forgetting the quotes in [[ $a = "$b" ]] when an equality comparison is intended, because an unquoted right-hand side is treated as a glob pattern instead; quote the right-hand side to force literal string comparison.
condition: you intend an equality comparison rather than pattern matching in [[ ]]

statement: Never parse the output of ls in scripts: ls mangles filenames with characters unsupported by the locale (replacing them with ?), filenames can themselves contain newlines that break line-based parsing, and the ls -l output format is not consistent across platforms; use globs and Bash file tests instead, or switch to a language like python or perl.
condition: programmatically obtaining or processing filenames
exception: using ls only to display output to a human user is acceptable

statement: Never test or filter filenames with grep, because a substring pattern such as matching '.txt' also matches 'story.txt.exe', and a pattern precise enough becomes too ugly and unreadable to trust; use globbing (pathname expansion) or a glob test in case or [[ ]] instead.
condition: matching or filtering filenames by name

statement: Do not use a for loop to read the lines of a file (for line in $(<file)); use a 'while read' loop instead, since a for loop word-splits and globs the content.
condition: reading a file line by line

statement: Do not use the external seq command to count; let Bash count with a C-style for loop for ((i=1; i<=10; i++)) or a brace expansion like {1..10}, since spawning an external, single-platform tool just to feed numbers back through word splitting is wasteful.
condition: generating a numeric counter or sequence

statement: When debugging, first diagnose the problem: understand exactly what goes wrong from the symptoms and error messages and state the problem as a clear sentence, which is also required before asking others for help.

Minimize the codebase to isolate a bug: copy the script and delete everything irrelevant (keeping only the suspect logic) until removing something makes the problem vanish, which pinpoints the cause and leaves a small 3-7 line stub that is far easier to reason about.
condition: the source of a bug is not obvious from reading the code

statement: Turn on Bash's trace mode (set -x, or bash -x) to print every command to stderr after all expansions have been applied but before it runs; watch the quoting Bash shows, because it reveals exactly which strings are passed as a single argument and thus exposes word-splitting problems.
condition: you need to see how a script actually executes

statement: Scope trace output to a region by bracketing it with set -x and set +x, and separate the trace from normal output by writing it to a chosen descriptor via BASH_XTRACEFD (bash 4.1+) or by sending stderr to a file with exec 2>>logfile.
condition: you want trace output only for part of a script or kept out of normal output

statement: Set PS4 (e.g. PS4='+$BASH_SOURCE:$LINENO:$FUNCNAME: ') before set -x to annotate trace lines with source file, line, and function; use single quotes so the value is expanded when the prompt is displayed rather than at assignment time.
condition: tracing across multiple scripts or functions

statement: Step through a script interactively by installing a DEBUG trap (trap 'debug_prompt' DEBUG) that reports $BASH_COMMAND and waits for confirmation before each command runs.
condition: you want to walk through commands one at a time

statement: When a script misbehaves, reread the manual or guide to re-check that commands and syntax actually do what you think, because people commonly misunderstand how for works, how word splitting works, and how often to quote.

When a script fails unexpectedly, first verify its header really is #!/bin/bash (not missing or #!/bin/sh) and that its lines have no carriage-return characters from Windows editors, which can be stripped with tr -d '\r' < myscript > tmp && mv tmp myscript.
condition: diagnosing why a script does not run as expected

statement: Bash aims to be a conformant implementation of the POSIX 1003.1 Shell and Utilities standard and is largely compatible with sh, so POSIX-conformant sh scripts generally run under Bash.
A '#' begins a comment: the shell ignores the '#' and the remainder of that line.
Bash has four quoting mechanisms - the escape character (backslash), single quotes, double quotes, and dollar-single ANSI-C quotes - and quoting removes the special meaning of characters or words.
An unquoted backslash preserves the literal value of the character that follows it, except that an unquoted backslash-newline pair is treated as a line continuation and removed from the input.
exception: the following character is a newline (line continuation)

statement: Single quotes preserve the literal value of every enclosed character, and a single quote cannot appear inside single quotes even when preceded by a backslash.

Inside double quotes the literal value of characters is preserved except for '$', backquote, backslash, and (when history expansion is on) '!'; '$' and backquote keep their special meaning, so parameter and command expansion still occur within double quotes.
When the shell is in POSIX mode, '!' has no special meaning inside double quotes even if history expansion is enabled.
condition: the shell is in POSIX mode

statement: Within double quotes a backslash keeps its special meaning only before '$', backquote, double-quote, backslash, or newline (and is removed in those cases); before any other character it is left unchanged.

A dollar-single-quoted string of the form $'...' expands backslash escape sequences per the ANSI C standard (such as backslash-n, backslash-t, backslash-xHH, backslash-uHHHH) and the expanded result is treated as single-quoted.

A $"..." string is translated according to the current locale via gettext; if the locale is C or POSIX, or no translation exists, the leading '$' is ignored and the string is treated as an ordinary double-quoted string.
condition: a matching translation and non-C/POSIX locale are available

statement: The special parameters '*' and '@' have special meaning when they appear inside double quotes.
A command's exit status is restricted to eight bits, so its maximum value is 255.
The return status of a simple command is its waitpid exit status, or 128+n when the command was terminated by signal n.
Unquoted metacharacters - space, tab, newline, and the characters | & ; ( ) < > - separate words, so any of them must be quoted to represent itself literally.
In a pipeline each command's standard output is connected through a pipe to the next command's standard input.
The '|&' pipeline operator connects both the standard output and standard error of the left-hand command to the next command's input, and is shorthand for '2>&1 |'.
By default a pipeline's exit status is the exit status of its last (rightmost) command.
exception: the pipefail option is enabled

statement: When the pipefail option is enabled, a pipeline's exit status is the value of the rightmost command that exited non-zero, or zero when every command succeeded.
condition: the pipefail option is enabled

statement: Prefixing a pipeline with the reserved word '!' negates (logically inverts) its exit status.

Each command in a multi-command pipeline runs in its own subshell (a separate process), unless the lastpipe option is enabled and job control is inactive, in which case the last pipeline element runs in the current shell process.
exception: lastpipe is enabled and job control is inactive (last element runs in the current shell)

statement: The reserved word 'time' before a pipeline prints its elapsed, user, and system time and can time shell builtins, functions, and pipelines that an external time command cannot; the TIMEFORMAT variable controls the output format.
In a list, '&&' and '||' have equal precedence, which is higher than that of ';' and '&' (which are equal to each other).
'command1 && command2' runs command2 only if command1 exits zero, and 'command1 || command2' runs command2 only if command1 exits non-zero.
Terminating a command with '&' runs it asynchronously in a background subshell; the shell does not wait for it and the command's return status is 0.
When job control is not active, an asynchronous command's standard input is redirected from /dev/null unless an explicit redirection is supplied.
condition: job control is not active
exception: an explicit input redirection is given

statement: Redirections attached to a compound command apply to every command inside it unless explicitly overridden.
An 'until' loop executes its body while the test commands return a non-zero status; a 'while' loop executes its body while the test commands return zero.
In a 'for name in words' loop, name is bound to each word in turn; if the 'in words' clause is omitted, the loop iterates over the positional parameters as if 'in "$@"' had been specified.
In the C-style 'for (( expr1; expr2; expr3 ))' loop, any omitted arithmetic expression behaves as if it evaluates to 1.

Reserved words are recognized only when unquoted and used as the first word of a command, except that 'in' is reserved as the third word of case/select and 'in' and 'do' are reserved as the third word of for.
Builtins such as cd, break, continue, and exec cannot be implemented as external programs because they directly manipulate the shell process itself.

An 'if' runs its test-commands and, on zero status, runs the consequent; otherwise each 'elif' test is tried in turn, and the 'else' clause runs only when the last tested condition returned non-zero; the return status is that of the last command executed, or zero if no condition tested true.
A 'case' executes the command-list of the first pattern that matches the word, scanning patterns from first to last.
When the nocasematch shell option is enabled, both 'case' matching and '[[ ==' / '!=' pattern matching ignore the case of alphabetic characters.
condition: nocasematch is enabled

statement: In 'case', the word and each pattern undergo tilde expansion, parameter expansion, command substitution, arithmetic expansion, process substitution, and quote removal before matching is attempted.

A 'case' clause ending in ';;' stops after the first match, ';&' falls through and runs the next clause's command-list unconditionally, and ';;&' re-tests the next clause's patterns and runs its command-list on a match.
A 'case' returns zero when no pattern matches; otherwise it returns the exit status of the last command-list executed.
Using '*' as the final 'case' pattern defines a default clause because that pattern always matches.

'select' prints a numbered menu of the expanded words to standard error, shows the PS3 prompt, reads a line into REPLY, sets name to the chosen word (null for a non-numeric line, re-displaying the menu on an empty line), returns 1 on EOF, and loops until 'break'.
The '(( expression ))' command evaluates the arithmetic expression and returns status 0 when the value is non-zero and status 1 when the value is zero, treating an empty expression as 0.
exception: an empty expression is treated as evaluating to 0

statement: Words between '[[' and ']]' do not undergo word splitting or filename expansion, though they still undergo tilde, parameter, arithmetic, command-substitution, process-substitution, and quote-removal expansions.
Conditional operators such as '-f' inside '[[ ]]' must be unquoted to be recognized as primaries.
Inside '[[ ]]', the '<' and '>' operators compare strings lexicographically using the current locale.
