With the '[[' '==' or '!=' operator (and '=' is identical to '=='), the right-hand string is treated as a pattern matched as if extglob were enabled; quoting any part of that pattern forces the quoted part to be matched literally.
With the '[[' '=~' operator the right-hand string is a POSIX extended regular expression; the match returns 0 on success, 1 on failure, and 2 if the regular expression is syntactically invalid.

Storing a '=~' regular expression in a shell variable and referencing it unquoted (for example '[[ $line =~ $pattern ]]') avoids shell-quoting problems, because quoting any part of the pattern forces it to be matched literally.
A '=~' match succeeds if the pattern matches any part of the string; anchor the pattern with '^' and '$' to require it to match the entire string.
Regular-expression anchors '^' and '$' in a '=~' pattern must not be quoted, because any shell quoting removes their special regular-expression meaning.
After a '=~' match, BASH_REMATCH index 0 holds the substring matching the whole regular expression and index n holds the substring matching the nth parenthesized subexpression.
BASH_REMATCH is set in the global scope, so declaring it as a local variable leads to unexpected results.
Inside '[[ ]]', the '&&' and '||' operators do not evaluate their second expression when the first already determines the result.
A '( list )' group runs the commands in a subshell, so variable assignments made inside it do not survive after the subshell completes.

A '{ list; }' group runs the commands in the current shell with no subshell; the braces are reserved words that must be separated from the list by whitespace, and the list must be terminated by a semicolon, '&', or newline before the closing brace.
The recommended coprocess form is 'coproc NAME { command; }', because a simple-command coprocess is always named COPROC.

A coprocess creates an array variable NAME where NAME[0] is the file descriptor reading the coprocess's standard output and NAME[1] is the descriptor writing its standard input, exposes its process id as NAME_PID, and can be waited on with the 'wait' builtin.
Shell functions execute in the current shell context with no new process created, in contrast to running a separate shell script.
A function is defined as 'fname () compound-command' or 'function fname [()] compound-command'; in POSIX mode fname must be a valid shell name and must not be one of the special builtins.

A function definition's exit status is zero unless a syntax error occurs or a readonly function of the same name already exists; when the function runs, its exit status is that of the last command executed in its body.
While a function executes, its arguments become the positional parameters and '$#' is updated to match, special parameter '$0' is unchanged, and FUNCNAME[0] holds the function name.
A function does not inherit the DEBUG and RETURN traps unless it has the trace attribute or 'set -o functrace' is enabled, and does not inherit the ERR trap unless 'set -o errtrace' is enabled.
condition: the function has the trace attribute, or functrace/errtrace is set

statement: Setting FUNCNEST to a numeric value greater than zero caps function nesting depth and aborts the entire command when exceeded; by default Bash imposes no limit on recursive function calls.
condition: FUNCNEST is set greater than 0

statement: The 'return' builtin ends the current function; a numeric argument sets its return status, otherwise the status is that of the last command before 'return'; the RETURN trap runs before execution resumes, and the positional parameters and '$#' are restored.
Variables declared with 'local' inside a function are visible only to that function and the commands it invokes, whereas ordinary variables are shared between a function and its caller.

Bash uses dynamic scoping for functions: a variable declared local in one function is also visible to (and shadows globals for) any function it calls, and the shadowed value is restored when the declaring function returns.

The 'unset' builtin follows dynamic scope: it unsets a current-scope local if one exists, otherwise it unsets the variable found in a calling scope; the localvar_unset shell option changes this behavior.
Functions can be exported to child shell processes with 'export -f', deleted with 'unset -f', and listed with 'declare -f' (definitions) or 'declare -F' (names).
A 'name=value' assignment subjects value to tilde, parameter, command-substitution, arithmetic, and quote-removal expansions but not word splitting or filename expansion.
If a variable has the integer attribute set, an assigned value is evaluated as an arithmetic expression even without using the '$((…))' syntax.
condition: the variable has the integer attribute

statement: The '+=' assignment operator appends: it concatenates strings, adds arithmetically for integer-attribute variables, appends after the highest index for indexed arrays, and adds key-value pairs for associative arrays without first unsetting the array.

A nameref created with 'declare -n ref=name' redirects references, assignments, unsets, and attribute changes to the variable it names, and is commonly used in a function to indirectly manipulate a variable whose name was passed as an argument.
A positional parameter with more than one digit must be enclosed in braces (for example '${10}'); without braces a digit after '$' refers only to positional parameters 1 through 9 or to '$0'.
Positional parameters cannot be changed with assignment statements; use the 'set' and 'shift' builtins to set and shift them.
Special parameters may only be referenced; assignment to them is not allowed.

Unquoted '$*' expands each positional parameter to a separate word subject to word splitting and globbing, while '"$*"' joins all positional parameters into a single word separated by the first character of IFS (a space if IFS is unset, nothing if IFS is null).

'"$@"' expands the positional parameters to separate individually-quoted words ("$1" "$2" ...), and expands to nothing when there are no positional parameters, making it the correct way to forward arguments.
'$?' expands to the exit status of the most recently executed foreground command.
'$$' expands to the process id of the shell, and inside a subshell it still expands to the process id of the invoking shell rather than the subshell.
'$!' expands to the process id of the job most recently placed in the background.
'$#' expands to the number of positional parameters in decimal.
'$0' expands to the name of the shell or script, set at initialization; when Bash is started with -c it is set to the first argument after the command string, if present.

Bash applies expansions in a fixed order: brace expansion; then tilde, parameter/variable, arithmetic, and command substitution (left to right); then word splitting; then filename expansion; and quote removal is always performed last.

Only brace expansion, word splitting, and filename expansion can increase the number of words; every other expansion turns one word into one word, except the expansions of '"$@"'/'$*' and '"${name[@]}"'/'${name[*]}'.

Brace expansion generates strings from a comma list ('{a,b,c}') or a sequence expression ('{x..y[..incr]}'), is performed before all other expansions, is strictly textual, and generates names whether or not the files exist.
A brace sequence expression uses integers or letters of the same type; it zero-pads terms when x or y has a leading zero, and letter sequences use the C locale.
condition: x and y are the same type (both integers or both letters)

statement: A well-formed brace expansion requires unquoted braces and at least one unquoted comma or a valid sequence expression, an incorrectly formed one is left unchanged, and the string '${' inhibits brace expansion to avoid conflicting with parameter expansion.

Tilde expansion replaces '~' with $HOME (or the executing user's home if HOME is unset), '~user' with that user's home, '~+' with $PWD, '~-' with $OLDPWD, and '~N'/'~+N'/'~-N' with directory-stack entries.
Results of tilde expansion are treated as quoted, so they are not subject to word splitting or filename expansion, and if the login name is invalid the tilde-prefix is left unchanged.

Bash performs tilde expansion on the parts of a variable assignment that follow the first '=' or a ':', so assignments to PATH, CDPATH, and MAILPATH may use tildes; in POSIX mode this applies only to declaration commands.
Braces in '${name}' protect the parameter name from following characters, so '${11}' expands the eleventh positional parameter whereas '$11' expands '$1' followed by a literal '1'.

Indirect expansion '${!parameter}' (the '!' must immediately follow the brace) expands parameter to obtain a variable name and then expands that name; if parameter is a nameref, '${!ref}' instead yields the name of the variable the nameref points to.
In parameter-expansion default/assign/error operators, including the colon (e.g. ':-') tests whether the parameter is unset or null, while omitting the colon tests only whether it is unset.
'${parameter:-word}' substitutes the expansion of word when parameter is unset or null and otherwise substitutes parameter's value, without assigning to parameter.
'${parameter:=word}' assigns the expansion of word to parameter when it is unset or null and then substitutes the result; positional and special parameters cannot be assigned this way.

'${parameter:?word}' writes word (or a default message) to standard error when parameter is unset or null and exits a non-interactive shell with non-zero status, providing a fail-fast check for required variables.
'${parameter:+word}' substitutes the expansion of word only when parameter is set and non-null, and otherwise substitutes nothing.

In substring expansion '${parameter:offset:length}', offset and length are arithmetic expressions, a negative offset counts from the end and must be separated from the colon by a space to avoid being read as ':-', and a negative length is an offset from the end.
Substring indexing is zero-based except when the positional parameters are used (which start at 1), and substring expansion applied to an associative array produces undefined results.
exception: the positional parameters are used, where indexing starts at 1

statement: '${#parameter}' yields the length in characters of the value, or the number of positional parameters when parameter is '@' or '*', or the number of elements when parameter is an array subscripted by '@' or '*'.

'${parameter#word}' and '${parameter##word}' delete the shortest and longest match of the pattern from the start of the value, while '${parameter%word}' and '${parameter%%word}' delete the shortest and longest match from the end.

'${parameter/pattern/string}' replaces the first match, '${parameter//pattern/string}' replaces every match, '${parameter/#pattern/string}' anchors the match at the start, '${parameter/%pattern/string}' anchors it at the end, and an empty string deletes matches.

In pattern substitution, quoting any part of the replacement string inhibits replacement there, the nocasematch option makes matching case-insensitive, and the patsub_replacement option makes an unquoted '&' in the replacement stand for the matched text.

'${parameter^pattern}' and '${parameter^^pattern}' uppercase the first or all matching characters, '${parameter,pattern}' and '${parameter,,pattern}' lowercase them, and an omitted pattern behaves like '?' matching every character.

The '${parameter@operator}' transform selects a single-letter operation such as Q (quote the value so it can be reused as input), E (expand backslash escapes as in $'...'), P (expand as a prompt), A (an assignment/declare that recreates the value), U/u/L (case changes), a (attribute flags), and K/k (key-value pairs for arrays).
'$(command)' runs the command in a subshell and substitutes its standard output with trailing newlines removed, and '$(< file)' is a faster equivalent of '$(cat file)'.

The backquote form of command substitution is deprecated in favor of '$(command)', in which every character between the parentheses is part of the command and none is treated specially, so nesting needs no backslash escaping.
When a command substitution appears within double quotes, Bash does not perform word splitting or filename expansion on its result.

The '${ command; }' form runs command in the current execution environment (so side effects such as 'exit' persist and local variables behave as in a function) and captures its output with trailing newlines removed, while '${| command; }' expands to the value of REPLY after command runs without needing any output.

'$(( expression ))' evaluates an arithmetic expression and substitutes the result; if the expression is invalid Bash prints an error to standard error, performs no substitution, and does not execute the command.

Process substitution '<(list)' exposes a command's output as a filename and '>(list)' exposes its input as a filename, running the list asynchronously; no space may appear between the '<' or '>' and the parenthesis or it is parsed as a redirection.

Word splitting is applied only to the results of parameter expansion, command substitution, and arithmetic expansion that did not occur within double quotes; words that were not expanded are not split.
The shell splits fields on each character of IFS; if IFS is unset it splits on space, tab, and newline, and if IFS is null no word splitting occurs at all.
condition: IFS is unset or null changes the behavior

statement: Leading and trailing IFS whitespace is trimmed and runs of IFS whitespace delimit fields, but a non-whitespace IFS character delimits a field on its own, so adjacent non-whitespace delimiters produce empty fields.
Explicit null arguments ('""' or "''") are retained and passed as empty strings, while an unquoted expansion of an unset or empty parameter is removed entirely.
After word splitting, unless noglob (-f) is set, an unquoted '*', '?', or '[' makes a word a filename-matching pattern that is replaced by a sorted list of matching filenames.
exception: the -f (noglob) option is set

statement: When a glob pattern matches no files, by default the word is left unchanged (literal), whereas with nullglob it is removed, with failglob Bash errors and does not run the command, and with nocaseglob matching ignores case.

In filename matching a leading '.' (or one right after a slash) must be matched explicitly unless dotglob is set, and the names '.' and '..' require a pattern beginning with '.' (or never match when globskipdots is enabled).
The GLOBIGNORE variable removes matching names from glob results, and setting it to a non-null value has the side effect of enabling dotglob-like matching for other dot-files.
In patterns '*' matches any string including the empty string, '?' matches any single character, '[...]' matches one bracketed character, and a backslash escapes the following character.

Character ranges in a '[...]' bracket expression depend on the current locale's collating order (LC_COLLATE/LC_ALL); to get the traditional C-locale range interpretation set LC_COLLATE or LC_ALL to C or enable the globasciiranges option.

Bracket expressions support POSIX character classes with the '[:class:]' syntax (such as alnum, alpha, digit, space, upper, lower, and word), where the 'word' class matches letters, digits, and underscore.
With the globstar option enabled, '**' matches files across directories and subdirectories recursively, and '**/' matches only directories and subdirectories.

With extglob enabled, the extended patterns '?(list)', '*(list)', '+(list)', '@(list)', and '!(list)' are recognized, and extglob must be enabled before parsing any construct (including functions and command substitutions) that contains such patterns.
condition: extglob is enabled before the construct is parsed

statement: Complicated extended pattern matching against long strings is slow, especially with alternations and multiple matches, so matching shorter strings or using arrays of strings can be faster.

Redirections are processed left to right and their order is significant, so 'command > file 2>&1' sends both standard output and standard error to the file while 'command 2>&1 > file' sends only standard output to the file because standard error was duplicated from the original standard output first.
If the word following a redirection operator expands to more than one word, Bash reports an error.

'[n]>word' creates or truncates the file for writing, and with the noclobber option set a plain '>' fails if the target already exists as a regular file, whereas '>|' forces the redirection regardless of noclobber.
condition: noclobber is enabled makes '>' fail on existing files

statement: '[n]>>word' opens the file for appending and creates it if it does not exist.
'&>word' (the preferred form) and '>&word' redirect both standard output and standard error to the file, equivalent to '>word 2>&1', and '&>>word' appends both.

Preceding a redirection with '{varname}' allocates a file descriptor of at least 10 into varname, and that descriptor persists beyond the command so its lifetime must be managed manually (controlled by the varredir_close option).
File descriptors greater than 9 should be used with care in redirections because they may conflict with descriptors the shell uses internally.
Redirections supplied to the 'exec' builtin (with no command) modify the file handles of the current shell execution environment rather than a child command.

Bash treats special redirection filenames specially: /dev/stdin, /dev/stdout, /dev/stderr, and /dev/fd/N duplicate file descriptors, while /dev/tcp/host/port and /dev/udp/host/port open the corresponding TCP or UDP socket.

In a here-document ('<<word') the delimiter must appear alone on a line; the body undergoes parameter, command, and arithmetic expansion when word is unquoted but is treated literally when any part of word is quoted, and '<<-' strips leading tab characters from the body and the closing delimiter.
condition: word is unquoted enables expansion; quoting any part makes the body literal

statement: A here-string ('<<< word') expands word (without filename expansion or word splitting) and supplies it to standard input as a single string with a trailing newline appended.

'[n]<&word' and '[n]>&word' duplicate file descriptors and close descriptor n when word is '-', '[n]<&digit-' and '[n]>&digit-' move a descriptor (duplicate then close the source), and '[n]<>word' opens a file for both reading and writing.

When executing a simple command, Bash saves assignments and redirections, expands the remaining words (first becomes the command name and the rest the arguments), performs redirections, then expands and applies the assignment values, all left to right.

Variable assignments preceding a command name affect the current shell only when no command name results; when a command name is present the assignments are placed only in that command's environment and do not change the current shell.
condition: no command name results leaves assignments in the current shell

statement: A simple command that is neither a builtin nor a shell function runs in a separate execution environment and cannot affect the shell's own environment; a subshell is a copy of the shell process.

Command substitutions, parenthesized groups, and asynchronous commands run in a subshell that duplicates the shell environment with caught traps reset, and pipeline builtins (except possibly the last when lastpipe is set) also run in a subshell, so their changes cannot affect the parent shell.
In POSIX mode a command-substitution subshell inherits the errexit (-e) option from the parent, but outside POSIX mode Bash clears -e in such subshells unless the inherit_errexit option is enabled.
condition: POSIX mode or inherit_errexit is enabled

statement: On invocation Bash creates a parameter for every environment variable and marks it for export; 'export', 'declare -x', 'unset', and 'export -n' add or remove environment entries, and assignments preceding a command are part of only that command's environment (or, before a function call, local to the function and exported to its children).
Command exit statuses range from 0 to 255, where zero means success and any non-zero value means failure, and the shell reserves values above 125 for special failure modes.

A command killed by fatal signal N exits with status 128+N, a command that is not found returns 127, a command found but not executable returns 126, and an expansion or redirection error yields a status greater than zero.
All Bash builtins return zero on success and non-zero on failure, and return exit status 2 to signal incorrect usage such as invalid options or missing arguments.

When interactive and with no traps set, Bash ignores SIGTERM and SIGQUIT, catches SIGINT (breaking out of executing loops and keeping 'wait' interruptible), and ignores SIGTTIN, SIGTTOU, and SIGTSTP when job control is active.
condition: the shell is interactive with no traps set

statement: Non-builtin commands inherit the shell's signal dispositions; a signal that 'trap' sets to be ignored is also ignored by child processes, and asynchronous commands run without job control additionally ignore SIGINT and SIGQUIT.
Bash exits by default on SIGHUP, and an interactive shell first resends SIGHUP (plus SIGCONT to stopped jobs) to all its jobs; use 'disown' or 'disown -h' to stop a particular job from receiving it.
With the huponexit option set, an interactive login shell sends SIGHUP to all jobs when it exits.
condition: the huponexit option is set and the shell is an interactive login shell

statement: When Bash is waiting for a command and receives a signal for which a trap is set, it defers running the trap until the command completes; but if it is waiting via the 'wait' builtin, 'wait' returns immediately with a status greater than 128 and the trap runs right after.

When job control is not enabled, Bash waits for a foreground command to finish before acting on a received SIGINT, and treats the SIGINT as meant for the shell only if the command itself terminated because of it.

When a script file is given as the first non-option argument (with neither -c nor -s), Bash reads and executes it as a non-interactive shell and then exits; if the filename contains no slash, Bash searches the current directory and then $PATH.
Bash attempts to detect binary files and refuses to execute a file it determines to be a binary.
When running a script, Bash sets '$0' to the script's filename and the positional parameters to the remaining arguments, leaving the positional parameters unset when none are supplied.

Executing an executable shell script starts a new Bash instance (equivalent to running 'bash filename arguments'); the child reinitializes itself but retains the command locations already hashed by the parent.

A '#!interpreter' first line selects the interpreter, but some older Unix systems limit the interpreter name plus a single argument to 32 characters, so relying on more than one interpreter argument is not portable.
Starting a script with '#!/bin/bash' ensures Bash interprets it even when launched from another shell, while '#!/usr/bin/env bash' locates the first bash found in $PATH.
A builtin command is executed directly within the shell process without invoking a separate program.

Most option-accepting builtins treat '--' as the end of options, but ':', 'true', 'false', and 'test'/'[' do not treat '--' specially, and 'exit', 'logout', 'return', 'break', 'continue', 'let', and 'shift' accept dash-leading arguments without needing '--'.
The ':' builtin does nothing beyond expanding its arguments and performing redirections and always returns zero, and 'true' returns zero while 'false' returns non-zero.

The '.' (source) builtin reads and executes commands from a file in the current shell context rather than a subshell, searches PATH (and, outside POSIX mode, the current directory) when the filename has no slash, and does not require the file to be executable.
Arguments passed to '.' (source) become the positional parameters while the file executes, and the positional parameters are left unchanged when no arguments are supplied.
'break [n]' exits the nth enclosing for/while/until/select loop and 'continue [n]' resumes the nth enclosing loop, where n must be at least 1.
When the target of 'cd' does not begin with a slash and CDPATH is set, 'cd' searches each colon-separated directory in CDPATH (a null entry meaning the current directory) for the target.
condition: the target does not begin with a slash and CDPATH is set

statement: 'cd -P' does not follow symbolic links (resolving them before processing '..'), the default '-L' resolves symlinks after processing '..', 'cd -' changes to $OLDPWD, and a successful 'cd' sets PWD to the new directory and OLDPWD to the previous one.
'eval' concatenates its arguments into a single space-separated command, then reads and executes that command and returns its exit status.

'exec command' replaces the shell with command without creating a new process (command may not be a builtin or function); if command cannot be executed, a non-interactive shell exits unless the execfail option is enabled.
exception: the execfail option is enabled, so the shell returns non-zero instead of exiting

statement: 'exec' with redirections but no command applies those redirections to the current shell environment.
'exit [n]' terminates the shell returning status n (or the last command's status if n is omitted), and any EXIT trap runs before the shell terminates.
'export [-f] name[=value]' marks a variable (or, with -f, a function) to be passed in the environment of subsequently executed commands, and 'export -n' removes the export attribute.

'getopts optstring name' parses one option per call from the positional parameters (or supplied arguments), setting name, OPTIND (the next argument index), and OPTARG (an option's argument); OPTIND is initialized to 1 only at shell startup and is not reset automatically, so it must be reset manually before re-parsing a new argument set in the same shell.

'getopts' uses silent error reporting when optstring begins with a colon (or when OPTERR is 0): on an invalid option it sets name to '?' (silent mode assigns the character to OPTARG), and on a missing required argument it sets name to '?' normally or to ':' with OPTARG set in silent mode.
condition: optstring begins with a colon or OPTERR is 0

statement: 'hash' remembers the full path of commands found through PATH so later lookups are skipped; 'hash -r' (and any assignment to PATH) forgets all remembered locations, and 'hash -p' records a location without searching.
'pwd -P' prints the physical current directory with symbolic links resolved, whereas the default '-L' may include symbolic links.
'readonly name[=value]' marks a name so its value cannot be changed by later assignment or unset, with -f for functions and -a/-A for indexed/associative arrays.

'return [n]' stops a function or sourced file returning status n (or the last command's status), truncated to its least significant 8 bits, runs the RETURN trap before resuming, and errors if used outside a function or sourced file.
'shift [n]' discards the first n positional parameters (default 1) and renumbers the rest; n must be between 0 and $#, and the parameters are unchanged when n is 0 or greater than $#.
condition: n is between 0 and the parameter count

statement: 'test'/'[' evaluates a conditional expression to status 0 (true) or 1 (false), requires each operator and operand to be a separate argument, requires a closing ']' for the '[' form, and does not treat '--' as an end-of-options marker.

POSIX has deprecated the '-a', '-o', and parenthesis operators of 'test', so scripts should restrict each 'test' to a single primary and combine conditions with the shell's '&&' and '||' list operators (for example 'test -n a && test -n b').
A one-argument 'test' is true if and only if the argument is not null, which is why an unquoted variable in '[ $x ]' can misbehave when the value is empty or contains blanks.
In 'test'/'[', the '<' and '>' operators sort lexicographically by ASCII outside POSIX mode, but sort using the current locale in POSIX mode or within '[['.

'trap action sigspec' runs action when the signal arrives; an action of '-' resets the signal to its startup disposition, while an empty-string action makes the shell and the commands it invokes ignore the signal.
condition: action is '-' resets, empty string ignores

statement: 'trap' with no arguments prints the current traps as a set of 'trap' commands that can be reused to restore the signal dispositions.

Special trap targets include EXIT (or 0) run when the shell exits, DEBUG run before each command, RETURN run when a function or sourced file finishes, and ERR run when a command returns non-zero under the same conditions as errexit (excluding while/until/if tests, non-final '&&'/'||' commands, non-final pipeline commands, and commands inverted with '!').
Trap signal names are case-insensitive and the 'SIG' prefix is optional, and 'trap -l' lists valid signal names and numbers.
Signals ignored on entry to a non-interactive shell cannot be trapped or reset, and trapped signals that are not ignored are reset to their original dispositions when a subshell is created.
condition: the shell is non-interactive and the signal was ignored on entry

statement: 'umask' sets the file-creation mask (a leading digit is octal, otherwise a symbolic mode), and each octal digit is subtracted from 7, so a umask of 022 yields 755 permissions.

'unset -v' removes a variable and 'unset -f' removes a function; with no option a variable is removed before a function, 'unset -n' unsets a nameref itself rather than its target, readonly names cannot be unset, and unsetting also removes the name from the environment passed to later commands.
'alias name=value' defines an alias, and a trailing space in the value causes the word following the alias to also be checked for alias expansion.

'bind -x keyseq:shell-command' runs a shell command when a key sequence is entered, exposing the line buffer as READLINE_LINE and the cursor and mark as READLINE_POINT and READLINE_MARK, and changes to those variables update the editing state.
'builtin shell-builtin args' runs the named builtin directly, which lets a shell function of the same name still invoke the builtin instead of calling itself recursively.
'caller [expr]' reports the line number, subroutine name, and source file of an active function or sourced-file call (frame 0 being the current one), which can be used to print a stack trace.

'command name' runs name while ignoring any shell function of that name, executing only a builtin or a command found in PATH, and 'command -p' uses a guaranteed-safe default PATH that finds the standard utilities.

'command -v name' prints a single word describing how name would be invoked and 'command -V' gives a verbose description, returning zero only when name is found, providing a portable way to test for a command.

'declare' (and its synonym 'typeset') assigns variable attributes: -i integer (arithmetic on assignment), -l or -u forcing lower or upper case, -r readonly, -x export, -a or -A for indexed or associative arrays, -n nameref, and -t trace.
'declare' used inside a function makes each name local (like 'local') unless the -g option is given, which forces the variable to be created or modified at global scope.
'declare -p name' displays a variable's attributes and value in a form that can be reused as input.
'local' may only be used within a function (it is an error otherwise) and restricts a variable's visible scope to that function and the commands it calls, accepting any option that 'declare' accepts.
'local -' makes shell options local to the function, so any options changed with 'set' after that call are restored to their prior values when the function returns.
'echo -e' enables interpretation of backslash escape sequences and '-E' disables it, the xpg_echo option controls the default, and 'echo' does not treat '--' as the end of options.

'enable -n name' disables a shell builtin so an external command of the same name is executed instead, and 'enable -f filename name' loads a new builtin from a shared object on systems that support dynamic loading.
'let expression' evaluates arithmetic on shell variables and returns 1 when the last expression evaluates to 0 and 0 otherwise, the same status inversion as the '(( ))' command.

'mapfile' (and its synonym 'readarray') reads lines from standard input (or file descriptor fd with -u) into an indexed array (MAPFILE by default), clears the array first unless an origin is given, uses -t to strip the trailing delimiter, and -d to set a non-newline delimiter.

'printf format arguments' formats output under control of format, '-v var' stores the result in a variable instead of printing, the format is reused until all arguments are consumed, and missing arguments are treated as zero or the empty string.

'printf %q' (and '%Q') outputs an argument quoted so it can be safely reused as shell input, '%b' expands backslash escapes as with 'echo -e', and '%(datefmt)T' formats a time whose argument is seconds since the epoch, with -1 meaning now and -2 meaning shell start.

'read' reads one line, splits it into words on the characters of IFS, and assigns them to the given names, with any extra words (and their delimiters) assigned to the last name and unfilled names left empty.
'read -r' treats backslash literally rather than as an escape character, so a backslash-newline is not a line continuation and backslashes in the input are preserved verbatim.
'read' with no name arguments assigns the whole line, minus the trailing delimiter, to the REPLY variable.

'read' options include -a to fill an array, -d to set the delimiter, -n or -N to read a fixed number of characters, -s for no echo, -p for a prompt, -u to read from a file descriptor, and -t for a timeout (which returns a status greater than 128 and only applies to terminals, pipes, or special files).
condition: a -t timeout applies only to terminals, pipes, or special files

statement: 'type -t name' classifies a command name as alias, keyword, function, builtin, or file, '-p' prints the executable path that a PATH search would find, and '-a' lists every location that defines the name, giving a reliable alternative to 'which'.

'ulimit' controls resource limits for the shell and its children; -H and -S select the hard and soft limit, a non-root user cannot raise a hard limit once set while a soft limit may rise up to the hard limit, and specifying neither -H nor -S sets both.
condition: raising a hard limit requires root; soft limits are capped by the hard limit

statement: Any arguments remaining after 'set' option processing replace the positional parameters, and 'set' with no options or arguments displays all shell variables and functions in a form that can be reused as input.

'set -e' (errexit) makes the shell exit when a command, pipeline, list, or compound command returns non-zero, except when the failing command is in a while/until test, an if/elif test, a non-final command of a '&&' or '||' list, a non-final command of a pipeline (subject to pipefail), or is inverted with '!'; a set ERR trap runs before the shell exits, and the option applies to each subshell separately.
exception: the failing command is in a test position, a non-final '&&'/'||' or pipeline command, or is inverted with '!'

statement: When a compound command or shell function runs in a context where errexit is being ignored, none of the commands inside it are affected by '-e' even if a command fails, which is why a function invoked as an if-test or '&&' operand does not abort on an internal failure.
condition: the compound command or function runs where errexit is already ignored

statement: 'set -u' (nounset) treats the expansion of an unset variable or parameter as an error that writes to standard error and exits a non-interactive shell, except for the special parameters '@' and '*' and arrays subscripted by '@' or '*'.
exception: '$@', '$*', and arrays subscripted by '@' or '*'

statement: 'set -x' (xtrace) prints a trace of each simple command and its expanded arguments to standard error after expansion and before execution, each line prefixed by the expanded value of PS4.
'set -o pipefail' makes a pipeline's return value the rightmost command to exit non-zero (or zero if all succeed); it is disabled by default.
'set -f' disables filename expansion, 'set -C' (noclobber) stops '>' from overwriting an existing file (overridden by '>|'), and 'set -B' (on by default) enables brace expansion.
'set -n' (noexec) reads commands without executing them so a script can be checked for syntax errors, and it is ignored by interactive shells.

'set -E' (errtrace) makes shell functions, command substitutions, and subshells inherit the ERR trap, and 'set -T' (functrace) makes them inherit the DEBUG and RETURN traps, none of which are inherited by default.
'set -a' (allexport) automatically gives the export attribute to every variable or function that is created or modified.
'set -P' (physical) makes commands like 'cd' use the physical directory structure without resolving symbolic links, instead of following the logical directory chain used by default.
'set -o posix' enables POSIX mode, changing Bash behavior to match the POSIX standard wherever the default differs.

'set -- arguments' sets the positional parameters to the given arguments even when some begin with '-', and unsets them when no arguments follow, providing a safe way to reset the positional parameters.
'set -m' (monitor) enables job control so all processes run in separate process groups and completed background jobs are reported.

'set -p' (privileged) mode does not process BASH_ENV or ENV, does not inherit functions from the environment, and ignores SHELLOPTS, BASHOPTS, CDPATH, and GLOBIGNORE from the environment, and is applied automatically when the effective and real user ids differ.

'shopt -s optname' enables and 'shopt -u optname' disables an optional shell behavior, 'shopt -q' reports the state only through its exit status, and shopt options are off by default unless otherwise noted.
Alias expansion (the expand_aliases option) is enabled by default only for interactive shells, so aliases are not expanded in non-interactive scripts by default.
condition: the shell is interactive or expand_aliases is explicitly enabled

statement: With the histappend option set, the history list is appended to the HISTFILE when the shell exits rather than overwriting the file.
With the checkhash option set, Bash verifies that a hashed command still exists before executing it and falls back to a normal PATH search if it does not.
With the localvar_inherit option set, a new local variable inherits the value and attributes (except nameref) of a same-named variable at a previous scope before any new value is assigned.

In POSIX mode the special builtins (including ':', '.', 'break', 'continue', 'eval', 'exec', 'exit', 'export', 'readonly', 'return', 'set', 'shift', 'trap', and 'unset') are found before shell functions during lookup, cause a non-interactive shell to exit on an error status, and let preceding assignment statements persist in the shell environment.
condition: the shell is executing in POSIX mode

statement: In PATH a zero-length (null) directory element, which can appear as two adjacent colons or as a leading or trailing colon, denotes the current directory, so an empty PATH entry causes the current directory to be searched for commands.

The '$_' parameter is set at startup to the invocation pathname, then expands to the last argument of the previous simple command, and is set to the full pathname of each executed command in its exported environment.
BASHPID expands to the process id of the current Bash process, which can differ from '$$' inside a subshell that does not re-initialize Bash, making it the reliable way to get the subshell's own pid.
BASH_SUBSHELL starts at 0 and is incremented by one within each subshell environment, so it reports the current subshell nesting depth.
BASH_COMMAND holds the command currently executing or about to execute, except during a trap where it holds the command that was running when the trap fired.

FUNCNAME, BASH_SOURCE, and BASH_LINENO are parallel call-stack arrays where FUNCNAME[0] is the current function (bottom element is 'main'), BASH_SOURCE[i] is the file defining FUNCNAME[i], and BASH_LINENO[i] is the line it was called from; FUNCNAME exists only while a function executes and the 'caller' builtin uses these to print a stack trace.

BASH_ENV names a startup file (its value expanded, not PATH-searched) that Bash reads before executing a non-interactive script, and ENV serves the same role for an interactive shell in POSIX mode, so both are security-sensitive influences on script startup.
EUID (effective user id), UID, and PPID (parent process id) are readonly variables, so a script can rely on EUID for a trustworthy privilege check that cannot be overwritten.

PIPESTATUS is an array holding the exit status of every command in the most-recently-executed foreground pipeline, letting a script inspect an individual pipeline command's status even without pipefail.
Each reference to RANDOM yields a random integer between 0 and 32767, and assigning a value seeds the generator, so seeding with the same constant reproduces the same sequence.
LINENO expands to the current line number in the executing script or function, with line numbers starting at 1.

EPOCHSECONDS expands to the whole number of seconds since the Unix epoch and EPOCHREALTIME expands to the seconds since the epoch as a floating-point value with microsecond granularity, and assignments to either are ignored.

If POSIXLY_CORRECT is present in the environment at startup Bash enters POSIX mode before reading startup files, and setting it while running enables POSIX mode as if 'set -o posix' had been executed.

GLOBSORT controls how filename-expansion results are sorted: a specifier such as name, numeric, size, mtime, atime, ctime, or blocks, optionally prefixed with '-' to reverse order, and 'nosort' to return results unsorted in filesystem order.

EXECIGNORE is a colon-separated list of shell patterns for full pathnames that PATH command search and completion should skip (for example shared libraries with the execute bit set), without affecting the test, '[', or '[[' commands.

The locale variables LC_ALL, LANG, LC_COLLATE, and LC_CTYPE determine collation order and character interpretation for filename expansion and pattern matching, so they change the meaning of range expressions and glob sorting.
Setting BASH_XTRACEFD to a valid file descriptor sends 'set -x' trace output to that descriptor instead of standard error, allowing trace output to be separated from a program's diagnostics.

BASH_VERSION is a string describing the running Bash and BASH_VERSINFO is a readonly array whose elements give the major, minor, patch, build, release-status, and machine-type components, supporting reliable version detection.
If HISTFILE is unset or null the shell does not save command history when it exits, which is relevant when handling sensitive commands.
SECONDS expands to the number of seconds since the shell started, and assigning to it resets the count so it later reads as the assigned value plus elapsed seconds.

SHELLOPTS and BASHOPTS are readonly lists of enabled options, and if either is present in the environment at startup Bash enables each listed option before reading any startup files, which propagates to exported child shells.

SRANDOM expands to a fresh 32-bit pseudo-random number on each reference using a non-linear source such as /dev/urandom or arc4random and cannot be seeded, making it stronger than RANDOM for unpredictability.

When TMOUT is greater than zero it becomes the default timeout for 'read' and 'select' on terminal input, and an interactive shell exits if a command line is not entered within TMOUT seconds after the prompt.
condition: TMOUT is set greater than zero

statement: All single-character 'set' options are also valid at shell invocation, and multi-character invocation options must appear before the single-character options to be recognized.
'bash -c string' reads and executes the command string then exits, and any arguments after the string are assigned to '$0' and then the positional parameters.

At invocation '-l' (or --login) makes a login shell, '-i' forces an interactive shell, '-s' reads commands from standard input (allowing positional parameters to be set), and '-r' makes a restricted shell.
A login shell is one whose zeroth argument begins with '-' or that was invoked with the --login option.
An interactive shell is one started with no non-option arguments (unless -s), without -c, whose standard input and standard error are both terminals, or one started with -i.
At invocation a '--' (or a lone '-') signals the end of options, and any following arguments are treated as a script filename and its arguments.

An interactive login shell reads /etc/profile then the first existing of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, or ~/.profile, while an interactive non-login shell reads ~/.bashrc, which is why ~/.bash_profile commonly sources ~/.bashrc.
When invoked under the name 'sh', Bash mimics historical sh startup and enters POSIX mode after reading startup files, and an interactive sh reads only the file named by the ENV variable.

If Bash starts with the effective user or group id not equal to the real id and without -p, it reads no startup files, does not inherit functions from the environment, ignores SHELLOPTS, BASHOPTS, CDPATH, and GLOBIGNORE from the environment, and resets the effective id to the real id.
condition: effective and real ids differ and -p is not supplied

statement: A script can detect an interactive shell by testing whether the '$-' special parameter contains 'i', or whether PS1 is set (it is unset in non-interactive shells).

An interactive shell does not exit on several errors that would terminate a non-interactive shell, including nounset ('set -u') expansion errors, '${var:?}' errors, redirection errors in builtins, a failed 'exec', a POSIX special-builtin error, and parser syntax errors.

The file-test primaries include -e (exists), -f (regular file), -d (directory), -r/-w/-x (readable/writable/executable), -s (size greater than zero), -L or -h (symbolic link), -p (FIFO), -S (socket), and -t (descriptor is a terminal).
Unless otherwise specified, file-test primaries follow symbolic links and test the link's target rather than the link itself.

'file1 -nt file2' is true when file1 is newer than file2 (or file2 is missing), '-ot' is true when file1 is older (or file1 is missing), and '-ef' is true when both refer to the same device and inode.
'-z string' is true when the string has length zero, and '-n string' (or a bare string operand) is true when its length is non-zero.
'-v varname' is true when the shell variable is set, and '-R varname' is true when it is set and is a name reference, providing a safe existence test.
'-o optname' is true when the named shell option is enabled.

The '==' (or '=') string operator performs pattern matching under '[[' but literal comparison under 'test' (where '=' should be used for POSIX conformance), while the arithmetic operators -eq/-ne/-lt/-le/-gt/-ge compare integers, and under '[[' their operands are evaluated as arithmetic expressions.
Shell arithmetic is evaluated in the largest available fixed-width integers with no overflow check (division by zero is trapped as an error), using C operators and precedence.
In an arithmetic context a shell variable may be referenced by bare name without the '$' syntax, and a null or unset variable referenced by name evaluates to 0.
Arithmetic integer constants with a leading 0 are octal and those with a leading 0x or 0X are hexadecimal, and the 'base#n' form uses an arbitrary base from 2 to 64.

Alias expansion substitutes a value for the first word of a simple command and re-checks the first word of the replacement for aliases, but an alias identical to one being expanded is not re-expanded, so 'alias ls="ls -F"' does not recurse.

Aliases are expanded when a line or function definition is read, not when it is executed, so an alias defined on the same line as another command or inside a compound command or function is not available until the next line or after the function runs; alias definitions should therefore be placed on their own line.
Aliases cannot take arguments, so a shell function should be used when arguments are needed, and for almost every purpose functions are preferable to aliases.

Bash supports one-dimensional indexed arrays (zero-based, arithmetic-integer subscripts) and associative arrays (arbitrary string keys), with no size limit and no requirement that indices be contiguous.
Assigning with 'name[subscript]=value' automatically creates an indexed array, while 'declare -a name' explicitly declares an indexed array and 'declare -A name' declares an associative array.
Arrays are assigned with the compound form 'name=(value ...)', where associative arrays require a subscript on each element (or an alternating key/value list) and associative keys may not be empty.
condition: associative arrays require explicit non-empty subscripts or key/value pairs

statement: An array element is referenced as '${name[subscript]}', and the braces are required to avoid conflicts with filename expansion.

'${name[@]}' expands each element to a separate word and '"${name[@]}"' quotes each element individually, whereas '"${name[*]}"' joins all elements into one word separated by the first character of IFS, and '"${name[@]}"' expands to nothing when the array is empty.
'${#name[@]}' (or '[*]') gives the number of array elements, while '${#name[subscript]}' gives the length of a single element.
'${!name[@]}' (or '[*]') expands to the list of assigned indices or keys of an array, which is how the keys of an associative array are enumerated.
Referencing an array variable without a subscript is equivalent to referencing index 0, so a bare '$name' yields only the first element rather than the whole array.
A negative index on an indexed array counts back from the end (one greater than the maximum index), so an index of -1 references the last element.

'unset name' destroys an entire array and 'unset name[subscript]' removes a single element, but an unquoted subscript argument such as 'unset a[4]' is subject to filename expansion and should be quoted (for example 'unset a[4]' written with quotes).
The directory stack is managed by 'pushd' (push a directory and change to it), 'popd' (pop and change to the new top), and 'dirs' (display it), with the current directory always at the top.

Prompt strings (PS0, PS1, PS2, PS4) support backslash escapes such as \u (user), \h (host), \w (working directory), \$ (which shows '#' for uid 0 and '$' otherwise), and \[ ... \] to bracket non-printing terminal control sequences.

After a prompt string's escapes are decoded it is further subjected to parameter expansion, command substitution, arithmetic expansion, and quote removal (under the promptvars option), which can cause unwanted side effects if the decoded text contains expansion-special characters.

A restricted shell (rbash, --restricted, or -r) forbids using 'cd', changing SHELL/PATH/HISTFILE/ENV/BASH_ENV, command names or source/history/hash filenames containing slashes, output redirection, the 'exec' builtin, importing functions or SHELLOPTS from the environment, and disabling restricted mode.

Restricted-shell limits are enforced only after startup files are read, and a shell script executed by rbash runs in an unrestricted shell, so restricted mode alone is not a complete security boundary and must be paired with a locked-down PATH, a non-writable working directory, and a cleaned environment.
Modern systems provide more secure ways to build a restricted environment, such as jails, zones, or containers.

POSIX mode (entered via --posix, 'set -o posix', POSIXLY_CORRECT in the environment, or invoking Bash as 'sh') changes dozens of Bash behaviors to conform more strictly to the POSIX standard where the Bash default differs.
In POSIX mode alias expansion is always enabled, even in non-interactive shells, unlike the default where aliases are not expanded in scripts.
In POSIX mode a shell function name may not be the same as a POSIX special builtin, and command lookup finds special builtins before shell functions, so a function cannot shadow a special builtin.
condition: the shell is in POSIX mode

statement: In POSIX mode many more error conditions cause a non-interactive shell to exit, including a special-builtin error, a variable-assignment error, an arithmetic or parameter-expansion error, a missing '.' source file, and a syntax error in a sourced file or an 'eval' string.
condition: the shell is in POSIX mode and non-interactive

statement: Enabling POSIX mode automatically sets the inherit_errexit, shift_verbose, and interactive_comments options.

Bash provides a shell compatibility level (older compat31..compat50 shopt options, or the BASH_COMPAT variable) that selects behavior from a previous version as a temporary migration aid; only one level is active at a time, and BASH_COMPAT is the only mechanism after bash-5.0.
condition: used only as a temporary migration aid

statement: Current Bash resets the loop state when entering a shell function or a subshell, so 'break' or 'continue' inside a function or subshell does not affect loops in the calling context (a change from older compatibility levels).
The shell associates one job with each pipeline and keeps a jobs table displayed by the 'jobs' builtin, with job numbers starting at 1.

Foreground processes (whose process group equals the terminal's) receive keyboard-generated signals such as SIGINT, whereas background processes are immune and are sent SIGTTIN or SIGTTOU (suspending them) if they read from, or with 'stty tostop' write to, the controlling terminal.

A job is referenced by a jobspec: '%n' by number, '%string' by command prefix, '%?string' by a substring of the command line, '%%'/'%+'/'%' for the current job, and '%-' for the previous job; an ambiguous prefix or substring is an error.
Naming a job by its jobspec alone (for example '%1') is equivalent to 'fg %1', and appending '&' (for example '%1 &') is equivalent to 'bg %1'.
Typing the suspend character (typically Control-Z) stops the foreground job and returns control to Bash, after which 'bg', 'fg', or 'kill' manipulate it, and sending SIGSTOP forces a process to stop.

Bash normally defers job status notifications until just before the next prompt unless 'set -b' is enabled, and after notifying about a terminated job it removes the job from the table though 'wait' with the job's process id still reports its exit status.

Attempting to exit Bash while jobs are stopped prints a warning, and a second immediate exit without an intervening command terminates the stopped jobs (the checkjobs option also warns about running jobs).
With job control enabled, the 'wait' builtin returns when a job changes state, whereas 'wait -f' waits until the job or process actually terminates before returning.
'bg [jobspec]' resumes a suspended job in the background as if it had been started with '&', defaulting to the current job.
'fg [jobspec]' resumes a job in the foreground and makes it the current job, defaulting to the current job.
'jobs' lists active jobs, with -l adding process ids, -p printing only the process-group-leader id, and -r or -s restricting output to running or stopped jobs.

'kill' sends a signal (SIGTERM by default) to a job or process id, accepts a case-insensitive signal name with or without the SIG prefix or a signal number, and 'kill -l [status]' lists signal names or maps an exit status above 128 to the terminating signal.
'wait [id ...]' waits for the given child processes or jobs and returns the exit status of the last id, and 'wait' with no arguments waits for all running background jobs and returns zero.

'wait -n' returns as soon as any one job or process completes (returning 127 when none of the ids is a child), and 'wait -p varname' stores the identifier of the job that finished, which is useful together with -n.
'disown [id]' removes a job from the active jobs table, while 'disown -h' keeps the job but marks it not to receive SIGHUP when the shell exits (with -a for all jobs and -r for running jobs).
'suspend' stops the current shell until it receives SIGCONT, and a login shell or a shell without job control cannot be suspended unless the -f option is supplied.
condition: the shell is a login shell or has no job control requires -f

statement: When job control is not active, the 'kill' and 'wait' builtins accept only process ids, not jobspecs, which matters in non-interactive scripts.

Command line editing is provided by the Readline library, enabled by default in interactive shells (unless --noediting) with Emacs-style bindings by default, and can be switched with 'set -o emacs' or 'set -o vi'.

Readline reads its init file from the path named by INPUTRC (defaulting to ~/.inputrc and then /etc/inputrc), the 'bind' builtin can also set bindings and variables, and C-x C-r re-reads the init file.

In a Readline inputrc file, blank lines are ignored, lines beginning with '#' are comments, lines beginning with '$' are conditional constructs, and other lines are variable settings ('set variable value') or key bindings.
A Readline boolean variable is set on when its value is empty, 'on' (case-insensitively), or '1', and off for any other value, and unrecognized variable names are silently ignored.
Setting 'editing-mode' to 'emacs' or 'vi' in the inputrc chooses the default keybinding set that Readline starts in.

A key binding is written 'keyname: function-name' (with no space before the colon), a macro is bound by using a quoted string on the right side, and '"keyseq": function' binds a whole key sequence written with Emacs-style escapes such as \C-, \M-, and \e.

Readline conditional directives let an inputrc branch on tests: '$if' can test mode=, term=, version, the application name, or a variable comparison, with '$else' and '$endif', and '$include file' reads another init file.

Useful Readline toggles include completion-ignore-case (case-insensitive completion), show-all-if-ambiguous (list matches on the first Tab), and enable-bracketed-paste (default on), which inserts pasted text literally so editing commands bound to sequences within the paste are not executed.

Default Emacs-mode line-editing bindings include C-a and C-e (start/end of line), C-k (kill to end of line), C-u (kill to start of line), C-w (kill the previous word), C-y (yank), and M-. or M-_ (insert the last argument of the previous command).
C-r starts an incremental reverse search through command history and C-s an incremental forward search, activating the matched region.
'edit-and-execute-command' (C-x C-e) opens the current command line in an editor ($VISUAL, then $EDITOR, then emacs) and executes the edited result as shell commands.

The 'complete' command (TAB) in Bash tries programmable completions for the command word first, then treats the text as a variable (leading '$'), username (leading '~'), hostname (leading '@'), or command, and finally falls back to filename completion.
'quoted-insert' (C-v or C-q) inserts the next character typed verbatim, which is how a literal control character or Tab is entered into the line.
'insert-comment' (M-#) prepends the comment-begin string (default '#') and accepts the line, turning the current command into a shell comment so it is stored in history without being executed.
'set -o vi' switches Readline to vi editing (the default is emacs); a new line begins in insert mode, and pressing ESC enters command mode where vi movement keys work and k/j move through history.

Programmable completion uses a compspec defined with the 'complete' builtin to generate a command's argument completions, with -E applying to an empty command line, -I to the initial command word, and -D as the default when no compspec exists for a command.

A 'complete -F function' completion function must place its results in the COMPREPLY array (one per element), and on invocation receives the command name as $1, the word being completed as $2, and the preceding word as $3, with COMP_WORDS, COMP_CWORD, COMP_LINE, and COMP_POINT also set.

Completion sources include -C command (whose printed lines become completions), -W wordlist (split on IFS and expanded), -G globpat (a filename pattern), -X filterpat (removes matching completions, or non-matching when prefixed with '!'), and -P/-S to add a prefix or suffix.

A completion function that returns exit status 124 after changing the command's compspec causes programmable completion to restart, which is how completions are loaded lazily (as in the bash_completion dynamic loader).

'compgen [option] [word]' generates the matches a compspec with the same options would produce and writes them to standard output (or, with -V, into an array variable), and is typically used inside completion functions.
'compopt' modifies the completion options of a named completion or of the currently-executing completion function.

The compspec '-o' options control completion behavior, including filenames (treat results as filenames, quoting them and adding slashes to directories), nospace (no trailing space), nosort, and the fallbacks bashdefault, default, dirnames, and plusdirs.

Command history is enabled by 'set -o history' (on by default in interactive shells), HISTSIZE bounds the in-memory list (default 500), and each command is stored after history expansion but before parameter expansion, subject to HISTIGNORE and HISTCONTROL.

On startup Bash reads history from HISTFILE (default ~/.bash_history) and on exit writes the last HISTSIZE entries, appending when histappend is set and otherwise overwriting, truncating to HISTFILESIZE lines, and saving nothing when HISTFILE is unset or null.

The 'history' builtin displays the list, 'history -c' clears it, 'history -d' deletes entries, and -a/-n/-r/-w append new lines to, read unread lines from, read into, or overwrite the history file, enabling history sharing across sessions.

'fc' lists or edits and re-executes ranges of history, 'fc -s pat=rep' re-runs the last matching command after a substitution (commonly aliased as r='fc -s'), and its editor is chosen by ${FCEDIT:-${EDITOR:-vi}}.
Bash is built with './configure', then 'make', optionally 'make tests' to run the test suite, then 'make install' (which may require elevated privileges).

Passing 'DESTDIR=path' to 'make install' installs the whole tree under that staging root without modifying the real system, which is how packagers build a sample install tree, while --prefix (default /usr/local) sets the real install prefix.

Many Bash runtime features are configure-time options that can be compiled out, including extended globbing, the '[[' command and its '=~' regex operator, arrays, process substitution, job control, /dev/tcp and /dev/udp net redirections, coprocesses, Readline/history, programmable completion, and the restricted shell, so a portable script should not assume every feature is present in every build.

Building with --enable-strict-posix-default makes Bash POSIX-conformant by default, and --enable-xpg-echo-default makes the 'echo' builtin expand backslash escapes by default, so identical scripts can behave differently across Bash builds.
An out-of-tree build (running configure from a separate build directory, which requires a VPATH-capable make such as GNU make) lets one source tree be compiled for multiple architectures at once.

A good Bash bug report, submitted with the 'bashbug' command, includes the Bash version, the hardware and operating system, the compiler used, a description of the behavior, and a short recipe that reproduces the bug.

Many common Bash constructs are extensions absent from the traditional Bourne/POSIX 'sh', so a script targeting '#!/bin/sh' must avoid them, including '[[ ]]', arrays, 'local', $'...' quoting, brace expansion, process substitution, the '+=' operator, the '${var/pat/rep}' and '${var:offset:length}' expansions, the C-style 'for (( ))', 'select', '(( ))' and 'let', '<<<' here-strings, '&>' redirection, 'mapfile', and the 'function' keyword.
Bash uses IFS to split only the results of expansion rather than all input words, which closes a longstanding shell security hole present in older Bourne shells.

In Bash a variable assignment preceding a command affects only that command, even for builtins and functions, whereas the traditional Bourne shell makes such assignments global unless the command is an external program.
Bash keeps separate namespaces for variables and functions, allowing a variable and a function to share the same name, unlike the traditional 'sh'.
Bash does not fork a subshell when redirecting into or out of a control structure such as an 'if' or 'while', so variables assigned inside a redirected loop persist in the current shell.
Bash does not allow unbalanced quotes and reports an error at end of input, whereas the historical SVR4.2 shell would silently insert a missing closing quote and hide the mistake.

The historical SVR4.2 shell exits a script if any builtin fails, but Bash exits a script only when a POSIX special builtin fails and only for certain failures enumerated by POSIX, so error-driven script termination differs between the shells.
Prefer Bash built-ins over external processes for common script tasks when a built-in equivalent is clear, because this can reduce dependencies and often improve runtime.

condition: when a backquote substitution or a quoted string straddles the boundary of a double-quoted string

statement: The shell reads input in terms of lines of unlimited length and parses them in two major modes: ordinary token recognition and here-document processing.

Alias substitution replaces a word only when it is the command-name word of a simple command and is an unquoted, valid alias name defined by alias and not undefined by unalias; reserved words in correct grammatical context are never candidates for alias substitution.
condition: when the word is the command-name word of a simple command and is an unquoted valid alias name
exception: reserved words used in correct grammatical context are not alias-substituted

statement: To prevent infinite recursive aliasing, a word is replaced by an alias value only if the shell is not already processing an alias of the same name.
condition: when the shell is not currently processing an alias of the same name

statement: If an alias value ends in a blank, the shell also checks the next command word for alias substitution, continuing until a word is reached that is not a valid alias or whose alias value does not end in a blank.
condition: when the alias value ends in a blank

statement: When used as specified by the standard, alias definitions are not inherited by separate invocations of the shell or by the utility execution environments the shell invokes.
The reserved words recognized by the shell are: ! { } case do done elif else esac fi for if in then until while.

A word is recognized as a reserved word only when none of its characters are quoted and it is used as the first word of a command, the first word following a reserved word other than case/for/in, the third word in a case command (where only 'in' is valid), or the third word in a for command (where only 'in' and 'do' are valid).
condition: when the word is unquoted and appears in one of the enumerated grammatical positions

statement: The tokens [[ ]] function and select may be recognized as reserved words on some implementations when unquoted, which causes unspecified results, so portable scripts cannot rely on their meaning.
condition: on some implementations when the characters are unquoted

statement: A parameter is set when it has an assigned value (a null value is a valid assigned value), and once a variable is set it can only be unset with the unset special built-in.
exception: a null value still counts as set

statement: A positional parameter is denoted by one or more decimal digits other than the single digit 0, and when a positional parameter has more than one digit the application shall enclose the digits in braces in parameter expansion.
condition: when the positional parameter number has more than one digit

statement: The special parameter @ expands to the positional parameters starting from one, producing one field per set positional parameter; within double-quotes each positional parameter is retained as a separate field rather than joined.
condition: the separate-field behavior applies when @ is expanded within double-quotes

statement: The special parameter * expands to the positional parameters, and where field splitting is not performed the parameters are joined into a single field separated by the first character of IFS, by a space if IFS is unset, or with no separation if IFS is set to a null string.
condition: when * is expanded in a context where field splitting is not performed

statement: The special parameter ? expands to the decimal exit status of the most recent pipeline.
The special parameter $ expands to the decimal process ID of the invoked shell, and inside a subshell $ expands to the same value as the current shell rather than the subshell's own process ID.
condition: the same-as-current-shell value applies inside a subshell

statement: A variable initialized from the environment shall be marked for export immediately.
condition: when the variable is initialized from the environment

statement: IFS is a list of characters used for field splitting, for expansion of the * special parameter, and for splitting lines into fields with the read utility; if IFS is not set the shell behaves as if IFS were space, tab, and newline, and the shell sets IFS to space/tab/newline when it is invoked.
exception: when IFS is unset, field and line splitting behave as if IFS were space/tab/newline

statement: Changing the value of LC_CTYPE after the shell has started does not affect lexical processing of shell commands in the current shell execution environment or its subshells; only invoking a new shell (for example exec sh) or running a shell script subjects it to the changed LC_CTYPE.
condition: when LC_CTYPE is changed after the shell has started
exception: invoking a new shell or shell script picks up the changed LC_CTYPE

statement: The ENV variable is subjected to parameter expansion only when an interactive shell is invoked and the result is used as the pathname of a file of commands to execute in the current environment; if the expanded value is not an absolute pathname the results are unspecified, and ENV is ignored when the real and effective user IDs or the real and effective group IDs differ.
condition: only when an interactive shell is invoked
exception: ENV is ignored when the real and effective user or group IDs differ

statement: Assignments to PWD may be ignored, and if an application sets or unsets the value of PWD the behaviors of the cd and pwd utilities become unspecified.
condition: when an application sets or unsets PWD

statement: The order of word expansion is: first tilde expansion, parameter expansion, command substitution, and arithmetic expansion (from beginning to end); then field splitting (unless IFS is null); then pathname expansion (unless set -f is in effect); and quote removal is always performed last.
Only field splitting or pathname expansion can create multiple fields from a single word; all other expansions within a single word expand to a single field.
exception: the expansion of the @ special parameter within double-quotes is the single exception

statement: If the complete expansion of a word results in an empty field, that empty field is deleted from the list of fields forming the expanded command.
exception: the empty field is retained when the original word contained single-quote or double-quote characters

statement: When an unquoted dollar-sign is followed by a character that is not a numeric character, a special-parameter name, a valid first character of a variable name, a left-curly-bracket, or a left-parenthesis, the result is unspecified.
condition: when an unquoted dollar-sign precedes a character outside the enumerated set

statement: A tilde-prefix is an unquoted tilde at the start of a word followed by the characters up to the first unquoted slash; if the tilde-prefix is just the tilde, it is replaced by the value of HOME, and if HOME is unset the results are unspecified.
condition: when the tilde-prefix contains only the tilde (null login name)
exception: if HOME is unset the result is unspecified

statement: The pathname resulting from tilde expansion is treated as if quoted, which prevents it from being altered by field splitting and pathname expansion.

In a ${expression} parameter expansion the expression runs until the matching close brace, and a close brace that is escaped by a backslash, is inside a quoted string, or belongs to an embedded arithmetic expansion, command substitution, or variable expansion is not counted when finding the match.

Braces around the parameter name are optional except for positional parameters with more than one digit or when the parameter is a name followed by a character that could be interpreted as part of the name; an unbraced name uses the longest valid name whether or not that variable exists.
condition: when a multi-digit positional parameter is used or a name is followed by a name-like character

statement: When a parameter expansion occurs inside double-quotes, neither pathname expansion nor field splitting is performed on the results of the expansion.
condition: when the parameter expansion occurs inside double-quotes

statement: The ${parameter:-word} Use Default form substitutes the expansion of word (or an empty string if word is omitted) when parameter is unset or null, and otherwise substitutes the value of parameter.
condition: when parameter is unset or null

statement: The ${parameter:=word} Assign Default form assigns the expansion of word to parameter when parameter is unset or null and then substitutes the final value; only variables, not positional or special parameters, can be assigned this way.
condition: when parameter is unset or null
exception: positional parameters and special parameters cannot be assigned with this form

statement: The ${parameter:?word} form, when parameter is unset or null, writes the expansion of word (or a default not-set message) to standard error and the shell exits with a non-zero status; otherwise it substitutes the value of parameter.
condition: when parameter is unset or null
exception: an interactive shell need not exit

statement: The ${parameter:+word} Use Alternative form substitutes null when parameter is unset or null, and otherwise substitutes the expansion of word.
condition: when parameter is unset or null

statement: In the default/assign/error/alternative parameter expansions, including the colon tests for a parameter that is unset or null, while omitting the colon tests only for a parameter that is unset (a set-but-null parameter passes the no-colon test).

The ${#parameter} form substitutes the length in characters of the value of parameter; if parameter is * or @ the result is unspecified, and if parameter is unset while set -u is in effect the expansion fails.
exception: the result is unspecified when parameter is * or @, and the expansion fails when parameter is unset under set -u

statement: The prefix/suffix removal parameter expansions match with shell pattern-matching notation rather than regular expressions; enclosing the whole expansion in double-quotes does not quote the pattern characters, whereas quoting characters within the braces does, and if parameter is #, *, or @ the result is unspecified.
exception: the result is unspecified when parameter is #, *, or @

statement: The pattern-removal parameter expansions delete a matched substring: ${parameter%word} removes the smallest matching suffix and ${parameter%%word} the largest suffix, while ${parameter#word} removes the smallest matching prefix and ${parameter##word} the largest prefix.

Command substitution runs the enclosed command in a subshell environment and replaces the substitution with the command's standard output, removing one or more trailing newlines; newlines embedded before the end are not removed but may be treated as field delimiters during field splitting depending on IFS and quoting.
If the output captured by a command substitution contains any null bytes, the behavior is unspecified.
condition: when the command output contains null bytes

statement: In backquoted command substitution the backslash keeps its literal meaning except before a dollar-sign, backquote, or backslash; the matching backquote is the first unquoted non-escaped one, an unescaped backquote inside a comment, here-document, embedded $() substitution, or quoted string gives undefined results, and nesting requires escaping the inner backquotes, so the $(command) form is preferable.
In the $(command) form, every character from the open parenthesis to the matching close parenthesis makes up the command, and a command consisting solely of redirections produces unspecified results.
exception: a substituted command that is only redirections yields unspecified results

statement: The results of a command substitution are not processed for further tilde expansion, parameter expansion, command substitution, or arithmetic expansion, and when the substitution is inside double-quotes neither field splitting nor pathname expansion is performed on its results.
condition: the no-field-split/no-pathname behavior applies when the substitution is inside double-quotes

statement: When an expansion begins with the two-character sequence dollar-paren-paren, arithmetic expansion takes precedence over a command substitution that starts with a subshell, so a conforming application must separate the dollar-paren and the inner open-paren with white space when writing a command substitution whose command is a subshell.
condition: when writing a command substitution whose command begins with a subshell

statement: Arithmetic expansion $((expression)) treats the expression as if double-quoted (except an inner double-quote is not special), expands its tokens for parameter expansion, command substitution, and quote removal, and then evaluates the result as an arithmetic expression and substitutes its value.

POSIX only requires arithmetic expansion to support signed long integer arithmetic and decimal, octal, and hexadecimal constants; the sizeof operator, prefix and postfix ++ and --, and selection/iteration/jump statements are not required, so portable scripts must not depend on them.

If an arithmetic expression is invalid, or a shell variable used in it holds contents the shell does not recognize as a valid integer, the arithmetic expansion fails and the shell writes a diagnostic message to standard error.
condition: when the expression is invalid or a used variable is not a recognized integer
