statement: Field splitting scans only the results of parameter expansion, command substitution, and arithmetic expansion that did not occur inside double-quotes, treating each character of IFS as a delimiter, and can turn one expansion into multiple fields.
exception: results that occurred inside double-quotes are not subject to field splitting

statement: Field splitting depends on IFS: when IFS is space/tab/newline or unset, leading and trailing runs of those characters are ignored and interior runs delimit fields; when IFS is null no field splitting is performed; otherwise IFS white space is ignored at the ends, and each non-white-space IFS character (with any adjacent IFS white space) or a run of IFS white space delimits a field.
exception: when IFS is set to a null string, no field splitting occurs

statement: After field splitting, unless set -f is in effect, each field on the command line is subjected to pathname expansion using pattern-matching notation qualified by the filename-expansion rules.
exception: pathname expansion is skipped when set -f is in effect

statement: Quote removal removes the backslash, single-quote, and double-quote characters that were present in the original word, unless those quote characters were themselves quoted.
exception: quote characters that were themselves quoted are not removed

statement: In a redirection of the form [n]redir-op word the optional file-descriptor number n must be delimited from any preceding text and immediately precede the operator; if n is quoted it is not recognized as part of the redirection, and if any part of the redirection operator is quoted no redirection is recognized at all.
exception: quoting the number or any part of the operator disables recognition of the redirection

statement: File descriptors are decimal numbers starting at zero; all implementations must support at least descriptors 0 through 9 for application use, and the values 0, 1, and 2 have the conventional meanings standard input, standard output, and standard error.

For the << and <<- here-document operators the following word undergoes only quote removal (other expansions are unspecified), while for other redirection operators the word undergoes tilde, parameter, command, and arithmetic expansion plus quote removal; pathname expansion is not performed on the word by a non-interactive shell, and an interactive shell may perform it only when it yields a single word.
When more than one redirection operator is specified with a command, the redirections are evaluated in order from beginning to end.
A failure to open or create a file causes the redirection to fail.

Output redirection with the > operator fails if the noclobber option (set -C) is set and the target is an existing regular file; otherwise the > and >| operators create the file if absent or truncate it to empty if it exists, and >| overrides noclobber.
condition: when the noclobber option is set and the file exists as a regular file
exception: the >| form overrides noclobber

statement: Appending output redirection [n]>>word opens the file as if with the O_APPEND flag and creates the file if it does not exist.

A here-document is treated as a single word beginning after the next newline and continuing until a line containing only the delimiter with no blank characters; it is unspecified whether the descriptor is a regular file, special file, or pipe, so portable applications cannot rely on it being seekable.

If any part of the here-document delimiter word is quoted, the delimiter is formed by quote removal and the here-document lines are not expanded; if no part is quoted, all lines are expanded for parameter expansion, command substitution, and arithmetic expansion, with the backslash behaving as it does inside double-quotes.
condition: expansion of here-document lines depends on whether any part of the delimiter word is quoted
exception: quoting any part of the delimiter word suppresses expansion of the here-document body

statement: The <<- here-document operator strips all leading tab characters from the input lines and from the line containing the trailing delimiter.

The [n]<&word and [n]>&word operators duplicate or close a file descriptor: if word is one or more digits the descriptor is made a copy of the one named by word, if word is '-' the descriptor is closed, digits that do not denote an already-open descriptor cause a redirection error, closing a descriptor that is not open is not an error, and any other word value gives unspecified behavior.
exception: any word value other than digits or '-' produces unspecified behavior

statement: An expansion error, variable assignment error, shell syntax error, special built-in utility error, or redirection error with a special built-in causes a non-interactive shell to exit while an interactive shell shall not exit; a command-not-found or a redirection error with a compound command or function may cause the shell to exit.
exception: an interactive shell does not exit on these errors

statement: An error in a special built-in utility causes a non-interactive shell to exit, whereas an error in an ordinary utility that is not a special built-in does not cause the shell to exit.

If a shall-exit or may-exit error occurs in a subshell environment, the shell exits (respectively may exit) from that subshell with a non-zero status and continues in the environment from which the subshell was invoked.
condition: when the error occurs in a subshell environment

statement: The exit status is 127 when a command is not found, 126 when the command name is found but is not an executable utility, and between 1 and 125 inclusive when a command fails during word expansion or redirection.

When reporting exit status through the special parameter ?, the shell reports the full eight bits of exit status, and a command that terminated because it received a signal is reported with a status greater than 128; unless otherwise stated, a command's exit status is that of the last simple command it executed.
A simple command is a sequence of optional variable assignments and redirections in any order, optionally followed by words and redirections, terminated by a control operator.

When a simple command is executed the shell performs, from beginning to end: saving the words recognized as variable assignments or redirections, expanding the remaining words (the first resulting field is the command name and the rest are arguments), performing the redirections, and expanding each variable assignment (tilde, parameter, command, arithmetic expansion, and quote removal) before assigning its value.

The order of performing redirections and performing variable assignments in a simple command may be reversed when no command name results from expansion or when the command name matches a special built-in utility.
condition: when no command name results or the command name is a special built-in utility

statement: If a simple command produces no command name, its variable assignments affect the current execution environment; if the command name is an ordinary utility (not a special built-in or function), the assignments are exported only for that command's execution environment and do not affect the current environment.

When the command name of a simple command is a special built-in utility, its variable assignments affect the current execution environment (they persist), unlike assignments prefixed to an ordinary command.
condition: when the command name is a special built-in utility

statement: When the command name is a function (not a standard utility implemented as a function), prefixed variable assignments affect the current execution environment during the function's execution, but whether the assignments and any gained export attribute persist after the function completes is unspecified.
condition: when the command name is a shell function

statement: If a variable assignment attempts to assign to a variable that has the readonly attribute set in the current shell environment, a variable assignment error occurs.
condition: when the target variable is readonly

statement: When a simple command has no command name, its redirections are performed in a subshell environment (so to affect the current environment the exec special built-in is required), and if a redirection performed in the current shell environment fails the command fails immediately with a non-zero exit status and a diagnostic message.
condition: when the simple command has no command name

statement: A simple command with no command name completes with the exit status of the last command substitution it performed, or with a zero exit status if it contained no command substitution.
condition: when the simple command has no command name

statement: When a command name contains no slash, the shell resolves it by the first successful step in this order: a special built-in utility, then a function known to the shell, then a specified set of regular built-in utilities (such as cd, read, umask, command), then a PATH search.
condition: when the command name contains no slash character

statement: If a command name matches one of an enumerated set of common non-standard built-in names (such as declare, local, source, typeset, let, pushd, popd, mapfile), the results are unspecified, so portable scripts cannot rely on those names.
condition: when the command name matches one of the listed non-standard built-in names

statement: Once a utility has been found through a PATH search, the implementation may remember its location and need not search again unless PATH is assigned to, and if the remembered location later fails the shell repeats the search.
exception: the search is repeated when PATH is assigned or the remembered location fails

statement: If a command name contains at least one slash, the shell executes the named file directly in a separate utility environment rather than performing a PATH search.
condition: when the command name contains at least one slash

statement: If executing a command fails with an ENOEXEC-equivalent error, the shell re-executes the file as a shell script by invoking a shell with that pathname as the first operand; if the executable is not a text file the shell may bypass this, write an error message, and return exit status 126.
condition: when execution fails with an ENOEXEC-equivalent error

statement: If a standard utility or conforming application is executed with file descriptor 0 not open for reading or with file descriptor 1 or 2 not open for writing, the execution environment is deemed non-conforming and the utility might not behave as the standard describes.
condition: when standard input is not open for reading or standard output/error is not open for writing

statement: A pipeline connects the standard output of each command except the last to the standard input of the next command through a pipe.

When a pipeline begins with the reserved word ! and the first command is a subshell, the application must separate the opening parenthesis from the ! with one or more blanks, because ! immediately followed by ( has unspecified behavior.
condition: when a negated pipeline's first command begins with a subshell parenthesis

statement: A pipeline assigns a command's standard input and standard output before any redirection operators that are part of that command are applied, so explicit redirections override the pipe connections.

The exit status of a pipeline is the exit status of its last command, unless the pipeline begins with the reserved word !, in which case the status is the logical NOT of the last command's status (zero becomes 1 and non-zero becomes 0).
exception: the ! reserved word inverts the last command's status

statement: The operators && and || have equal precedence and are evaluated with left associativity, so an AND-OR list is evaluated strictly left to right rather than giving && higher precedence.

A semicolon separator or terminator (or a newline) causes the preceding AND-OR list to be executed sequentially, while an ampersand separator or terminator causes the preceding AND-OR list to be executed asynchronously.
A command terminated by an ampersand is executed asynchronously in a subshell and the shell does not wait for it to finish before executing the next command.

When job control is disabled, the standard input of an asynchronous list is assigned (before any explicit redirections) to a file with the same properties as /dev/null; this does not happen when job control is enabled, and an explicit redirection of standard input always overrides it.
condition: when job control is disabled (set -m off)
exception: an explicit standard-input redirection overrides this behavior, and it does not happen when job control is enabled

statement: When an asynchronous list element starts, the process ID of its last command becomes known in the current shell environment (available through $!), and it remains known until the application waits for it or until another asynchronous list is invoked before $! is expanded.
The exit status of an asynchronous list is zero regardless of the outcome of the backgrounded command.

In an AND list joined by &&, each subsequent command is executed only if the previous command's exit status is zero, execution stops at the first non-zero status, commands are expanded only if they are executed, and the list's exit status is that of the last command executed.

In an OR list joined by ||, each subsequent command is executed only if the previous command's exit status is non-zero, execution stops at the first zero status, and the list's exit status is that of the last command executed.

A compound command may be followed by redirections on the same line as its terminator, and each such redirection applies to all commands within the compound command that do not explicitly override it.
exception: an inner command that specifies its own redirection overrides the compound redirection

statement: A grouping command written as ( compound-list ) executes the list in a subshell environment, so variable assignments and built-in commands that affect the environment do not remain in effect after the list finishes.

A conforming application must separate the two leading parentheses of a subshell grouping command with white space, because a shell that implements the ((expression)) arithmetic-evaluation extension may otherwise treat the doubled parenthesis as arithmetic evaluation rather than a grouping command.
condition: when a grouping command begins with two adjacent open parentheses

statement: A brace group written as { compound-list; } executes the list in the current process environment rather than a subshell, and the closing brace is a reserved word that must be preceded by a control operator such as a semicolon or newline.

A for loop expands the words after in to a list of items, sets the named variable to each item in turn and runs the body each time, does not run the body at all if the expansion yields no items, and treats an omitted in word... as equivalent to in "$@"; its exit status is that of the last command executed, or zero if there were no items.
exception: omitting the in word... clause defaults the item list to the positional parameters "$@"

statement: A case construct expands the word (tilde, parameter, command, arithmetic expansion, and quote removal) and executes the compound-list of the first pattern that matches using pattern-matching notation; once the first match is found no further patterns are expanded, patterns sharing an action are delimited by |, each action is terminated by ;; (optional for the last), and the exit status is zero if nothing matched otherwise the last command executed.

An if construct executes the if compound-list and runs the then list when its status is zero; otherwise it runs each elif list in turn, running that elif's then list on a zero status, and finally the else list if none succeeded; its exit status is that of the then or else list actually executed, or zero if none was.
A while loop repeatedly executes its body as long as the condition compound-list has a zero exit status, and its exit status is that of the last body execution, or zero if the body never ran.
An until loop repeatedly executes its body as long as the condition compound-list has a non-zero exit status, and its exit status is that of the last body execution, or zero if the body never ran.

A function is defined with the form fname ( ) compound-command [redirections]; the application must ensure fname is a valid name and is not the name of a special built-in utility, and the implementation maintains separate name spaces for functions and variables.

No word expansions are performed on a function's compound-command or redirections at the time it is declared; the expansions, redirections, and any inner variable assignments are performed anew each time the function is called.

When a function is called its operands temporarily become the positional parameters and the special parameter # is updated to their count while the special parameter 0 is unchanged; on completion the positional parameters and # are restored, and executing the return special built-in inside the function ends it and resumes execution after the call, with the invocation's exit status being that of the last command executed.
The word expansion rules are applied to WORD tokens immediately before the associated command is executed, not at the time the command is parsed.

Because quotation-mark characters are still retained in the token when reserved-word recognition happens, a quoted string can never be recognized as a reserved word, and reserved words are recognized only in certain input positions such as after a newline or semicolon.

A word preceding the command name is treated as a variable assignment (ASSIGNMENT_WORD) only when all characters before the first unquoted equals-sign form a valid name; if the token begins with an equals-sign it is not treated as an assignment.
condition: when the characters before the first unquoted equals-sign form a valid name
exception: a token beginning with an equals-sign is not an assignment word

statement: When job control is disabled and the shell executes an asynchronous list, the commands in that list inherit a signal action of ignored (SIG_IGN) for SIGINT and SIGQUIT; in all other cases commands inherit the shell's own signal actions unless changed by the trap special built-in.
condition: when job control is disabled and the command is part of an asynchronous list

statement: A trap set for a signal that is received while the shell is waiting for a foreground command to complete is not executed until after that foreground command has completed.
condition: when the signal arrives while the shell waits for a foreground command

statement: When the shell is waiting via the wait utility for asynchronous commands, receiving a signal for which a trap is set makes wait return immediately with an exit status greater than 128, after which the trap for that signal is taken.
condition: when the shell is waiting on asynchronous commands via the wait utility

statement: If multiple signals that have associated trap actions are pending for the shell, the order in which those trap actions are executed is unspecified.
condition: when multiple trapped signals are pending simultaneously

statement: A shell execution environment comprises its open files, the working directory, the file-creation mask, current traps, shell parameters (variables), shell functions, options, the process IDs of the last commands of known asynchronous lists, and shell aliases.

A utility that is not a special built-in is invoked in a separate environment initialized from the parent shell, into which only variables that have the export attribute (plus those explicitly exported for the command) are passed as environment variables.

When the invoked utility is a shell script, traps caught by the shell are reset to their default values for the utility and traps ignored by the shell remain ignored; when the utility is not a shell script, the shell's trap actions are mapped into the corresponding signal-handling actions for the utility.
A utility does not change the environment of the shell process unless the utility's own description explicitly specifies it (as cd and umask do).
exception: utilities such as cd and umask are documented to change the shell environment

statement: A subshell environment is created as a duplicate of the shell environment except that signal traps not being ignored are reset to their default action, and changes made in the subshell environment do not affect the parent shell environment.
exception: traps that are being ignored are not reset in the subshell

statement: Command substitutions, commands grouped with parentheses, and asynchronous lists are executed in a subshell environment, and each command of a multi-command pipeline is also in a subshell environment (although as an extension an implementation may run any or all pipeline commands in the current environment).
exception: as an extension, some or all commands of a pipeline may run in the current environment

statement: Shell pattern-matching notation is related to but different from regular-expression notation, so glob patterns must not be treated as regular expressions.

In a pattern, a backslash escapes the following character and the escaping backslash is discarded; if a pattern ends with an unescaped backslash, it is unspecified whether the pattern matches nothing or is treated as invalid.
exception: a pattern ending in an unescaped backslash has unspecified behavior

statement: Pattern matching is based on the bit pattern used to encode a character rather than its graphic representation; any quoted character matches itself, and the shell special characters always require quoting to be matched literally.

When unquoted and outside a bracket expression, a question-mark matches any single character, an asterisk matches any string including the null string, and an open bracket introduces a pattern bracket expression.
condition: when the character is unquoted and outside a bracket expression

statement: In a shell pattern bracket expression the exclamation-mark replaces the circumflex used in regular expressions to introduce a non-matching list, and a bracket expression that starts with an unquoted circumflex produces unspecified results.
exception: a bracket expression starting with an unquoted circumflex is unspecified

statement: Where pattern matching is used without shell quote removal (such as find's -name primary invoked via exec, or the fnmatch pattern argument), special characters are escaped by preceding them with a backslash (which is discarded), and a doubled backslash represents one literal backslash.
condition: when pattern matching is performed in a context where shell quote removal does not occur

statement: An asterisk in a pattern is greedy: it matches a string of zero or more characters, matching the greatest possible number of characters that still allows the remainder of the pattern to match.

During filename expansion, a slash in a pathname must be matched explicitly by a slash in the pattern and is never matched by an asterisk, a question-mark, or a bracket expression, and a slash cannot appear inside a pattern bracket expression, so filename patterns do not match across directory separators.
condition: when pattern matching is used for filename expansion

statement: During filename expansion, a leading period in a filename must be matched explicitly by a period as the first character of the pattern or immediately after a slash; it is not matched by an asterisk, a question-mark, or a bracket expression containing a non-matching list, range, or character class.
condition: when pattern matching is used for filename expansion

statement: Filename-expansion patterns are matched against existing filenames: each pathname component containing a pattern character requires read permission on its directory, each non-pattern component except the last requires search permission, and the resulting matches are sorted according to the collating sequence of the current locale.
condition: when pattern matching is used for filename expansion

statement: If a filename-expansion pattern does not match any existing filename or pathname, the pattern string is left unchanged rather than removed or replaced.
condition: when a filename-expansion pattern matches no existing files

statement: An error in a special built-in utility may cause a shell executing it to abort, whereas an error in a regular built-in does not; if the shell does not abort on a special built-in error, that built-in's exit value is non-zero.
The special built-in utilities need not be provided in a form accessible through the exec family of functions.

For special built-ins that do not conform to the Utility Syntax Guidelines, the requirement to recognize and discard a leading -- argument does not apply, and a conforming application must not pass -- to them.
condition: for special built-ins that do not conform to the Utility Syntax Guidelines

statement: The break utility exits from the nth enclosing for, while, or until loop (defaulting to n=1), after which execution continues with the command following the exited loop; if n exceeds the number of enclosing loops the outermost loop is exited, and if there is no enclosing loop the behavior is unspecified.
exception: with no enclosing loop the behavior is unspecified

statement: A loop lexically encloses a break or continue command only if the command runs in the same execution environment as the loop's do-group and is contained in a compound-list associated with the loop and is not in the body of a function defined within the loop, so break and continue driven from a function, a dot-script, or a trap can produce unspecified behavior.
exception: a break or continue in a function body, sourced script, or trap may not be lexically enclosed by the loop

statement: The colon (:) null utility only expands its arguments and performs no action, returning a zero exit status; because it is a special built-in, variable assignments prefixed to it persist and any redirections associated with it are still performed.

The continue utility returns to the top of the nth enclosing for, while, or until loop (defaulting to n=1), re-testing a while or until condition or performing a for loop's next assignment; if n exceeds the number of enclosing loops the outermost loop is used, and with no enclosing loop the behavior is unspecified.
exception: with no enclosing loop the behavior is unspecified

statement: The dot utility executes the commands from the given file in the current shell environment rather than in a subshell.

If the dot utility's file contains no slash, the shell searches PATH to find it, but unlike normal command search the file need not be executable; if no readable file is found a non-interactive shell aborts while an interactive shell writes a diagnostic (not treated as a syntax error), and the exit status is non-zero on no-readable-file or parse failure, otherwise the last command's value or zero.
condition: when the file operand contains no slash

statement: The dot utility does not search the current directory for its file unless the value of PATH permits it, a deliberate choice to avoid the trojan-horse susceptibility that leaving the current directory out of PATH is meant to prevent.

The eval utility constructs a command by concatenating its arguments separated by single spaces, and the shell then reads and executes that constructed command, giving the text a second round of shell parsing and expansion.

The eval utility returns a zero exit status when there are no arguments or only null arguments; otherwise it returns the exit status of the command defined by the concatenated arguments, or non-zero if that concatenation could not be parsed as a command and the shell is interactive.

Because eval is not required to recognize the -- end-of-options delimiter, when its arguments might begin with a hyphen the first argument should be prefixed with a harmless string such as a leading space so the intended commands are not misread as options.
condition: when eval arguments might begin with a hyphen

statement: When exec is given no command, it performs the redirections in the current shell execution environment, opening, closing, or copying file descriptors that then persist for the rest of the shell.
condition: when exec is invoked without a command

statement: When exec is given a command, it replaces the shell with that command without creating a new process, so it does not return to the shell; if the command is not found the exit status is 127, if found but not executable it is 126, and a redirection error makes the shell exit with a value in the range 1 to 125.
condition: when exec is invoked with a command

statement: When exec is used with no command to open file descriptors greater than 2 through redirections, it is unspecified whether those descriptors remain open when the shell later invokes another utility, so a script concerned about child shells misusing them should close them explicitly.
condition: when file descriptors above 2 are opened via exec redirections

statement: The exit utility causes the shell to leave its current execution environment with the specified status; in a subshell it exits only the subshell and execution continues in the invoking environment, and if n is not an unsigned decimal integer between 0 and 255 the exit status is undefined.
exception: in a subshell environment exit leaves only the subshell

statement: A trap set on EXIT is executed before the shell terminates, except when the exit utility is invoked inside that EXIT trap itself, in which case the shell exits immediately.
exception: when exit is called from within the EXIT trap the shell exits immediately without re-running it

statement: When exit is given no operand, the exit status is the exit value of the last command executed (or zero if none was executed), and when exit runs inside a trap action the last command is considered to be the one that executed immediately before the trap action.
An exit status value larger than 255 might be truncated by the shell and be unavailable even to a parent process that uses waitid to retrieve the full exit value.
condition: when an exit value greater than 255 is used

statement: The export special built-in gives the export attribute to the named variables so they appear in the environment of subsequently executed commands, and a name followed by =word also sets that variable's value.

The export -p option writes all exported variables to standard output in a form suitable for re-input to the shell to reproduce the same exports, whereas invoking export with no arguments gives unspecified results.
exception: export with no arguments is unspecified

statement: Combining an assignment with export as in export X=$(command) leaves $? at zero because export itself succeeded (setting X to the command's output), and execution continues even under set -e, so to detect a command-substitution failure the assignment must be separated from the export.
condition: when a command substitution is combined with export in a single command

statement: The readonly special built-in gives the readonly attribute to the named variables so their values cannot be changed by subsequent assignment and they cannot be unset, and a name followed by =word also sets the value.
The readonly -p option writes all read-only variables in a form suitable for re-input to the shell, whereas invoking readonly with no arguments gives unspecified results.
exception: readonly with no arguments is unspecified

statement: The standard allows but does not require the readonly attribute to persist across separate shell invocations, and functions are deliberately never read-only across invocations to preclude spoofing of security-relevant shell scripts.
The return utility stops execution of the current function or dot script, and if the shell is not currently executing a function or dot script the results are unspecified.
exception: invoking return outside a function or dot script is unspecified

statement: The return utility sets the special parameter ? to n or, if n is omitted, to the exit status of the last command executed; if n is not an unsigned decimal integer or is greater than 255 the results are unspecified, and inside a trap action the last command is the one that executed immediately before the trap.

With no options or arguments, set writes the names and values of all shell variables, one per line in the current locale's collation order, quoted so the output is suitable for re-input to the shell, though read-only variables cannot be reset.

set options are enabled with a leading hyphen-minus and disabled with a leading plus-sign, all options default to off unless stated otherwise or set at invocation, and setting shell attributes and setting positional parameters are independent actions that may be combined in one invocation.

Under set -a (allexport) every variable that is assigned gains the export attribute; an assignment preceding an ordinary utility does not persist that attribute after the utility completes, an assignment preceding a special built-in does persist, and an assignment not preceding a utility (or made by getopts or read) persists until the variable is unset.
condition: when set -a is in effect
exception: an assignment preceding an ordinary utility does not persist the export attribute after that utility

statement: Under set -e (errexit) the shell exits immediately when a command fails, but with exceptions: the failure of an individual command within a multi-command pipeline does not trigger it (only the pipeline's own failure does), -e is ignored while executing the condition list of while/until/if/elif, a pipeline beginning with !, or any non-final command of an AND-OR list, and it does not apply to a non-subshell compound command whose failure happened while -e was being ignored.
condition: when set -e is in effect
exception: -e is ignored in condition lists, negated pipelines, and non-final AND-OR commands, and individual pipeline-member failures do not trigger it

statement: Because set -e is ignored whenever a command is a non-final element of an AND-OR list, calling a function as in start || handle_error suppresses -e throughout the function body, so a failing command inside the function does not stop it and the function's exit status can still be zero; application writers should therefore avoid relying on set -e inside functions.
condition: when a function is invoked as a non-final command of an AND-OR list under set -e

statement: Under set -n (noexec) the shell reads commands but does not execute them, which is used to check a script for syntax errors, though an interactive shell may ignore this option.
condition: when set -n is in effect
exception: an interactive shell may ignore -n

statement: set -C (noclobber) prevents the > redirection operator from overwriting an existing file (the >| operator overrides it for an individual file), and set -f (noglob) disables pathname expansion.

Under set -x (xtrace) the shell writes a trace of each command to standard error after expanding it and before executing it, and it is unspecified whether the command that turns tracing off is itself traced.
condition: when set -x is in effect

statement: Under set -u (nounset) the shell writes a message to standard error and fails the expansion when it tries to expand an unset parameter, except that this deliberately does not apply to the @ and * special parameters so that scripts using them with no arguments are not treated as errors.
condition: when set -u is in effect and an unset parameter is expanded
exception: the @ and * special parameters are exempt from -u

statement: set -v causes the shell to write its input to standard error as it is read, set -h locates and remembers the utilities invoked by a function at the time the function is defined rather than when it runs, and set -m (monitor) runs jobs in their own process groups and reports their status and is enabled by default for interactive shells.

set -o with no option-argument writes the current option settings in an unspecified format, whereas set +o writes them in a format suitable for re-input to the shell to restore the same option settings.

The set -o long option names include allexport, errexit, monitor, noclobber, noglob, noexec, notify, nounset, verbose, and xtrace (each equivalent to a single-letter option), plus ignoreeof (prevent an interactive shell exiting on end-of-file so the user must exit explicitly), nolog (keep function definitions out of the command history), and vi (enable vi command-line editing).

When set is given arguments, all existing positional parameters are unset before the new arguments are assigned to positional parameters in order, and the special parameter # is updated to the new count.
If the first argument to set is a lone hyphen, the results are unspecified.
condition: when the first argument to set is '-'

statement: The special argument -- immediately after set delimits the arguments when the first would begin with a plus or hyphen and prevents an inadvertent listing of all variables when there are no arguments; set -- with no further arguments unsets all positional parameters and sets the special parameter # to zero.

The shift utility shifts the positional parameters so that parameter 1 takes the value of parameter (1+n) and so on, unsets the highest n parameters, and updates the special parameter #; n must be an unsigned decimal integer no greater than the current number of positional parameters, defaults to 1, and if n is 0 the parameters are left unchanged.
exception: an n of 0 leaves the positional parameters unchanged

statement: If the shift operand n is invalid or greater than the number of positional parameters, this may be treated as a syntax error and a non-interactive shell may exit; if the shell does not exit, a non-zero exit status is returned.
condition: when the shift operand is invalid or exceeds the number of positional parameters

statement: The times utility writes the accumulated user and system CPU times for the shell and for all of its child processes, and is a special built-in required of all conforming shells.

If the first operand of trap is an unsigned decimal integer, the shell treats all operands as conditions and resets each to its default; otherwise the first operand is the action and the remaining operands are conditions.

In trap, an action of '-' resets each condition to its default, an action that is the null string makes the shell ignore each condition when it arises, and any other action is read and executed when a condition arises; a new trap overrides the previous action, and after the trap action completes the special parameter ? is restored to the value it had before trap was invoked.

A trap condition may be EXIT, 0 (equivalent to EXIT), or a signal given by its symbolic name without the SIG prefix (such as HUP, INT, QUIT, TERM), and setting a trap for SIGKILL or SIGSTOP produces undefined results.
exception: setting a trap on SIGKILL or SIGSTOP is undefined

statement: The environment in which the shell executes a trap on EXIT is identical to the environment immediately after the last command executed before the EXIT trap was taken.
Each time trap is invoked, its action argument is processed in a manner equivalent to eval action, so the action text is re-parsed and expanded when the trap fires rather than when it is set.

Signals that were ignored on entry to a non-interactive shell cannot be trapped or reset (though no error need be reported for the attempt), whereas an interactive shell may reset or catch signals ignored on entry, and traps remain in place until explicitly changed by another trap command.
condition: for signals ignored on entry to a non-interactive shell
exception: an interactive shell may reset or catch signals ignored on entry

statement: On entering a subshell, traps that are not being ignored are reset to their default actions (except that a command substitution containing only a single trap command need not alter them), but the trap command can still be used within the subshell to set new traps.
condition: when a subshell environment is entered
exception: a command substitution containing only a single trap command need not have its traps reset

statement: The trap command with no operands writes to standard output the commands associated with each condition, formatted with quoting so the output is suitable for re-input to the shell, which allows saving and restoring traps with an idiom such as saving the output of trap and later re-evaluating it.

Only XSI-conformant systems are required to also accept numeric signal numbers as trap conditions (1 for SIGHUP, 2 for SIGINT, 3 for SIGQUIT, 6 for SIGABRT, 9 for SIGKILL, 14 for SIGALRM, 15 for SIGTERM), so portable scripts should use symbolic signal names instead of numbers.
condition: numeric signal numbers as trap conditions are guaranteed only on XSI-conformant systems

statement: The trap utility returns a non-zero exit status when a signal name or number is invalid and zero otherwise, but for both interactive and non-interactive shells an invalid signal name or number is not considered a syntax error and does not cause the shell to abort.

The trap and kill utilities consistently omit the SIG prefix from signal names, and although an implementation may permit the SIG prefix or lowercase names as an extension, no known historical shell accepts the SIG prefix, so portable scripts should use bare uppercase signal names.

For a trap action that must run the contents of a variable, trap 'eval " $cmd"' condition executes cmd when the trap fires, whereas trap '$cmd' condition fails if cmd contains special characters such as quoting or redirections, and trap " $cmd" condition works but expands cmd when the trap command is set rather than when the action later runs.
condition: when a trap action needs to execute the contents of a shell variable

statement: The ERR trap, which fires whenever set -e would cause an exit, is a KornShell extension that the standard allows but does not mandate, so portable scripts cannot rely on it.

The unset utility removes named variables or functions: with -v it unsets a variable and removes it from the environment (read-only variables cannot be unset), and with -f it unsets a function definition.
exception: read-only variables cannot be unset

statement: When unset is given neither -f nor -v, the name refers to a variable, and if no variable by that name exists it is unspecified whether a function of that name is unset, so a portable script must use unset -f to unset a function.
condition: when unset is invoked without -f or -v

statement: Unsetting a variable or function that was not previously set is not considered an error and does not cause the shell to abort.
Assigning VARIABLE= is not equivalent to unsetting the variable because it sets the variable to an empty string, and the special parameters are not among the variables that unset can remove.
Treat a standard command synopsis as program name plus optional options and arguments, where bracketed items are optional and italic placeholders must be replaced with real values.
condition: When reading or explaining command syntax from this guide.

statement: Use a lone dash as a conventional filename to mean standard input for input positions or standard output for output positions only for commands that support that convention.
condition: When a command documents support for single-dash file operands.

statement: Use a double dash before path operands that begin with a dash so later tokens are treated as filenames rather than options.
condition: When a command supports the end-of-options marker and a filename could be parsed as an option.

statement: If a command lacks double-dash support, prefix a leading-dash filename with a path such as ./ to stop the dash from being the first character.
condition: When working with a leading-dash filename and the command does not support --.

statement: Use --help or --version only for commands that advertise those options; they print usage or version information and then exit.
condition: When a command supports these common options.

statement: Do not include the displayed shell prompt or command output when copying an example command; type only the command text intended for the user.
condition: When transcribing examples from command-line documentation.

statement: A trailing backslash may be used to continue a long shell command on the next physical line.
condition: When entering a long command in an interactive shell or script.

statement: The echo command is useful for demonstrating shell expansion because the shell processes variables and other substitutions before echo prints its arguments.
condition: When explaining or testing shell expansion behavior.

statement: Use curl with -O followed by an archive URL and then extract the archive with tar -xf to download and unpack the guide practice files.
condition: When setting up the Linux Pocket Guide practice files.

statement: Use the provided reset script rather than manual edits to restore the guide practice files, unless the files were obtained through git and should be reset through git instead.
condition: When restoring the book practice tree.
exception: If the practice files were cloned with git and the intent is to restore repository state.

statement: A Linux system can usually be approached through a shell program, and command-line work depends on distinguishing the shell from the terminal window that hosts it.
condition: When orienting a user in a graphical Linux environment.

statement: The core command-line material in the guide is intended to apply across Linux distributions even though distributions vary in included programs, files, and defaults.
Parse a Linux command as a program name followed by options and arguments, and explain each part separately when troubleshooting usage.
condition: When analyzing a simple shell command.

statement: Do not assume short options are globally standardized; the same flag can mean different things in different programs.
Prefer consulting a command-specific help source before transferring an option meaning from another command.
condition: When an option is unfamiliar or overloaded across commands.

statement: Combined short options are convenient but not universal, so expand them into separate options when a program rejects the grouped form.
condition: When a command does not accept combined short flags.

statement: Treat arguments as command-specific operands that may be filenames, directories, users, hosts, IP addresses, regular expressions, or arbitrary strings rather than assuming they are always filenames.
Use pipelines to connect the standard output of one command to the standard input of another command for composable processing.
condition: When a task can be decomposed into producer and consumer commands.

statement: Use sudo only for commands that require administrative privileges, because it grants superuser authority and can damage the system.
condition: When an operation is blocked by permissions or modifies protected system state.

statement: Expect sudo to prompt for a password in some cases before running the protected command.
Track the shell current directory because relative paths are resolved from that directory.
condition: When using relative paths in shell commands.

statement: Use an absolute path when the target must be unambiguous from the filesystem root.
condition: When two locations could share the same basename or current directory is uncertain.

statement: Use cd to change the shell current directory and pwd to verify it before running path-sensitive commands.
condition: When navigation state matters for a command.

statement: Use . for the current directory and .. for its parent when constructing relative paths.
condition: When navigating or referencing nearby filesystem locations.

statement: Avoid spaces and shell-special characters in filenames when possible because they require quoting or escaping in shell commands.
Use cd with no arguments, $HOME, a lone tilde, or a tilde plus username to navigate to home directories as appropriate.
condition: When referring to personal home directories.

statement: Interpret common system directory names by combining scope, category, and application components rather than treating every path as opaque.
condition: When reasoning about unfamiliar Linux system paths.

statement: Expect /usr/local to contain locally installed system files that were not supplied by the distribution.
Expect bin directories to hold executable programs and sbin directories to hold programs intended for superuser administration.
Treat /etc paths as system configuration locations and use an application subdirectory there to infer the service being configured.
condition: When inspecting system configuration files.

statement: Treat /proc and /sys file metadata cautiously because their apparent sizes and timestamps may not reflect the kernel information they expose.
condition: When inspecting kernel-related pseudo-filesystems.

statement: Use /proc files such as cpuinfo, version, uptime, process-number directories, and self to inspect live kernel or process information.
condition: When read-only kernel/process visibility is needed.

statement: Use ls -l to inspect file owner, group, and permission bits before changing access or diagnosing permission failures.
condition: When a file access question arises.

statement: Remember that directory permissions differ operationally from file permissions: read lists entries, write creates or deletes entries, and execute permits entering the directory.
condition: When troubleshooting directory access.

statement: Use chown, chgrp, and chmod for owner, group, and permission changes respectively.
condition: When modifying file ownership or access bits.

statement: Verify the active login shell with the SHELL variable, and run bash explicitly if bash-specific behavior is desired in a non-bash shell.
condition: When a command relies on bash behavior.

statement: Treat shell wildcard expansion as a preprocessing step performed by the shell before the target program starts.
condition: When explaining why patterns work with many commands.

statement: Quote or escape wildcard characters when the literal pattern must reach the program unchanged.
condition: When a command itself needs to receive metacharacters rather than expanded filenames.

statement: Remember that shell patterns do not match leading dot filenames unless the dot is supplied explicitly.
condition: When matching hidden files with shell globs.

statement: Use brace expansion for generating literal argument lists or ranges without requiring matching files to exist.
condition: When constructing repetitive command arguments.

statement: Export a shell variable only when child processes must see it as an environment variable.
condition: When a variable value must be available to invoked programs.

statement: Prefix a command with VAR=value to override an environment variable only for that command invocation.
condition: When a temporary per-command environment change is needed.

statement: Use printenv to inspect environment variables exposed to subprocesses.
condition: When diagnosing inherited environment state.

statement: Use type or which to find the executable path that the shell will resolve through PATH.
condition: When diagnosing command lookup or shadowing.

statement: Modify PATH in the current shell for a temporary command-search change and in a shell startup file for a persistent change.
condition: When adding a directory to the command search path.

statement: Use type to distinguish filesystem commands, shell builtins, and aliases before assuming where a command comes from.
condition: When diagnosing command lookup or unexpected command behavior.

statement: Treat standard output and standard error as separate streams even when both appear on the display.
Use < to feed a command standard input from a file when the command reads from stdin.
condition: When a command accepts standard input.

statement: Use > to create or overwrite an output file and >> to append to an output file.
condition: When redirecting standard output to a file.

statement: Redirect standard error with descriptor 2 so error messages can be captured separately from standard output.
condition: When stderr and stdout need different handling.

statement: Use separate stdout and stderr redirections when the two streams need different destinations, and combined redirection only when they should share one file.
condition: When capturing command output streams.

statement: Use semicolons for unconditional command sequencing on one line.
condition: When later commands should run regardless of earlier exit status.

statement: Use && for dependent command sequences that should stop after the first failure.
condition: When each command depends on the previous command succeeding.

statement: Use || for fallback command sequences that should stop after the first success.
condition: When later commands are alternatives after earlier failures.

statement: Use pipes for commands that can stream producer output directly into consumer input.
condition: When the downstream command reads from standard input.

statement: Use command substitution to replace a command expression with its output inside another command line.
condition: When a command argument must be computed dynamically.

statement: Prefer $(...) over backticks for command substitution when nesting may be needed.
condition: When writing command substitutions in shell commands.

statement: Use process substitution when a program requires filename arguments but the data should come from another command pipeline.
condition: When a command cannot consume the needed data through stdin but can read file operands.

statement: Quote filenames or arguments containing whitespace so the shell treats the text as one argument.
condition: When shell words contain spaces or other separators.

statement: Use single quotes when shell contents must remain literal, and double quotes when variables or substitutions should still be evaluated.
condition: When choosing shell quoting style.

statement: Escape a shell metacharacter with backslash when the literal character must be passed to the command.
condition: When only one special character needs literal treatment.

statement: Use control-V before a control character such as Tab when that control character must be entered literally at the shell prompt.
condition: When interactive shell editing would otherwise intercept the key.

statement: Set bash command-line editing mode with set -o emacs or set -o vi, and put the setting in a bash configuration file for persistence.
condition: When choosing persistent command-line editing keystrokes.

statement: Use shell history expansion cautiously because history expressions re-run or substitute previous commands.
condition: When using !!, !N, or related history shortcuts.

statement: Use Tab completion to reduce filename typing errors and double-Tab to inspect ambiguous completions.
condition: When typing pathnames interactively.

statement: Use jobs to inspect shell-tracked jobs, and remember job control is a shell abstraction above operating-system processes.
condition: When managing foreground, background, or suspended interactive commands.

statement: Append & to run a command as a background job while keeping the shell prompt available.
condition: When the job does not require foreground interaction.

statement: Use Ctrl-Z to suspend a foreground job, then bg to continue it in the background or fg to resume it in the foreground.
condition: When temporarily stopping an interactive foreground command.

statement: Expect some interactive jobs to be unsuitable for background execution if they need terminal input.
condition: When moving interactive jobs to the background.

statement: Use disown only when the shell should stop tracking a job while leaving the underlying process running.
condition: When a long-running job should outlive shell job control.

statement: Use tmux for multiple shell sessions over a plain terminal or SSH connection; prefer ordinary terminal windows on a graphical desktop when available.
condition: When multiple simultaneous shells are needed.

statement: Detach from tmux instead of killing it when the shell sessions should continue running.
condition: When leaving a tmux session that should be resumed later.

statement: If tmux shells lack expected aliases or variables, arrange for the login startup file to source the interactive shell configuration.
condition: When tmux starts login shells that skip .bashrc.

statement: Use Ctrl-C to interrupt a foreground command, but use kill or application-specific controls for programs that catch or ignore Ctrl-C.
condition: When stopping a running foreground command.

statement: Recover a damaged terminal state after an interrupted command by getting a prompt with Ctrl-J and running reset.
condition: When the shell stops echoing keystrokes or behaves oddly after interruption.

statement: Terminate an interactive shell with exit or Ctrl-D on an empty input line.
condition: When intentionally closing a shell session.

statement: Put login-time bash commands in one login startup file and interactive-shell commands in .bashrc to avoid confusing shell startup behavior.
condition: When tailoring bash behavior persistently.

statement: Use man for command documentation, man -k for keyword search, info for hypertext documentation, --help for short usage, and /usr/share/doc for package-supplied supporting files.
condition: When the pocket guide does not contain enough detail.

statement: Pipe long help output through less so it can be read page by page.
condition: When command help or search results exceed the screen.

statement: Check for an alias when ls behavior differs from the documented command, then bypass, remove, or redefine the alias as needed.
condition: When ls output or options behave unexpectedly.

statement: Use ls -a for hidden dotfiles, ls -l for attributes, and ls -d when you need information about a directory itself rather than its contents.
condition: When inspecting files and directories with ls.

statement: Use cp -a or cp -r for recursive directory copies, choosing -a when preserving attributes and links matters.
condition: When copying directory hierarchies.

statement: Use cp -i or mv -i when overwrites should be confirmed interactively, and use force options only when unconditional overwrite is intended.
condition: When replacing existing destination files.

statement: Treat rm -r, especially with -f or sudo, as destructive because it can remove large directory trees or critical system files.
condition: When deleting directories recursively.

statement: Choose a hard link when a second pathname should continue to refer to the same file data even if the original pathname is renamed or deleted.
condition: When the link and original are on the same device and the target is not a directory in ordinary use.

statement: Choose a symbolic link when the link must point to a path, a directory, or a file on another device.
condition: When pathname indirection is acceptable.

statement: Expect symbolic links to break if the target path is renamed or removed because they store a path rather than an inode.
Use readlink, or readlink -f for chains, to resolve where a symbolic link ultimately points.
condition: When diagnosing symlink targets.

statement: Use ln -i, -f, or -b deliberately because link creation can ask before replacing, replace unconditionally, or back up an existing target.
condition: When the intended link target path already exists.

statement: Use cd with no argument to return to the current user home directory.
condition: When navigating back to the home directory.

statement: Use cd - to return to the previous directory visited by the current shell.
condition: When toggling between two working directories.

statement: Use pwd when a script or interactive task must confirm the absolute current directory.
condition: When current-directory ambiguity would affect later relative paths.

statement: Use basename and dirname for path string manipulation; do not expect them to verify that the path exists or to change the shell directory.
condition: When extracting a final path component or parent path text.

statement: Use mkdir -p for nested directory paths whose parents may not yet exist.
condition: When creating a directory hierarchy in one command.

statement: Use mkdir -m only when an explicit initial directory mode is needed; otherwise the shell umask influences the permissions.
condition: When creating directories with controlled permissions.

statement: Use rmdir only for empty directories, and use rmdir -p only when all named parent directories should also be removed and are empty.
condition: When removing empty directory paths.

statement: Use rm -ri rather than rm -rf when recursively deleting a nonempty directory that should be reviewed interactively.
condition: When deletion is recursive and confirmation is desired.

statement: Use cat for short files or concatenation pipelines, and switch to less when output is longer than the screen.
condition: When displaying text file contents.

statement: Use cat options such as tab, newline, nonprinting-character, or numbering display when invisible characters or line positions matter.
condition: When inspecting text formatting problems.

statement: Use less as the terminal pager for long files or lengthy pipeline output, with search and navigation rather than dumping everything to the terminal.
condition: When output needs interactive paging.

statement: Use less -S when long lines should stay unwrapped, and less -N when line numbers are useful during inspection.
condition: When reviewing wide or line-referenced text.

statement: Use nl instead of cat -n when line-number formatting or selective numbering is needed.
condition: When numbering text output with control over format or which lines count.

statement: Use head or tail for previews of the beginning or end of a file or pipeline rather than opening the whole stream.
condition: When only an initial or final sample is needed.

statement: Use tail -f to monitor lines appended to an active logfile and stop it with Ctrl-C.
condition: When following an actively written text log.

statement: Use strings to extract readable text from binary files, and combine a minimum length with grep when searching for meaningful embedded strings.
condition: When exploring binary file contents for readable fragments.

statement: Use od for binary inspection when byte offsets, numeric bases, character formats, or fixed-width byte rows matter.
condition: When binary data must be viewed in a controlled representation.

statement: Use od character output for binary files that may contain recognizable text signatures.
condition: When checking binary headers or embedded characters.

statement: Learn enough of nano, Emacs, and Vim to recover when a program unexpectedly invokes one of them on an important file.
condition: When administering Linux systems interactively.

statement: Use touch or output redirection to create an empty file quickly without opening an editor.
condition: When a placeholder file is needed at the command line.

statement: Set both VISUAL and EDITOR to the preferred filename-accepting editor because programs may consult either variable.
condition: When configuring the default editor.

statement: Use nano help if basic save or quit commands are unclear because nano exposes its command list from within the editor.
condition: When editing with nano.

statement: Run Emacs with -nw when a terminal session should not open a graphical Emacs window.
condition: When invoking Emacs from a graphical desktop but wanting terminal-only behavior.

statement: Remember Vim has distinct insert and command modes, and switch modes explicitly before typing text or issuing editing commands.
condition: When editing with Vim.

statement: Use du to measure disk blocks consumed by files or directory trees, and add -s when only totals are wanted.
condition: When estimating disk usage rather than logical file length.

statement: Use human-readable du output for interactive review and explicit byte/block units for scripts that need stable units.
condition: When reporting disk usage.

statement: Use file or mimetype as a content-based guess, not proof, of a file type.
condition: When identifying unknown files.

statement: Use file -L or mimetype -L when the type of a symlink destination matters more than the symlink object itself.
condition: When classifying symbolic links.

statement: Use file -z when compressed content should be inspected rather than merely identified as compressed data.
condition: When classifying compressed files.

statement: Use touch to update access and modification timestamps or to create an empty file only when creation is acceptable.
condition: When manipulating file timestamps.

statement: Use touch -c to avoid creating a missing file while attempting timestamp changes.
condition: When a missing file should remain absent.

statement: Verify nontrivial touch timestamp expressions with stat because the accepted date formats are flexible.
condition: When setting arbitrary timestamps.

statement: Use chown with sudo in most ownership-change cases because ordinary users usually cannot change file owners.
condition: When changing file ownership.

statement: Use chown user:group or numeric IDs only after confirming the intended account and group identity.
condition: When setting owner and group together.

statement: Use --reference with chown, chgrp, or chmod when a file should inherit owner, group, or mode from an existing reference file.
condition: When matching metadata to another file.

statement: Use recursive ownership or group changes only when every item in the tree should receive the new metadata.
condition: When using chown -R or chgrp -R.

statement: Use chmod numeric modes for absolute common permissions and symbolic modes for targeted relative changes.
condition: When changing file or directory permissions.

statement: Use conditional execute X in large chmod operations to affect directories and already-executable files without making ordinary files executable.
condition: When recursively adjusting execute bits.

statement: Avoid setuid and setgid unless their privilege effect is deliberately required and understood because they can create security exposure.
condition: When changing executable permission bits.

statement: Use the sticky bit on shared writable directories when users should not be able to remove or rename each other’s files merely because the directory is writable.
condition: When administering shared temporary or collaboration directories.

statement: Use umask 0022, 0002, or 0077 as simple defaults for respectively public-readable, group-writable, or private newly created files and directories.
condition: When choosing a shell default creation mode.

statement: Remember umask removes permissions from the default file and directory modes rather than directly setting final permissions.
Use lsattr and chattr only with awareness of filesystem-specific extended attributes.
condition: When inspecting or changing ext-style file attributes.

statement: Treat immutable or append-only attributes as stronger protection than ordinary mode bits because even root operations may be blocked until the attribute is removed.
condition: When diagnosing files that cannot be changed or deleted.

statement: Use find for precise one-off searches or complex criteria over a directory tree, and locate for repeated fast searches over a relatively stable indexed tree.
condition: When choosing a file-location command.

statement: Escape find patterns so the shell does not expand them before find receives them.
condition: When using find -name, -path, or related pattern predicates.

statement: Use find type predicates to restrict results to regular files, directories, symlinks, devices, pipes, or sockets.
condition: When a search should return only certain filesystem object classes.

statement: Use find time, size, owner, group, permission, and depth predicates to narrow a search before performing actions.
condition: When locating files by metadata.

statement: Use find expression operators carefully because implicit AND, OR, negation, grouping, and comma evaluation affect which files match.
condition: When combining multiple find predicates.

statement: Use find -print0 with xargs -0 when filenames may contain whitespace or other characters that would break whitespace-delimited parsing.
condition: When piping found filenames into another command.

statement: Prefer find -ok over -exec when each matching file operation should be confirmed interactively.
condition: When applying a potentially risky command to found files.

statement: Treat find -delete as destructive and ensure the match expression is correct before enabling it.
condition: When deleting files directly from find results.

statement: Use xargs to turn long stdin lists into command invocations when command substitution could exceed shell command-line length limits.
condition: When processing large lists of filenames or operands.

statement: Test xargs pipelines with harmless commands such as ls or grep before substituting destructive commands.
condition: When building a new xargs command pipeline.

statement: Use xargs -n1 when each input line must produce a separate command execution.
condition: When command batching would change semantics.

statement: Build a locate index with updatedb for a chosen directory when the distribution’s default index is missing, stale, or too broad.
condition: When using locate on a custom or unindexed tree.

statement: Run updatedb with permission-aware indexing when users should only see indexed files they are allowed to access.
condition: When creating a shared locate database as root.

statement: Use type rather than which when aliases, builtins, or shell keywords may explain command behavior.
condition: When diagnosing commands in bash or another shell with type.

statement: Use whereis for executables, documentation, or source files in known system locations, but verify results because its search directories may not cover the needed path.
condition: When looking beyond PATH for related files.

statement: Use grep to select lines matching a regular expression from files or standard input.
condition: When line-oriented text needs to be filtered by pattern.

statement: Use grep -v, -l, -L, -c, -o, or -n to change whether grep reports nonmatches, filenames, counts, matching substrings, or line numbers.
condition: When the default matching-line output is not the desired report.

statement: Use grep context options when adjacent lines are needed to interpret a match.
condition: When a matching line alone lacks enough context.

statement: Use recursive grep carefully, choosing symlink-following behavior explicitly with -r versus -R.
condition: When searching directory trees.

statement: Use extended regular expressions through grep -E when the pattern syntax should be less backslash-heavy.
condition: When extended regex syntax is desired.

statement: Use fixed-string matching through grep -F when search strings should not be interpreted as regular expressions.
condition: When matching literal punctuation or a list of strings.

statement: Treat egrep and fgrep as equivalent conveniences for grep -E and grep -F, but prefer the explicit grep options for modern scripts.
condition: When writing new shell commands that need portability.

statement: Check for non-Linux line endings when grep end-of-line matches behave unexpectedly.
condition: When $ patterns fail or look inconsistent on files from Windows or macOS.

statement: Use tr -d to remove carriage returns when converting DOS-style text for Linux text utilities.
condition: When a text file contains carriage returns before newlines.

statement: Use cut with character offsets for character columns, byte offsets for byte positions, and field mode plus a delimiter for delimited records.
condition: When extracting columns from line-oriented text.

statement: Use cut ranges and comma-separated selections to extract multiple columns without a heavier parser.
condition: When fixed positions or simple delimiters are sufficient.

statement: Use cut -s when undelimited input lines should be suppressed rather than passed through unchanged.
condition: When field extraction should ignore non-record lines.

statement: Use paste to merge corresponding lines from multiple files into columns, and use paste -s to transpose file contents sideways.
condition: When combining line-oriented files columnwise.

statement: Use column for display formatting, but do not rely on default column layout for stable scripts because terminal width can affect it.
condition: When presenting text in columns.

statement: Use column -t with explicit separators and headings when ragged text should become a readable table.
condition: When formatting simple tabular text for humans.

statement: Use column JSON output only when table mode and column headings are supplied.
condition: When converting simple table-like text to JSON.

statement: Use tr for simple character-to-character translation, deletion, squeezing, or complement operations.
condition: When transformation can be expressed as character sets.

statement: Use sed, awk, Perl, or another programming language instead of tr for transformations that require line structure or richer logic.
condition: When character translation is not expressive enough.

statement: Use expand or unexpand to normalize tabs and spaces, and inspect ambiguous whitespace with cat -T or od -c.
condition: When whitespace representation matters.

statement: Use sort numerical modes for numbers and lexical mode for text, because alphabetic sorting can place 10 before 9.
condition: When sorting numeric-looking lines.

statement: Use sort keys and delimiters when the ordering criterion is a field or subfield rather than the whole line.
condition: When sorting structured text records.

statement: Repeat sort keys to define fallback ordering from most important to least important key.
condition: When multiple sorting criteria are required.

statement: Use sort -c to validate sorted input without rewriting it.
condition: When checking ordering in a script or pipeline.

statement: Use uniq only on adjacent duplicate lines, and sort first when all equal lines should be considered together.
condition: When deduplicating line-oriented text.

statement: Use uniq -c after sorting to count repeated lines.
condition: When summarizing duplicate frequency.

statement: Use tac to reverse line order, and concatenate first if multiple files should be reversed as one combined stream.
condition: When reversing chronological or ordered line streams.

statement: Use shuf -n to select random subsets and shuf -e or -i to randomize command-line strings or integer ranges.
condition: When random ordering or sampling is needed.

statement: Use shuf -r only with a limit when unbounded repeated random output is not desired.
condition: When sampling with replacement.

statement: Use tee inside a pipeline when intermediate data should be saved while still flowing to downstream commands.
condition: When debugging or preserving a pipeline stage.

statement: Use tee -a when the intermediate output should append to existing files rather than overwrite them.
condition: When recording pipeline data incrementally.

statement: Use awk or sed for pattern-driven line processing before escalating to a full programming language.
condition: When grep/cut/tr/sort pipelines are insufficient but the task remains line-oriented.

statement: Use compressed-file variants such as zgrep, zless, zcmp, and zdiff instead of manually uncompressing when the operation maps directly to grep, less, cmp, or diff.
condition: When inspecting or comparing compressed files.

statement: Use tar to package many files or directories into one archive, and choose -c, -t, or -x according to whether the task is creating, listing, or extracting an archive.
condition: When working with TAR archives.

statement: Always supply tar -f with the archive pathname or device being read or written.
condition: When tar should operate on a named archive rather than default media.

statement: Use tar -C to extract archive contents into a chosen directory instead of the current directory.
condition: When controlling extraction destination.

statement: Choose tar compression flags according to the archive format: -z for gzip, -j for bzip2, and -Z for classic Unix compression.
condition: When creating or extracting compressed TAR archives.

statement: Use decompression-to-stdout forms such as gunzip -c, zcat, bunzip2 -c, bzcat, or uncompress -c when compressed data should feed a pipeline without replacing files.
condition: When streaming compressed content through commands.

statement: Remember that basic gzip, bzip2, and classic compress commands replace the original file with the compressed or uncompressed counterpart unless a stdout option is used.
condition: When preserving original compressed or uncompressed files matters.

statement: Use zip -r for directory trees, unzip -l to inspect archive contents, and unzip to extract ZIP archives.
condition: When working with Windows-style ZIP files.

statement: Use 7z when a 7-Zip archive is needed or when extracting archive types beyond the common Linux compression tools.
condition: When handling .7z, LZMA, CAB, or other formats supported by 7-Zip.

statement: Prefer the native Linux commands for gzip, bzip2, or ZIP formats when those formats are the only requirement.
condition: When choosing between 7z and format-specific tools.

statement: Use munpack to extract MIME attachments from a saved message file and mpack to create MIME-encoded attachment files.
condition: When handling email attachments at the command line.

statement: Use GPG symmetric encryption only when the same passphrase can safely be used for encryption and decryption and the passphrase will not be lost.
condition: When choosing gpg -c.

statement: Use GPG public-key encryption when a file should be encrypted to a recipient key and decrypted with the matching private key.
condition: When encrypting for a recipient rather than a shared passphrase.

statement: Use GPG signing together with encryption when the recipient must verify who encrypted or sent the file.
condition: When authenticity as well as confidentiality matters.

statement: Use gpg --list-public-keys and --list-secret-keys to inspect the available key material before encrypting, signing, or decrypting.
condition: When diagnosing GPG key availability.

statement: Use ASCII armor output for GPG data that must be inserted into text channels such as email bodies.
condition: When binary OpenPGP output is inconvenient.

statement: Choose line-oriented comparison tools such as diff or comm for text and byte-oriented comparison such as cmp for binary files.
condition: When selecting a file comparison method.

statement: Avoid insecure checksum algorithms such as MD5 and SHA-1 for production integrity checks; use shasum with SHA-256 or stronger instead.
condition: When checksums may inform security or production decisions.
