statement: Use diff quiet mode when only equality status matters, unified format when producing patch-like output, and recursive mode when comparing directory trees.
condition: When tailoring diff output to a task.

statement: Use whitespace, blank-line, or case-ignoring diff options only when those differences should be intentionally disregarded.
condition: When comparing text with nonsemantic formatting differences.

statement: Use comm only on sorted input files, because its three-column comparison assumes sorted lines.
condition: When comparing line membership across two files.

statement: Suppress comm columns to report only lines unique to one file or common to both.
condition: When set-like line comparison output is needed.

statement: Use cmp silent mode in scripts where exit status should communicate same or different without printing output.
condition: When checking binary or exact file equality programmatically.

statement: Use shasum --check with a saved checksum file to detect whether files have changed since checksums were recorded.
condition: When validating file integrity against a prior digest set.

statement: Use pandoc for broad markup/document format conversion, but expect imperfect results that may need manual cleanup.
condition: When converting between supported document formats.

statement: Use pandoc -o for output files, especially binary outputs, and add -f or -t when format inference from filenames is insufficient.
condition: When converting files with pandoc.

statement: Use hxnormalize before hxselect for cleaner HTML extraction with CSS selectors.
condition: When selecting data from imperfect HTML.

statement: Use hxselect -c when only element contents are needed rather than the enclosing HTML tags.
condition: When extracting text from matched HTML elements.

statement: Use jq filters to select JSON fields, nested values, array elements, derived lengths, or computed aggregate values.
condition: When extracting or manipulating JSON data at the command line.

statement: Use jq with no explicit filter or with the identity filter to pretty-print one-line JSON for inspection.
condition: When making JSON readable.

statement: Use jq -f when a JSON filter is complex enough to keep in a separate file.
condition: When command-line quoting would make a jq filter unwieldy.

statement: Use xmllint --noout to validate XML without printing it, and inspect the exit code for success or failure.
condition: When checking XML well-formedness in a command-line workflow.

statement: Use xmllint --xpath to extract XML values or elements with XPath expressions.
condition: When querying XML content.

statement: Use csvtool for simple CSV column extraction, row/column counts, row formatting, header removal, and separator changes.
condition: When working with comma- or delimiter-separated records.

statement: Use split for fixed-size chunks by line count, byte count, or separator, and reassemble ordered pieces with cat when needed.
condition: When a file is too large for a tool or medium.

statement: Choose split prefixes and suffix options deliberately so generated part names sort and reassemble in the intended order.
condition: When file pieces will be handled later by globbing or scripts.

statement: Use csplit instead of split when division points are structural regular-expression matches rather than equal sizes.
condition: When splitting structured text such as HTML, XML, or source code.

statement: Use csplit silent, prefix, and suffix options when generated part files must have controlled names or quiet operation.
condition: When scripting structural file splitting.

statement: Use pdftotext only when a PDF contains real text; run OCR first when the PDF is image-only.
condition: When extracting text from PDFs.

statement: Use lpq to identify print job IDs before canceling specific jobs with lprm.
condition: When removing jobs from a print queue.

statement: Specify a printer queue with -P when printing, listing, or canceling jobs for a nondefault printer.
condition: When more than one printer or queue may be involved.

statement: Use look for prefix dictionary lookup, aspell for interactive correction, and spell for batch reporting of unrecognized words.
condition: When choosing a text spellchecking tool.

statement: Use superuser privileges only when necessary for administration, because root can modify or destroy the whole system.
condition: When deciding whether to use sudo, su, or a root shell.

statement: Prefer sudo over su on multiuser systems when available because sudo can use per-user authentication, precise privilege rules, and command logging.
condition: When choosing a privilege-escalation method.

statement: Exit a superuser shell as soon as the privileged work is done, and use whoami if the current identity is uncertain.
condition: When operating after sudo -s, sudo bash, or su.

statement: Use sudo -u or su with a username only when intentionally running as another non-root user and the authentication prerequisites are met.
condition: When executing commands under another user identity.

statement: Distinguish operating-system processes from shell jobs because process commands use PIDs while job-control commands use shell job abstractions.
condition: When selecting tools for monitoring or control.

statement: Use ps with filters for user, command name, terminal, PID, full command lines, or process trees according to the diagnostic question.
condition: When inspecting running processes.

statement: Prefer pgrep over ps piped through grep when a process list of matching PIDs is needed.
condition: When passing matching processes to another command.

statement: Use pgrep -f or -x deliberately depending on whether matching should use full command lines or exact process names.
condition: When searching processes by pattern.

statement: Interpret uptime load averages as average runnable process counts over 1, 5, and 15 minutes rather than as percentages.
condition: When evaluating uptime output.

statement: Use w to connect logged-in users to terminals, origins, idle state, CPU time, and current processes.
condition: When reviewing interactive user activity.

statement: Use top for interactive monitoring and top -b -n1 when a single snapshot should be redirected or piped.
condition: When capturing process resource usage.

statement: Use top interactive help before killing or changing behavior from inside top.
condition: When operating top interactively.

statement: Use the available column from free as the practical estimate of free RAM because the kernel may reserve memory for cache.
condition: When interpreting Linux memory output.

statement: Send a normal kill signal first, and reserve kill -KILL or -9 for processes that ignore the normal termination request.
condition: When terminating a process.

statement: Treat kill -KILL as a last resort because it prevents clean program shutdown and may leave resources or state inconsistent.
condition: When choosing a process signal.

statement: Use kill -l and signal documentation when a process needs a signal other than the default termination signal.
condition: When sending nondefault signals.

statement: Use pkill when the intended operation is to signal all matching processes by program pattern rather than a single known PID.
condition: When terminating or signaling by process name.

statement: Use timeout to impose a maximum runtime on commands that should not run indefinitely.
condition: When a command may hang or exceed an acceptable duration.

statement: Use timeout -k to escalate to a KILL signal only after a grace period following the initial signal.
condition: When a timed-out command might ignore the first signal.

statement: Use nice to start CPU-intensive work at lower priority so other users and processes remain responsive.
condition: When launching resource-heavy commands.

statement: Avoid large negative nice values unless administrative priority changes are truly required because they can interfere with important system processes.
condition: When raising process priority.

statement: Use renice for already-running processes and remember ordinary users can only lower priority for their own processes.
condition: When changing priority after launch.

statement: Use nohup with backgrounding when a command should continue after the launching shell exits.
condition: When a long-running command must survive logout.

statement: Capture or redirect nohup output deliberately because stdout or stderr may be written to nohup.out.
condition: When running nohup commands that produce output.

statement: Use flock with a shared lock file to prevent concurrent instances of the same command or script.
condition: When scheduled or repeated commands must not overlap.

statement: Use flock -n for immediate failure or -w for bounded waiting when another instance already holds the lock.
condition: When choosing lock contention behavior.

statement: Use sleep to delay a later command in a shell sequence by seconds, minutes, hours, or days.
condition: When a simple fixed delay is sufficient.

statement: Quote or escape shell-special characters in watch commands because watch passes the command to the shell.
condition: When repeatedly executing a command with watch.

statement: Use watch -d or -g when the task is to highlight or stop on changing command output.
condition: When monitoring periodic output changes.

statement: Use at for one-time future jobs and remember aliases are not available to at jobs even though the environment is preserved.
condition: When scheduling commands for a single future time.

statement: Use atq and atrm to inspect and remove scheduled at jobs by job number.
condition: When managing pending one-time jobs.

statement: Use crontab for recurring scheduled jobs and at for one-time future jobs.
condition: When choosing a scheduler for command execution.

statement: Use crontab -e to edit, crontab -l to inspect, and treat crontab -r as destructive because it deletes the crontab without confirmation.
condition: When managing a user crontab.

statement: Use absolute command paths in crontab entries so cron executes the intended programs despite PATH differences.
condition: When writing recurring cron jobs.

statement: Put long or messy cron commands into scripts and invoke those scripts from crontab.
condition: When a recurring job needs complex shell logic.

statement: Use systemctl poweroff, reboot, or suspend for whole-system state changes on systemd systems.
condition: When controlling local machine power state through systemd.

statement: Use systemctl status before or after service changes to verify the current state and diagnose failures.
condition: When managing a named service.

statement: Use systemctl enable or disable to control startup eligibility separately from start, stop, restart, and reload runtime actions.
condition: When managing services across boot and current runtime.

statement: Use reload instead of restart only when the service supports rereading configuration without a full stop and start.
condition: When applying configuration changes to a running service.

statement: Omit the .service suffix in systemctl service names when convenient because systemctl accepts the shortened service name.
condition: When naming ordinary services.

statement: Never power off a Linux system by cutting power when a graceful shutdown command is available, because the filesystem needs orderly shutdown.
condition: When shutting down a Linux computer.

statement: Run shutdown as superuser and supply either relative minutes, an absolute clock time, or now for the scheduled time.
condition: When halting or rebooting with shutdown.

statement: Use shutdown -k to test warning broadcasts without actually shutting down.
condition: When notifying users or rehearsing shutdown messaging.

statement: Use shutdown -c to cancel a pending shutdown.
condition: When a scheduled shutdown should no longer occur.

statement: Recognize that shutdown without halt or reboot options may enter single-user maintenance mode rather than powering off.
condition: When invoking shutdown with no action option.

statement: Use reboot for immediate reboot only after considering that some distributions allow non-root users to run it.
condition: When rebooting a local system.

statement: Use logname for the original login name and whoami for the current effective user, especially after sudo.
condition: When identity may differ from login identity.

statement: Use id to inspect effective and real user IDs, group IDs, and group memberships.
condition: When diagnosing permissions or group access.

statement: Use who or users to list current logins, choosing who for detailed terminal/origin information and users for a compact username list.
condition: When checking who is logged in.

statement: Use tty to identify the terminal device associated with the current shell.
condition: When terminal-specific information is needed.

statement: Use last with filters and alternate log files to inspect login history, current-at-time sessions, failed-login data, or shutdown/runlevel events.
condition: When auditing login history.

statement: Use printenv with variable names to inspect selected environment values rather than dumping the whole environment.
condition: When diagnosing a specific environment variable.

statement: Give every local account a strong password because each account can become an entry point to the system.
condition: When creating or maintaining user accounts.

statement: Create user accounts with explicit useradd options rather than relying on weak defaults.
condition: When adding a local user account.

statement: Use useradd -m when a new account should receive a home directory initialized from the skeleton directory.
condition: When creating an interactive user account.

statement: Avoid manually assigning numeric user IDs unless there is a clear administrative reason.
condition: When creating accounts with useradd.

statement: Before deleting a user, consider locking the account and backing up the user’s files because userdel does not remove files unless -r is used.
condition: When removing a user account.

statement: Use usermod -aG when adding group memberships so existing supplementary groups are preserved.
condition: When adding a user to additional groups.

statement: Avoid changing login names or system accounts unless dependencies are understood.
condition: When using usermod -l or modifying root/daemon-style accounts.

statement: Use usermod -L and -U to lock and unlock login access without deleting the account.
condition: When disabling or restoring an account.

statement: Use passwd for the current user’s password and sudo passwd for another user’s password.
condition: When changing login passwords.

statement: Use password-expiration options only as part of a coherent security policy.
condition: When configuring passwd aging controls.

statement: Use chsh only with shells listed in /etc/shells, and chsh -l to list permissible login shells.
condition: When changing a login shell.

statement: Use groups to inspect group membership before diagnosing group-based access failures.
condition: When file or device permissions depend on group membership.

statement: Use usermod -aG or a root edit of /etc/group to add users to a group, and use chgrp to change group ownership of files.
condition: When granting group-based access.

statement: Use groupadd -f when group creation should not fail noisily if the group already exists.
condition: When idempotently ensuring a group exists.

statement: Use newgrp to activate a newly granted group membership in a fresh shell without logging out and back in.
condition: When group membership has changed during the current login session.

statement: Before deleting or renaming a group, find files owned by that group because groupdel and groupmod do not update existing file ownership.
condition: When changing or removing groups.

statement: Treat group ID changes as risky because files with the old group ID may become invalidly owned and require cleanup.
condition: When using groupmod -g.

statement: Identify the Linux distribution before choosing package-manager commands, because package tools and package formats vary by distro.
condition: When installing or updating software packages.

statement: Distinguish system package managers from container-style package managers such as Snap and Flatpak because they install and isolate software differently.
condition: When choosing a software installation source.

statement: For each distro package manager, refresh package metadata before search, install, or update operations.
condition: When using tools such as emerge, pacman, zypper, apt, aptitude, or dnf.

statement: Use package-manager query commands to learn whether a package is installed, what files it owns, and which package owns an installed file before making changes.
condition: When auditing installed software.

statement: Use package-manager download-only operations when packages must be staged without installing them yet.
condition: When separating retrieval from installation.

statement: Use distro-native package managers for system software updates and removals rather than manually deleting installed files.
condition: When maintaining packages installed under system directories.

statement: For Gentoo Portage work, install gentoolkit before relying on extra commands such as equery.
condition: When using Portage command-line workflows.

statement: When Portage refuses removal because of dependencies, inspect the dependent packages and include intended removals explicitly rather than forcing blind deletion.
condition: When depclean reports blockers.

statement: Treat Flatpak and Snap packages as containerized applications with bundled dependencies and limited host filesystem access.
condition: When reasoning about Flatpak or Snap behavior.

statement: Use Flatpak remotes before installation and run Flatpak applications by their package IDs.
condition: When installing and launching Flatpak software.

statement: Use flatpak --user instead of sudo flatpak when the package should be installed only for the current user.
condition: When choosing Flatpak installation scope.

statement: Define a shell alias only as a convenience wrapper for long Flatpak run IDs, not as a substitute for understanding the real command.
condition: When making Flatpak command-line launches easier.

statement: Inspect archive contents before extracting source tarballs or ZIPs because archives can overwrite valuable or sensitive paths.
condition: When unpacking downloaded source archives.

statement: Extract downloaded source archives into a new directory rather than directly into an important working location.
condition: When unpacking source distributions.

statement: Use git clone for source distributed through a Git repository, then build from the local repository copy.
condition: When obtaining software from GitHub-like services.

statement: Read INSTALL or README before building source code because package-specific instructions can override the generic configure/make pattern.
condition: When building software from source.

statement: Use configure --prefix to install software under a writable user directory and avoid later superuser installation.
condition: When building source as an ordinary user.

statement: If configure fails, read its output to identify missing prerequisite software before retrying.
condition: When source configuration fails.

statement: Use make to build after successful configuration and make install only after the build succeeds.
condition: When using the conventional source-build workflow.

statement: Use sudo make install only for intentional system-wide installation, because omitting --prefix normally requires superuser privileges later.
condition: When installing built software into system locations.

statement: Add a user-local installation bin directory to PATH when installed commands should be found by future shells.
condition: When installing software under a user-controlled prefix.

statement: Distinguish disks, partitions, filesystems, mount points, and directories when explaining Linux storage operations.
condition: When diagnosing storage or filesystem tasks.

statement: Treat /dev names such as sda, md, and nvme devices as block-device identifiers and verify the exact target before storage operations.
condition: When operating on disk or partition device files.

statement: Mount a filesystem on a directory to make its files reachable in the unified directory tree.
condition: When accessing a partition or removable medium.

statement: Avoid mounting over a nonempty directory unless hiding that directory’s current contents until unmount is intended.
condition: When choosing a mount point.

statement: Use df on a file or directory to identify the mounted filesystem that contains it.
condition: When checking capacity for a path.

statement: Use df inode mode when a filesystem appears full despite available disk blocks.
condition: When diagnosing file-creation failures with free space remaining.

statement: Filter df pseudo-filesystem types when the goal is to review real disk capacity.
condition: When df output is cluttered by tmpfs, devtmpfs, squashfs, or similar entries.

statement: Use lsblk to map block devices, partitions, sizes, mount points, and filesystem details before mounting or formatting.
condition: When identifying storage devices.

statement: Use lsblk JSON or selected output columns when scripts need structured block-device information.
condition: When parsing block-device data programmatically.

statement: Use /etc/fstab entries to mount known filesystems by device or mount directory instead of repeating full mount details.
condition: When the filesystem table already defines the mount.

statement: Unmount writable removable media before unplugging it to reduce filesystem damage risk.
condition: When removing USB drives or similar media.

statement: Do not unmount filesystems currently in use; the safety refusal should prompt closing processes or changing directories first.
condition: When umount reports that a target is busy.

statement: Unmount a filesystem before running fsck manually so no other process modifies it during the check.
condition: When checking or repairing a non-root filesystem.

statement: Boot from rescue media before using fsck to repair the root filesystem.
condition: When the root filesystem needs repair.

statement: Use fsck -N to preview checks and fsck -r for interactive repairs; avoid automatic repair unless the consequences are understood.
condition: When repairing filesystem errors.

statement: Prefer graphical partitioning tools for complex disk layout changes because command-line partitioning and formatting are error-prone.
condition: When doing more than a simple filesystem operation.

statement: Export a partition table to a different device before risky partitioning so it can be restored if needed.
condition: When preparing for risky partition table changes.

statement: Treat mkfs as destructive and verify the device name before formatting.
condition: When creating a filesystem on a partition.

statement: Use mkfs dry-run, labels, and block-size options only after selecting the appropriate filesystem-specific mkfs command.
condition: When formatting a storage device.

statement: For ext2/ext3/ext4 resizing, unmount and check the filesystem, adjust the partition in the correct order for growth or shrinkage, then run resize2fs with the intended size or partition size.
condition: When resizing a standard Linux ext filesystem.

statement: Use e2label to assign or print ext filesystem labels that can make /etc/fstab references more convenient.
condition: When labeling ext2/ext3/ext4 filesystems.

statement: Practice RAID, LVM, and ZFS storage commands on spare drives or virtual machines because mistakes can wipe filesystems without confirmation.

statement: Inspect /proc/mdstat and mdadm --detail to verify RAID state, rebuild progress, degraded arrays, and failed devices.

statement: After creating a RAID array, format and mount the array device rather than the individual member partitions.

statement: Persist a RAID array by saving mdadm detail output into the mdadm configuration, updating initramfs, reboot-testing, and only then adding fstab mounting.
condition: When configuring an mdadm array to survive reboots.

statement: Do not add a RAID array to /etc/fstab until reboot and manual mount testing show that the RAID configuration is correct.
condition: When configuring automatic RAID mounts.

statement: Replace a failed RAID member by failing and removing it, powering down for physical replacement, copying the partition table from a good member, randomizing GUIDs, and adding the new partition.

statement: Use distinct placeholder names and re-identify actual devices before destructive RAID replacement commands to avoid operating on the wrong drive.

statement: Destroy a RAID array by unmounting it, stopping the md device, zeroing member superblocks, removing configuration references, and updating initramfs.

condition: When taking a quick or cautious look at a web page.

condition: When capturing web page content from the command line.

condition: When using Lynx or similar text browsers.

condition: When retrieving web content for local storage.

statement: Use wget spider mode when checking existence of pages without downloading them.
condition: When validating remote links or availability.

statement: Use wget recursive, depth, conversion, page-requisite, accept, reject, include, and exclude options deliberately when mirroring websites.
condition: When downloading more than a single URL.

statement: Check which echo implementation is active because shell builtins and /bin/echo can differ in behavior.
condition: When relying on echo option or escape semantics.

statement: Use echo for simple messages, but use printf when formatted output, width, numeric bases, or escaped shell-safe strings matter.
condition: When producing output in scripts.

statement: Treat mismatched printf format specifications and arguments as bugs even though printf may produce default or repeated output.
condition: When writing printf commands.

statement: Use yes only when it is safe for every prompt of a command to receive the same repeated affirmative or string response.
condition: When automating interactive prompts.

statement: Use seq for numeric streams and choose lower bound, increment, separator, padding, or printf-like formatting as needed.
condition: When generating numbers for pipelines or scripts.

statement: Use clear or Ctrl-L to clear the visible terminal without changing shell state.
condition: When resetting the display during interactive work.

statement: Use xclip or xsel only in environments that provide compatible clipboards; use Wayland or terminal-multiplexer mechanisms otherwise.
condition: When accessing clipboard data from the shell.

statement: Choose the correct X selection, especially primary versus clipboard, because different paste mechanisms read different selections.
condition: When moving text between shell and graphical applications.

statement: Use xsel when clipboard appending, clearing, or swapping is needed beyond basic xclip read/write.
condition: When manipulating X selections from the command line.

condition: When evaluating expressions in shell commands.

statement: Prefer shell arithmetic $((...)) over expr for simple inline arithmetic in bash-like shells.
condition: When arithmetic is needed inside a command line.

statement: Interpret expr Boolean results as 0 for false and 1 for true, with numeric zero and empty string treated as false.
condition: When using expr in conditional logic.

statement: Use bc for arbitrary-precision decimal arithmetic, base conversion, variables, functions, or calculator scripts.
condition: When shell arithmetic or expr is insufficient.

statement: Set bc scale when decimal precision matters because division is truncated to the current scale.
condition: When doing fractional calculations in bc.

statement: Remember demonstration bc functions may not handle all mathematical cases such as imaginary roots unless explicitly coded.
condition: When adapting example bc scripts.

statement: Use dc only when stack-based reverse Polish notation is acceptable or desired.
condition: When choosing a command-line calculator.

statement: Use cal with explicit month and four-digit year when displaying calendars other than the current month.
condition: When printing calendars.

statement: Treat cal behavior as somewhat implementation-dependent across systems.
condition: When relying on cal options or output shape.

statement: Use date format strings beginning with plus to produce predictable timestamp output for scripts or reports.
condition: When formatting dates and times.

statement: Account for locale when interpreting date output because default results depend on country and language settings.
condition: When parsing or comparing date command output.

statement: Use date -d for an arbitrary date string, date -r for a file timestamp, and date -s only as superuser to set system time.
condition: When selecting date command modes.

statement: Use seconds-since-epoch format when a numeric, timezone-independent timestamp is needed for scripts.
condition: When producing machine-comparable times.

condition: When verifying the exact contents of a Git commit.

statement: Use git reset to unstage changes without necessarily discarding working-tree edits.

statement: Use git restore for unstaged working-tree rollback, and reserve git reset --hard only for intentional destruction of all uncommitted changes.

statement: Use branches to isolate a line of work, merge it back when ready, and delete the branch after it is no longer needed.

condition: When deleting a remote Git branch.

statement: Use revision IDs from git log to refer to specific Git commits in commands.

statement: Add new files explicitly in Subversion before committing them.

statement: Use SVN revision numbers and ranges from svn log when inspecting or merging specific historical changes.
condition: When working with Subversion history.

statement: Join the docker group or use sudo only according to the local Docker installation model.

statement: Use docker stop/start/restart/pause/unpause/kill according to whether the container should stop cleanly, resume, suspend processes, or be forcibly killed.

statement: Use docker exec to run a command inside an existing container and docker logs with follow, tail, or since options to inspect container output.

statement: Use ffmpeg help listings for encoders or specific encoder details when supported formats or options are unclear.

condition: when evaluating a computer for Linux compatibility before installation

condition: for contemporary Linux distributions covered by the book

condition: when using terminal-window clipboard copy and paste

condition: for Unix-like systems such as Linux

condition: when storage devices are attached to a Linux system
statement: Additional storage devices become part of the Linux tree by being mounted at chosen points in that tree.

condition: in an interactive shell session
statement: A command-line user is always located in a current working directory.

condition: when a regular user logs in or opens a terminal emulator

condition: when directory path arguments are supplied

A relative pathname starts from the current working directory rather than from the filesystem root.

condition: when absolute and relative pathnames lead to the same target
statement: For equivalent pathnames, users should normally choose the form that requires the least typing.

Running cd - changes back to the previous working directory.

condition: when the shell supports tilde expansion
statement: A tilde followed by a username names that user's home directory for cd targets.

condition: unless an option such as ls -a requests hidden names

condition: for most command-line programs introduced by the book
statement: Most commands follow a pattern of a command name followed by behavior-modifying options and target arguments.
Short command options usually use a single dash and one character, while GNU-style long options usually use two dashes and a word.

condition: when a command supports clustered short options
statement: Many commands allow multiple short options to be combined behind one dash.
Command options are case sensitive like Linux filenames.
The ls -l long format exposes file attributes such as type, permissions, link count, owner, group, size, modification time, and name.

condition: when a user needs to know what kind of data a file contains
statement: The file command should be used to identify a file's contents instead of relying only on its name.

condition: for Unix-like systems such as Linux
statement: A central Unix-like design idea is that many system resources are represented through the file abstraction.

condition: when the user wants to inspect a text file from the command line
statement: The less command is the appropriate tool introduced here for viewing text files without editing them.
Plain text differs from word-processor documents because it stores characters and basic control codes rather than rich formatting structure.
Many Linux configuration files and scripts are stored as plain text, so reading text files helps users understand system behavior.

condition: when viewing a file with less
statement: Inside less, users can page or line-scroll through a file, search forward, open help, and quit without changing the file.

condition: when reasoning about standard Linux filesystem locations
statement: Most Linux distributions approximately follow the Linux Filesystem Hierarchy Standard, though exact directory layout can vary by distribution.

condition: when exploring unfamiliar Linux system directories
statement: A practical system-tour workflow is to enter a directory, list details with ls -l, identify interesting files with file, and inspect text files with less.

condition: when terminal output becomes garbled after viewing a non-text file
statement: The reset command can recover a terminal display that was scrambled by attempting to view non-text data.

condition: when exploring without administrative privileges
statement: Regular users are generally protected from damaging system areas during read-only exploration.

condition: on Linux systems following the standard layout
statement: The /etc directory is the central location for system-wide configuration files and those files should generally be readable text.

condition: in normal Linux configurations
statement: The /home tree normally contains per-user home directories where ordinary users can write their own files.

condition: on Linux systems
statement: The /dev directory exposes device nodes, applying the file abstraction to hardware devices.

condition: on Linux systems using procfs
statement: The /proc directory is a kernel-maintained virtual filesystem rather than ordinary files stored on disk.

condition: when investigating system state from the command line
statement: Reading files under /proc can reveal how the kernel views hardware and system state.

condition: on typical Linux systems
statement: The /usr tree contains programs and support files used by regular users and is often the largest tree on a Linux system.

condition: when installing programs outside the distribution package set for all users
statement: Locally compiled or non-distribution software intended for system-wide use normally belongs under /usr/local.

condition: on typical Linux systems
statement: The /var tree is the standard location for data that changes over time, such as logs, queues, spools, and databases.

condition: when monitoring system activity
statement: Log files under /var/log are important operational records and should be checked periodically, subject to access permissions.
Symbolic links let one pathname refer indirectly to another pathname.

condition: when programs need a stable resource name while installed versions change
statement: Symbolic links are useful for stable names that point to versioned files because the link can be retargeted during upgrades or rollback.
Hard links also allow multiple names for a file, but they work differently from symbolic links.

condition: when file operations are complex or pattern-based
statement: Command-line file manipulation becomes especially powerful when operations need selection criteria that graphical file managers handle poorly.

condition: when a command takes filenames as arguments
statement: Shell wildcards allow commands that accept filenames to operate on groups of names selected by patterns.

condition: in shell filename expansion patterns
statement: The asterisk wildcard matches any sequence of characters, including an empty sequence.

condition: in shell filename expansion patterns
statement: The question-mark wildcard matches exactly one character.

condition: in shell filename expansion patterns
statement: Bracket wildcard expressions match one character from an allowed or disallowed set.

condition: when writing wildcard patterns that should behave predictably across configurations
statement: POSIX character classes such as digit, upper, lower, alpha, and alnum are safer than traditional A-Z style ranges for portable filename patterns.

condition: when using shell wildcards on filenames
statement: Hidden dotfiles are excluded from ordinary wildcard expansion unless the pattern explicitly accounts for dot-prefixed names.

condition: when the file manager supports wildcard filtering or selection
statement: Wildcard support in some graphical file managers can apply command-line selection ideas inside GUI workflows.
The mkdir command creates one or more directories named by its arguments.

condition: when reading the book's command syntax notation
statement: An ellipsis in command documentation means the preceding argument can be repeated.
The cp command copies either one item to another item or multiple items into an existing directory.

condition: when preserving attributes matters during a copy
statement: Use cp -a when a copy should preserve directory contents and file attributes such as ownership and permissions.

condition: when an existing file might be overwritten by cp
statement: Use cp -i when copying over an existing destination should require confirmation before overwriting.

condition: when copying a directory and its contents
statement: Use cp -r or cp -a when copying directories recursively.

condition: when copying many files into a directory and only updates are desired
statement: Use cp -u to skip destination files that already exist and are at least as new as the source files.
The mv command either renames an item or moves items into a directory, and the original pathname disappears after success.

condition: when moving or renaming could replace an existing file
statement: Use mv -i when an existing destination should not be overwritten without confirmation.
The rm command removes one or more named files or directories.

condition: when rm is invoked with interactive mode
statement: The rm -i option requires confirmation before deleting a file.

condition: when deleting directories with rm
statement: The rm -r option recursively deletes directories and their contents and is required for deleting directories with rm.

condition: when rm is invoked with force mode
statement: The rm -f option suppresses prompts and ignores missing operands, overriding interactive behavior.

condition: when deleting with rm on Unix-like systems
statement: Users should treat rm deletions as permanent because Unix-like systems do not provide a general undelete command for rm.

condition: when using shell wildcards with rm
statement: Wildcards with rm must be checked carefully because a small spacing error can expand from a narrow deletion to all files in a directory.

condition: when preparing an rm command that contains wildcards
statement: Before running rm with a wildcard, users should test the same pattern with ls to see which names will be affected.
The ln command creates hard links by default and symbolic links when invoked with -s.

condition: for ordinary filesystem files
statement: Every file has at least one hard link because a filename is a directory entry linked to file data.

condition: when creating hard links
statement: A hard link cannot refer to a file on a different filesystem.

condition: when creating hard links
statement: A hard link may not refer to a directory.

condition: when a file has multiple hard links
statement: Deleting one hard link removes that name but does not free the file data until all hard links to the inode are deleted.

condition: when choosing a link type for ordinary user workflows
statement: Modern practice generally favors symbolic links over hard links for routine linking needs.
A symbolic link is a special file containing a text pointer to another file or directory.

condition: when an operation follows a symbolic link
statement: Writing through a symbolic link affects the linked target rather than the link file itself.

condition: when removing a symbolic link with rm
statement: Deleting a symbolic link with rm deletes the link itself rather than the target.

condition: when the referenced file or directory no longer exists
statement: A symbolic link becomes broken when its target is removed while the link remains.

condition: when the link and its target move together within a directory tree
statement: Relative symbolic-link targets are often preferable because the containing directory tree can usually be moved or renamed without breaking the links.
Symbolic links can refer to directories as well as regular files.

condition: when learning commands such as cp, mv, rm, and ln
statement: A safe playground directory in the user's home directory is an appropriate place to practice destructive or confusing file-manipulation commands.

condition: when a command accepts a pathname destination
statement: The current-directory dot can be used as a copy or move destination for the working directory.

condition: when cp or mv are invoked without interactive protection
statement: The cp and mv commands overwrite existing destinations silently unless interactive options are used.

condition: when verifying whether names are hard links to the same file
statement: After creating hard links, ls -li can confirm shared identity by showing identical inode numbers.

condition: when operating on symbolic links
statement: Most file operations through symbolic links act on the target, but rm is an important exception.

condition: when checking a command name in the shell
statement: The type command identifies how the shell interprets a command name.

condition: in the shell command model described by the book
statement: A command name can resolve to an executable program, a shell builtin, a shell function, or an alias.

condition: when the command is an executable program
statement: The which command identifies the executable file that would run for a command name.

condition: when investigating builtins or aliases
statement: The which command is not the right tool for shell builtins or aliases that do not correspond to executable programs.

condition: when the command being investigated is a bash builtin
statement: The bash help command is the appropriate documentation source for shell builtins.

condition: when reading command synopsis notation
statement: Square brackets in command syntax mark optional elements, while vertical bars mark mutually exclusive alternatives.

condition: when requesting usage help from executable programs
statement: Many executable programs support --help for concise usage and option information.

condition: when using man documentation
statement: Man pages are reference documentation for command-line programs and commonly include a synopsis, purpose, and option descriptions rather than tutorial examples.

condition: when the default man lookup returns the wrong topic type
statement: When a man-page topic exists in multiple sections, the desired section number should be supplied to man.

condition: when looking for relevant commands by topic
statement: The apropos command and man -k search manual-page summaries for a keyword.
The whatis command returns a one-line manual-page description for a specified keyword.

condition: for programs documented by GNU info files
statement: GNU info pages are hyperlinked, node-based documentation viewed with the info reader.

condition: when local package documentation is needed
statement: The /usr/share/doc tree is a common place to find package documentation, often viewable as plain text, Markdown, HTML, or compressed text.

condition: when documentation is compressed with gzip
statement: The zless command can display gzip-compressed text documentation without manually decompressing it first.

condition: when commands are separated with semicolons
statement: Semicolons let multiple shell commands be written on one command line and executed in sequence.

condition: when creating a new alias
statement: Before defining an alias, the proposed alias name should be checked with type to avoid unintentionally shadowing an existing command.

condition: when using the alias command syntax described by the book
statement: An alias definition binds a name directly to a quoted replacement string with no whitespace around the equals sign.

condition: within the shell session where the alias exists
statement: After an alias is defined, the shell can use the alias name anywhere it expects a command name.
The unalias command removes an alias definition.

condition: when a user wants a default behavior for a familiar command
statement: Aliases are often used to add a preferred option to a commonly used command.
Running alias without arguments lists the aliases currently defined in the shell environment.

condition: when an alias is created only at the command line
statement: Aliases defined interactively disappear when the shell session ends unless they are added to startup configuration.

condition: for well-behaved Unix-style command-line programs
statement: Programs commonly separate normal results on standard output from status and error messages on standard error.

condition: in a normal interactive shell session
statement: By default, standard input is attached to the keyboard and standard output and standard error are attached to the screen.

condition: when redirecting stdout
statement: The greater-than redirection operator sends standard output to a file instead of the screen.

condition: when stdout is redirected with >
statement: The greater-than redirection operator rewrites the destination from the beginning, so it can truncate an existing file even when the command produces no standard output.

condition: when using shell redirection alone
statement: A redirection operator without a preceding command can create an empty file or truncate an existing file.

condition: when redirecting stdout with >>
statement: The double-greater-than redirection operator appends standard output to a file and creates the file if it does not exist.

condition: when several commands should write to the same log or file
statement: Brace-grouped commands can share one redirection as a single output stream.

condition: when using shell brace groups for command sequencing
statement: Brace command groups require whitespace around the braces and a semicolon or newline after the final command.

condition: when using descriptor-based redirection
statement: The shell file descriptors for standard input, standard output, and standard error are 0, 1, and 2 respectively.

condition: when only stderr should be captured or suppressed
statement: Standard error can be redirected separately by placing file descriptor 2 immediately before the redirection operator.

condition: when using > file 2>&1 style redirection
statement: To capture standard output and standard error in one file using traditional redirection, stdout must be redirected before stderr is duplicated to stdout.

condition: in recent bash versions
statement: Bash supports &> for redirecting standard output and standard error to one file and &>> for appending both streams.

condition: when command output or errors are intentionally unwanted
statement: Redirecting output to /dev/null discards that output.

condition: when cat is given filename arguments
statement: The cat command copies one or more files to standard output.

condition: when split file names sort into the desired order
statement: The cat command can concatenate split files into one output file when shell expansion supplies the parts in sorted order.

condition: when cat is invoked without operands
statement: When cat receives no file arguments, it reads standard input until end-of-file and copies that input to standard output.

condition: when creating a small text file from the command line
statement: Redirecting cat output with > can create a short text file from typed standard input.

condition: when redirecting stdin
statement: The less-than redirection operator changes standard input from the keyboard to a file.

condition: when using the pipe operator
statement: A pipeline connects the standard output of one command to the standard input of another command.

condition: when a command produces more output than fits on one screen
statement: Piping command output to less is a convenient way to page through output that would otherwise scroll past.

condition: when distinguishing redirection from pipelines
statement: The > operator connects a command to a file, whereas the pipe operator connects one command to another command.

condition: when redirecting output to a pathname
statement: The > operator must be treated carefully because it silently creates or overwrites files, including executable files if run with sufficient permissions.

condition: when composing filter commands in pipelines
statement: Pipeline filters take input, transform it, and write output for the next stage.

condition: when downstream processing needs sorted text
statement: The sort command can combine multiple command outputs into one ordered stream in a pipeline.

condition: when uniq receives sorted data
statement: The uniq command removes duplicate lines from a sorted input stream by default.

condition: when finding repeated lines in sorted input
statement: The uniq -d option reports duplicate lines instead of suppressing them.

condition: when each input line represents an item to count
statement: The wc command reports line, word, and byte counts, and wc -l is useful in pipelines for counting items.

condition: when searching text with grep
statement: The grep command prints lines that match a specified text pattern, with options for case-insensitive, filename-only, inverted, and whole-word matching.

condition: when only part of text output is needed
statement: The head and tail commands select the beginning or ending portion of a file or stream, and -n adjusts how many lines are selected.

condition: when monitoring a growing file such as a log
statement: The tail -f option follows appended file content in real time until interrupted.

condition: when a pipeline stage should be saved without stopping the pipeline
statement: The tee command copies standard input both to standard output and to one or more files, allowing intermediate pipeline capture.

condition: when a command line contains expandable shell syntax such as wildcards
statement: Bash performs qualifying command-line expansions before executing the command, so commands receive expanded arguments rather than the original expansion syntax.

condition: when the command line contains wildcard patterns
statement: Pathname expansion is the shell mechanism that turns wildcard patterns into matching pathnames before command execution.

condition: when expanding filename patterns
statement: Pathname expansion normally excludes hidden dotfiles unless the pattern explicitly begins with a dot.

condition: when expanding hidden-file patterns with .*
statement: Using dot-star for hidden files can accidentally include the current and parent directory entries on shells where globskipdots is not set.

condition: when inspecting hidden files safely
statement: Use a more specific hidden-file pattern or ls -A when hidden files should be listed without including dot and dot-dot.

condition: when tilde expansion is applied at the beginning of a word
statement: A leading tilde expands to the current user's home directory, while a leading tilde plus username expands to that user's home directory.

condition: when using shell arithmetic expansion
statement: Arithmetic expansion uses the $((...)) form and evaluates integer arithmetic in the shell.

condition: when division is performed inside arithmetic expansion
statement: Shell arithmetic expansion supports integer results only, so division truncates rather than producing decimals.

condition: when a command line contains brace expansion syntax
statement: Brace expansion generates multiple text strings from comma lists or ranges before commands run.

condition: when writing brace expansion patterns
statement: Brace expansion patterns must not contain unquoted whitespace.

condition: when many similarly named directories or files are needed
statement: Brace expansion is useful for creating structured sets of pathnames, such as year-month directory trees.

condition: when a variable reference such as $USER is expanded
statement: Parameter expansion substitutes the value of a named variable into the command line.

condition: when the referenced variable is unset or unavailable
statement: A misspelled variable name in parameter expansion expands to an empty string rather than remaining visibly misspelled.

condition: when examining available variables
statement: The printenv command can list available environment variables for inspection.

condition: when using $(...) or supported legacy backquote syntax
statement: Command substitution uses a command's output as part of another command line.

condition: when the substitution expression runs a pipeline
statement: Command substitution can contain a whole pipeline, not just a single simple command.

condition: when command text contains characters the shell would otherwise treat specially
statement: Quoting is the shell mechanism for selectively suppressing expansion and word splitting.

condition: when command arguments are not quoted
statement: Unquoted spaces, tabs, and newlines act as word delimiters rather than literal text in shell word splitting.

condition: inside double-quoted shell text
statement: Double quotes suppress word splitting, pathname expansion, tilde expansion, and brace expansion while still allowing parameter, arithmetic, and command substitution.

condition: when a pathname contains spaces
statement: Double quotes should be used around filenames that contain embedded spaces so the shell treats the name as one argument.

condition: when command-substitution output must retain formatting or remain one argument
statement: Quoting command substitutions preserves embedded spaces and newlines as one argument instead of splitting them into many arguments.

condition: inside single-quoted shell text
statement: Single quotes suppress all shell expansions inside the quoted text.

condition: when only one character needs quoting
statement: A backslash can escape a single character to remove its shell-special meaning.

condition: when a filename contains shell-special characters
statement: Backslash escaping can protect special characters in filenames from shell interpretation.

condition: when an alias should be suppressed for one invocation
statement: A leading backslash before a command name can bypass an alias and run the underlying command lookup.

condition: inside single-quoted shell text
statement: Inside single quotes, a backslash is treated as an ordinary character.

condition: when producing control-code output such as tabs, newlines, or alerts
statement: Echo interprets backslash escape sequences only when enabled with -e or when using the shell's ANSI-C quoted form.

condition: when learning or troubleshooting shell command lines
statement: A solid understanding of expansion and quoting is essential to using the shell predictably and effectively.

condition: in interactive bash command editing
statement: Bash uses Readline for command-line editing, so cursor movement, editing, and cut-paste key bindings can reduce typing.

condition: when using Readline key sequences under a GUI terminal
statement: Some Alt-key Readline bindings may be intercepted by a graphical interface, while virtual consoles should receive them reliably.

condition: when requesting completion with Tab
statement: Tab completion succeeds only when the partially typed text identifies an unambiguous completion.

condition: when using bash completion
statement: Shell completion can apply to pathnames, variables, usernames, commands, and known hostnames depending on the word prefix and position.

condition: when completion has multiple possible matches
statement: A second Tab press or Alt-question-mark can show possible completions when the partial input is ambiguous.

condition: when every possible completion is wanted on the command line
statement: Alt-asterisk inserts all possible completions, which is useful when multiple matches should become arguments.

condition: when relying on advanced completion behavior
statement: Programmable completion lets bash or a distribution add application-specific completion rules, but not every distribution enables the same set.

condition: for interactive bash sessions using the default history facility
statement: Bash stores command history in the user's home directory and uses it to reduce repeated typing.

condition: when searching command history by text
statement: Piping history through grep is a practical way to find earlier commands containing a remembered fragment.

condition: when using bash history expansion
statement: History expansion can rerun a command by expanding an event designator such as a history line number.

condition: when searching command history interactively
statement: Reverse incremental search with Ctrl-r finds earlier history entries as text is typed; Enter runs the match and Ctrl-j copies it for editing.

condition: when bash history expansion is enabled
statement: History expansion uses exclamation-point forms to substitute commands from the shell history.

condition: when using !string or !?string forms
statement: Users should be cautious with prefix and substring history expansion because it can recall an unintended command from history.

condition: when previewing a history expansion before execution
statement: Appending :p to a history expansion prints the expansion and stores the result in history instead of immediately executing it.

condition: in Unix-style operating systems such as Linux
statement: Linux multi-user design protects users from each other and restricts system-level changes to administrative authority.

condition: when operating Linux as an ordinary user most of the time
statement: Even on a single-user personal computer, separate administrative privileges improve safety by limiting system-level modifications.

condition: for files and directories in the Unix security model
statement: Unix permissions model access around file owners, group members, and everyone else.
The id command reports the current user identity, primary group, and group memberships.

condition: on conventional Linux systems
statement: Linux account, group, and password-related identity data are stored in text files such as /etc/passwd, /etc/group, and /etc/shadow.

condition: in the Unix/Linux account model
statement: The superuser account always has user ID 0.

condition: when interpreting long directory listings
statement: The first character in ls -l file attributes identifies the file type, such as regular file, directory, symbolic link, character device, or block device.

condition: when interpreting permissions of symbolic links
statement: Symbolic-link mode bits displayed as rwxrwxrwx are dummy values; the target file's permissions control access.

condition: when interpreting file permission bits
statement: For regular files, read permits opening and reading, write permits writing or truncating, and execute permits running the file as a program.

condition: when interpreting directory permission bits
statement: For directories, read permits listing names, write permits creating, deleting, or renaming entries only with execute, and execute permits entering and accessing metadata.

condition: when reasoning about file removal or rename permissions
statement: Deleting or renaming a file is governed by permissions on the containing directory rather than by write permission on the file itself.

condition: when changing permissions with chmod
statement: Only a file or directory owner or the superuser can change its mode with chmod.

condition: when using numeric chmod modes
statement: Octal chmod notation maps each digit to a three-bit read, write, execute permission set.

condition: when applying a standard three-digit chmod mode
statement: Three octal chmod digits set permissions for owner, group owner, and others in that order.

condition: when reading or writing chmod numeric modes
statement: Common octal permission values are 7 for rwx, 6 for rw-, 5 for r-x, 4 for r--, and 0 for no permissions.

condition: when using symbolic chmod modes
statement: Symbolic chmod notation specifies who is affected, whether permissions are added, removed, or assigned, and which permission bits are involved.

condition: when a symbolic chmod expression has no u, g, o, or a selector
statement: If symbolic chmod omits a user class, all classes are assumed.

condition: when preserving the rest of an existing mode matters
statement: Symbolic chmod is useful for changing one permission attribute without disturbing unrelated permission bits.

condition: when considering recursive permission changes
statement: chmod --recursive should be used cautiously because it applies to both files and directories even though they often need different modes.

condition: when new filesystem objects are created under a shell umask
statement: The umask command controls default permissions for newly created files by masking away permission bits.

condition: when interpreting umask values
statement: A umask bit set to 1 removes the corresponding permission bit from the default mode.

condition: when deciding whether to change umask
statement: Most users should leave the distribution-provided umask alone unless they have a specific security requirement.

condition: when setuid is applied to an executable file
statement: The setuid bit on an executable makes the program run with the file owner's effective user ID, commonly root for privileged helpers.

condition: when granting setuid privileges
statement: Setuid programs should be kept to an absolute minimum because they raise security risk.

condition: when setgid is applied to a directory
statement: The setgid bit on a directory causes new files created there to inherit the directory's group ownership.

condition: when a common group collaborates in one directory
statement: Directory setgid is useful for shared group directories where all members need access to newly created files.

condition: when the sticky bit is applied to a directory
statement: On Linux directories, the sticky bit prevents users from deleting or renaming entries unless they own the file, own the directory, or are superuser.

condition: when a shared writable directory needs deletion protection
statement: The sticky bit is commonly used to control shared directories such as /tmp.

condition: when alternate user privileges are needed
statement: Users can take on another identity by logging in as that user, using su, or using sudo.

condition: when su authentication and account configuration permit it
statement: The su command can start a shell as another user or execute a single command as another user.

condition: when invoking su as a login shell
statement: Using su with a login-shell option loads the target user's environment and changes to that user's home directory.

condition: when invoking su without an explicit target user
statement: If no user is specified, su assumes the superuser account.

condition: when running a single command through su -c
statement: A command passed to su -c should be quoted so expansion happens in the target shell rather than the caller's shell.

condition: when sudo is configured in sudoers
statement: sudo lets an administrator grant ordinary users controlled permission to run commands as another user, usually root.

condition: under the sudo behavior described in the book
statement: sudo authenticates with the invoking user's password rather than requiring the superuser password.

condition: unless sudo options override the default behavior
statement: sudo normally runs a command without starting a new shell or loading another user's environment.

condition: when checking what sudo permits
statement: The sudo -l option lists sudo privileges granted to the invoking user.

condition: when performing tasks that require elevated privileges
statement: Unix-style administration should grant superuser privileges only when they are needed rather than making everyday work administrative.

condition: when deciding whether to use root for normal sessions
statement: Operating routinely as root reduces Linux security by giving user-run programs broad system authority.

condition: for modern Linux distributions described by the book
statement: Most modern Linux distributions favor sudo-based privilege grants over routine root logins.

condition: on distributions following the Ubuntu default model
statement: Ubuntu-style sudo setup disables direct root login by leaving the root account without a password and gives the initial user sudo access.

condition: when changing file ownership with chown
statement: The chown command changes the owner and group owner of files or directories and requires superuser privileges.

condition: when using chown owner:group syntax
statement: A chown argument can set only owner, owner plus group, only group, or owner plus that owner's login group depending on colon placement.

condition: when copying files into another user's area with sudo
statement: Files copied with sudo may become owned by root and need chown before the intended user can edit them normally.

condition: in most sudo configurations
statement: sudo commonly caches authentication for several minutes after a successful password entry.

condition: when only group ownership needs changing
statement: The chgrp command changes group ownership and remains available as a narrower alternative to chown.

condition: when multiple users need shared file access
statement: A shared writable directory should use a group containing all collaborators, rather than relying on world-writable access.

condition: when preparing a shared group for directory access
statement: groupadd creates a group, and usermod with append and group options adds users to that group.

condition: when the directory is under a system-wide location such as /usr/local/share
statement: Creating shared directories outside a user's home directory typically requires superuser privileges.

condition: when building a collaborative directory
statement: To make a directory group-shareable, set its group owner to the shared group and grant group write permissions.

condition: when group members need shared access to nested files and directories
statement: Setting setgid on a shared directory makes newly created entries inherit the directory group, keeping collaboration group ownership consistent.

condition: when the shared tree is hierarchical and group collaboration is expected
statement: A shared directory that contains nested directories may require a 0002 umask so group members can write into each other's created directories.

condition: when setting umask from the shell
statement: An interactively changed umask lasts only for the current session unless it is made persistent in startup configuration.
The passwd command changes the current user's password when run without a username.

condition: when password quality checks reject or warn on a new password
statement: The passwd command warns against weak passwords such as ones that are too short, too similar to previous passwords, dictionary-based, or easy to guess.

condition: when managing another account password
statement: A user with superuser privileges can pass a username to passwd to set another user's password.

condition: on a running Linux system
statement: Linux represents running programs and kernel activities as processes managed by the kernel.

condition: during Linux system startup
statement: System startup launches init as PID 1, and systemd or older init scripts start system services.

condition: when describing many Linux services
statement: Daemon programs run in the background without a user interface to provide system services.

condition: in the Linux process model
statement: A process can launch child processes, forming parent-child process relationships.

condition: while managing processes
statement: The kernel tracks each process with a process ID, memory allocation, execution readiness, and ownership identities.

condition: when inspecting processes with ps
statement: The ps command reports a process snapshot rather than a continuously updated view.

condition: when ps is run without additional options
statement: Plain ps shows only processes associated with the current terminal session.

condition: when viewing all processes owned by the current user
statement: ps x lists the user's processes even when they do not have a controlling terminal.

condition: when a broad process snapshot is needed
statement: ps aux lists processes for every user and adds verbose resource and ownership columns using BSD-style option behavior.

condition: when ps produces many rows or long command lines
statement: Long ps output is easier to inspect by piping it to less and widening the terminal for long lines.

condition: when interpreting ps state output
statement: The STAT column in ps indicates process state, including running, sleeping, uninterruptible sleep, stopped, zombie, high priority, and low priority.

condition: when investigating one known process ID
statement: A PID argument to ps can produce a detailed snapshot for one specific process.

condition: when monitoring process activity dynamically
statement: The top command provides a continuously updated process display sorted by activity and includes system summary information.

condition: when diagnosing system slowness from the command line
statement: top is often preferable to graphical system monitors for slowdown investigation because it is faster and uses fewer resources.

condition: when launching an interactive or graphical program from a terminal without backgrounding it
statement: A foreground command keeps the shell prompt unavailable until the program exits or is interrupted.

condition: when a foreground terminal program should be stopped
statement: Ctrl-C sends an interrupt request that asks many command-line programs to terminate and returns control to the shell if they exit.

condition: when a command can run without occupying the foreground terminal
statement: Appending an ampersand to a command launches it in the background and returns the shell prompt.

condition: when job control is active
statement: When a job is started in the background, the shell reports both a job number and the process ID.

condition: when using shell job control
statement: The jobs command lists jobs launched from the current terminal.

condition: when a job is running in the background
statement: A background job does not receive terminal keyboard input such as Ctrl-C until it is brought back to the foreground.

condition: when resuming direct terminal control of a job
statement: The fg command brings a background or stopped job to the foreground, using a percent-prefixed job number when needed.

condition: when terminal job-control stop is supported
statement: Ctrl-Z stops a foreground process without terminating it.

condition: when a stopped job should continue without occupying the prompt
statement: The bg command resumes a stopped job in the background.

condition: when troubleshooting or customizing a graphical program launch
statement: Launching a graphical program from the command line can expose startup errors and command-line options that may be hidden from a GUI launcher.

condition: when interpreting nice or top priority fields
statement: Process niceness controls scheduling priority, with lower niceness meaning higher CPU priority.

condition: when adjusting niceness
statement: Only the superuser may increase a process priority, while regular users may only lower priority for processes they own.

condition: when starting a process with adjusted scheduling priority
statement: The nice command launches a process with a specified niceness value.

condition: when adjusting a running process priority
statement: The renice command changes niceness for an already running process identified by PID.

condition: when considering negative niceness or higher priority
statement: Increasing a process priority is rarely necessary and can starve essential system processes of CPU time.

condition: when using kill
statement: The kill command sends signals to processes rather than inherently performing only termination.

condition: when sending a signal from the shell
statement: kill can address a process by PID or by shell jobspec.

condition: when using kill PID with no signal option
statement: If kill is invoked without an explicit signal, it sends TERM by default.

condition: when using terminal job-control keys
statement: Ctrl-C sends an interrupt signal to the foreground program, and Ctrl-Z sends a terminal-stop signal.

condition: when a signal is delivered to a process
statement: A program may handle or ignore many signals, which lets it clean up or save work when signaled.

condition: when gentler termination signals fail
statement: KILL should be used only as a last resort because the kernel terminates the process without giving it a chance to clean up.

condition: when asking a process to terminate normally with kill
statement: TERM is the normal default termination signal for kill when a process is able to receive signals.

condition: when continuing a stopped process
statement: CONT resumes a stopped process and is the signal used by bg and fg.

condition: when using the STOP signal
statement: STOP pauses a process without letting the target ignore the signal.

condition: when sending signals with kill or killall
statement: Processes may be signaled only by their owner or by the superuser.

condition: when a terminal hangup should not terminate the command
statement: The nohup command launches a program so it continues running after its controlling terminal closes.

condition: when terminating or signaling multiple matching processes
statement: The killall command sends a signal to multiple processes selected by program name and optionally by user.

condition: when shutting down Linux
statement: A proper system shutdown terminates processes orderly and syncs mounted filesystems before power-off or reboot.

condition: when using shutdown
statement: The shutdown command can halt, power down, or reboot the system with a specified delay and broadcasts a warning to logged-in users.

condition: when monitoring process-related system load
statement: Command-line process-management tools are preferred for many Linux diagnostics because they are fast and have a small resource footprint.

condition: during a shell session
statement: The shell environment stores data that programs can use to discover configuration and adjust behavior.

condition: in a bash shell session
statement: Bash maintains shell variables, environment variables, aliases, and shell functions as part of the session context.

condition: when examining the shell environment
statement: printenv displays environment variables, while set displays shell variables, environment variables, and shell functions.

condition: when inspecting all environment content
statement: Piping set or printenv to less is useful because environment listings are usually long.

condition: when examining command aliases
statement: Aliases are inspected separately with alias because set and printenv do not list them.

condition: when the shell resolves executable command names
statement: The PATH variable is a colon-separated directory list searched when an executable command name is entered without a pathname.

condition: when bash starts a new session
statement: Login and non-login shell sessions read different startup files, and non-login shells also inherit environment variables from their parent process.

condition: when choosing where to put ordinary bash customizations
statement: For ordinary users, ~/.bashrc is usually the most important startup file because non-login shells read it and login startup files often source it.

condition: when looking for bash startup files in the home directory
statement: Startup files whose names begin with a dot are hidden and require options such as ls -a to list them.

condition: when reading shell startup files
statement: Lines beginning with # in shell startup files are comments for humans and are not executed by the shell.

condition: when setting up personal command scripts or programs
statement: Appending $HOME/bin to PATH prepares the shell to find private programs stored in a bin directory under the user's home directory.

condition: when child programs need a variable value
statement: The export command makes a shell variable available to child processes as an environment variable.

condition: when a shell launches a child process
statement: Shell variables are local to the current shell instance and are not copied into child processes.

condition: when a shell launches a child process
statement: Environment variables are copied into child processes when they are launched.

condition: when a child process changes its own variables or environment
statement: A child process cannot alter the environment of its parent process.

condition: when one invocation needs a special environment setting
statement: A variable assignment placed immediately before a command runs that command with a temporary environment value.

condition: when the same temporary environment value should accompany a command routinely
statement: Temporary environment assignments can be wrapped in an alias for repeated use of the same command setting.

condition: when customizing a user's bash environment
statement: PATH additions and new environment variables generally belong in .bash_profile or the distribution-equivalent login startup file.

condition: when customizing aliases, shell options, or interactive shell behavior
statement: Most other ordinary bash customizations generally belong in .bashrc.

condition: when modifying shell startup files
statement: Users should restrict startup-file customization to files in their home directory unless they are administering defaults for all users.

condition: when changing configuration stored as plain text
statement: Text editors are the standard tool for modifying shell startup files and most Linux configuration files.
