condition: when choosing a tool for configuration files
statement: A text editor differs from a word processor by editing pure text and often providing features for program or configuration editing.

condition: when opening a new pathname in an editor
statement: A text editor invoked with a nonexistent filename treats the target as a new file to create.

condition: when modifying important configuration files
statement: Before editing an important configuration file, create a backup copy with an understandable name.

condition: when creating configuration-file backups with cp
statement: Because cp overwrites existing files silently by default, backup filenames should be chosen carefully or protected with interactive options.

condition: when editing with nano
statement: In nano, Ctrl-X exits and Ctrl-O writes the current file.

condition: when modifying configuration files
statement: Configuration-file changes should include comments explaining the reason for the change for future readers.

condition: when maintaining system or user configuration
statement: Keeping a log of configuration changes is useful because the reason for a change may be forgotten over time.

condition: when experimenting with configuration choices
statement: Commenting out a configuration line deactivates it while preserving the information, and uncommenting can activate prepared examples.

condition: after editing .bashrc
statement: Changes to .bashrc take effect in new sessions unless the file is reread explicitly.

condition: when applying shell file contents without starting a child shell
statement: The source command, or dot shorthand, reads commands from a file into the current shell.

condition: when choosing a fallback editor for remote or damaged systems
statement: vi is worth learning because it is nearly always available on Unix-like systems, including systems without a working GUI.

condition: when editing text from a terminal
statement: vi is lightweight and fast, making it suitable for quick command-line editing tasks.

condition: on typical Linux distributions
statement: Most Linux systems provide vim as an enhanced vi replacement and may link or alias it as vi.

condition: when vim compatibility mode blocks expected enhanced behavior
statement: If vim starts in vi-compatible mode, using vim directly, adding an alias, or setting nocp in ~/.vimrc can enable enhanced vim behavior.

condition: when vim features used by the book are unavailable
statement: If a distribution installs only a minimal vim, missing lesson features can be resolved by installing the full vim package.

condition: when editing in vi or vim
statement: vi is modal: normal mode treats keys as commands, while insert mode enters text.

condition: when text entry is complete or the user is disoriented
statement: Pressing Esc is the standard way to leave insert mode and return to normal mode in vi.

condition: when leaving vi
statement: The :q command exits vi, and :q! forces exit when unsaved changes would otherwise block quitting.

condition: when invoking vi with a pathname
statement: Starting vi with a filename opens that file or creates a new file with that name if it does not exist.

condition: when adding text in vi
statement: The i command enters insert mode before the current cursor position.

condition: when saving work in vi
statement: The :w command writes the edited file to disk from vi command-line mode.

condition: when using vi normal-mode commands
statement: Many vi movement and editing commands can be prefixed with a number to repeat the command that many times.

condition: when reversing recent edits
statement: The u command undoes the last change in vi, with vim supporting multiple undo levels.

condition: when appending text in vi
statement: The a command appends after the cursor, while A moves to the end of the current line and appends there.

condition: when inserting a new line in vi
statement: The o command opens a new line below the current line, and O opens a new line above it.

condition: when deleting text in vi
statement: The x command deletes characters at the cursor, while d combined with a movement command deletes a larger text range.

condition: when using d deletions in vi
statement: The d command also cuts deleted text into a paste buffer for later insertion.

condition: when yanking text in vi
statement: The y command copies text using the same movement-combination style as d.

condition: when pasting in vi
statement: The p command pastes buffered text after the cursor, and P pastes it before the cursor.

condition: when combining lines in vi
statement: The J command joins the current line with the line below it.

condition: when searching within one line in vi
statement: In vi normal mode, f followed by a character searches the current line for the next occurrence of that character.

condition: after a line character search in vi
statement: A semicolon repeats the previous vi character search within the line.

condition: when searching an entire file in vi
statement: The slash command searches forward through a vi file for a word, phrase, or regular-expression pattern.

condition: after a slash search in vi
statement: The n command repeats the previous vi file search.

condition: when using vi search-and-replace
statement: vi substitution commands operate over an explicit line range, with percent meaning the whole file and an omitted range meaning only the current line.

condition: when using vi substitution
statement: The g flag in a vi substitution replaces every match on each affected line instead of only the first match on each line.

condition: when replacements should be reviewed before application
statement: Adding c to a vi substitution requests confirmation for each replacement.

condition: when editing related files together
statement: vi can open multiple files in one editing session when multiple filenames are supplied on the command line.

condition: when changing buffers with unsaved changes
statement: vi prevents switching away from a modified buffer unless changes are saved or the switch is forced with an exclamation point.

condition: when multiple buffers are open
statement: :bn and :bp move to the next and previous buffers in a vi editing session.

condition: when tracking multiple open files in vim
statement: :buffers lists the files currently open in vim buffers.

condition: when selecting among multiple vi buffers
statement: :buffer followed by a buffer number switches directly to that file buffer.

condition: when adding a file to an existing editing session
statement: :e followed by a filename opens an additional file in the current vi session.

condition: when moving text between files in the same vi session
statement: vi yank and paste commands can copy text from one open buffer into another.

condition: when inserting an entire file into the current vi buffer
statement: :r followed by a filename inserts that file below the current cursor line.

condition: when leaving vi after saving
statement: ZZ and :wq both save the current file and exit vi.

condition: when using vi save-as behavior
statement: :w followed by a filename writes a copy under that name without changing the file currently being edited.

condition: when configuring interactive bash editing mode
statement: Bash can use vi-style command-line editing when set -o vi is enabled.

condition: when a user wants persistent vi-style command-line editing
statement: Adding set -o vi to .bashrc makes vi-style command-line editing persistent for future shells.

condition: when leaving vi-style shell editing
statement: set -o emacs restores the default emacs-style bash command-line editing mode.

condition: when investing effort in command-line editing skills
statement: Learning vi has compounding value because vi-style editing influences other Unix tools such as less and bash command-line editing.

condition: when customizing the shell prompt
statement: The PS1 environment variable defines the visible primary bash prompt.

condition: when constructing PS1
statement: Prompt strings can include bash backslash escapes for information such as user, host, working directory, time, command count, and privilege marker.

condition: when comparing prompt output across systems
statement: Different Linux distributions may define different default PS1 strings.

condition: when trying alternative prompt designs interactively
statement: Before experimenting with PS1, save the old value in another shell variable so it can be restored during the session.

condition: when designing a custom prompt
statement: A prompt string should usually include a visible separator or trailing space so the cursor does not run into the prompt text.

condition: when PS1 contains terminal-control characters
statement: Non-printing prompt sequences must be wrapped with \[ and \] so bash can calculate prompt length correctly for cursor positioning.

condition: when the terminal emulator interprets ANSI control sequences
statement: ANSI escape codes embedded in PS1 can change terminal colors and other display attributes.

condition: when adding color to PS1
statement: After setting a color in a prompt, reset terminal attributes so user-entered text does not inherit unintended styling.

condition: when relying on advanced prompt escape sequences
statement: Some terminal emulators may ignore particular display or cursor-control escape codes.

condition: when using terminal cursor-control escape codes in PS1
statement: A complex prompt can draw information elsewhere on the terminal screen by saving cursor position, moving the cursor, writing control output, and restoring position.

condition: when a prompt design should survive new shell sessions
statement: A custom prompt can be made persistent by adding the PS1 assignment and export to .bashrc.

condition: when evaluating Linux distributions
statement: A Linux distribution's packaging system and support community are more important quality factors than superficial desktop differences.

condition: when managing distribution-provided software
statement: Package management is the standard method for installing and maintaining software on contemporary Linux systems.

condition: when the needed software is available from the distribution
statement: Installing distributor-provided precompiled packages is generally faster and easier than downloading and compiling source code manually.

condition: when maintaining Linux software
statement: Command-line package tools are worth learning because they can perform tasks that graphical package managers may handle poorly or not at all.

condition: when selecting package files for installation
statement: Packages are generally built for a specific distribution family and should not be assumed compatible across distributions.

condition: when identifying a distribution packaging family
statement: Most mainstream distributions use either Debian-style .deb packages or Red Hat-style .rpm packages.

condition: when reasoning about what a package installs
statement: A package file contains the software files plus metadata and may include pre-installation or post-installation scripts.

condition: when tracing how upstream software becomes a distribution package
statement: Package maintainers adapt upstream source code into distribution packages and may patch it for better distribution integration.

condition: when installing software through package tools
statement: Distribution repositories provide centrally maintained packages built for that distribution.

condition: when choosing repositories to enable
statement: Testing and development repositories may contain packages that are not yet intended for ordinary general use.

condition: when software is unavailable from the distribution repository
statement: Third-party repositories can provide legally or policy-constrained software, but they are independent and must be manually configured.

condition: when installing software packages
statement: Package dependencies are required supporting components such as shared libraries that a package needs in order to function.

condition: when using tools such as apt or dnf
statement: High-level package tools perform repository metadata search and dependency resolution.

condition: when using tools such as dpkg or rpm directly
statement: Low-level package tools install or remove package files but do not provide the same dependency-resolution workflow as high-level tools.

condition: on Debian-style package systems
statement: Debian-style systems use dpkg as a low-level tool and apt, apt-get, or aptitude as high-level tools.

condition: on Red Hat-style package systems
statement: Red Hat-style systems use rpm as the low-level package tool and dnf or yum as high-level tools.

condition: when using apt against repositories
statement: Debian apt workflows need apt update periodically to synchronize the local repository database before package operations.

condition: when using dnf as described by the book
statement: dnf updates its local package database automatically when enough time has elapsed.

condition: when changing installed system packages
statement: Installing or removing system-wide software requires superuser privileges regardless of the package tool.

condition: when locating packages by name or description
statement: Repository search uses apt search on Debian-style systems and dnf search on Red Hat-style systems.

condition: when installing a package from a configured repository
statement: Repository installation uses apt install on Debian-style systems and dnf install on Red Hat-style systems.

condition: when installing a downloaded package file outside a repository workflow
statement: Direct package-file installation uses dpkg -i for Debian package files and rpm -i for RPM package files.

condition: when installing downloaded packages with dpkg or rpm directly
statement: Direct low-level package-file installation can fail on missing dependencies because dependency resolution is not performed.

condition: when uninstalling packages through high-level tools
statement: Package removal uses apt remove on Debian-style systems and dnf erase on Red Hat-style systems.

condition: when applying repository updates
statement: System package updates use apt update followed by apt upgrade on Debian-style systems and dnf update on Red Hat-style systems.

condition: when listing installed packages
statement: Installed package listing uses dpkg -l on Debian-style systems and rpm -qa on Red Hat-style systems.

condition: when determining whether a specific package is installed
statement: Package status checks use dpkg -s on Debian-style systems and rpm -q on Red Hat-style systems.

condition: when viewing a package description
statement: Package information lookup uses apt show on Debian-style systems and dnf info on Red Hat-style systems.

condition: when identifying which package installed a file
statement: File-to-package ownership can be traced with dpkg -S on Debian-style systems and rpm -qf on Red Hat-style systems.

condition: when using formats such as Snap, Flatpak, or AppImage
statement: Distribution-independent package formats bundle applications with dependencies to reduce per-distribution packaging work.

condition: when evaluating Snap, Flatpak, or AppImage tradeoffs
statement: All-in-one package formats can consume more disk space, load more slowly, and integrate less well with the base distribution.

condition: when choosing package formats for applications
statement: The book does not recommend all-in-one package formats until their performance issues are resolved.

condition: when installing software available in distribution repositories
statement: Linux software installation is usually easier when open-source programs are packaged by distributions and delivered through repositories.

condition: when comparing Linux driver installation with other platforms
statement: Linux device drivers are generally part of the kernel rather than installed from separate driver disks.

condition: when selecting hardware for Linux compatibility
statement: Users should avoid hardware whose vendor withholds both Linux driver source code and technical documentation.

condition: when managing storage devices
statement: Mounting attaches a storage device to the single Linux filesystem tree so the operating system can use it.

condition: when comparing desktop and server storage management
statement: Desktop Linux systems often mount removable storage automatically, while servers commonly require more manual storage configuration.

condition: when inspecting boot-time filesystem mounts
statement: /etc/fstab lists filesystems that should be mounted at boot time.

condition: when interpreting fstab device fields
statement: Modern fstab entries may identify devices by label or UUID so hot-pluggable hardware is recognized despite changing device filenames.

condition: when reading /etc/fstab entries
statement: fstab records the mount point, filesystem type, mount options, dump frequency, and fsck check order for each listed filesystem.

condition: when inspecting mounted filesystems
statement: Running mount without arguments lists currently mounted filesystems.

condition: when interpreting mount output
statement: A mount listing shows the device, mount point, filesystem type, and mount options.

condition: when mount output is cluttered
statement: Filtering mount output with grep can make device-backed mounts easier to inspect on systems with many virtual or snap loop mounts.

condition: when mounting, formatting, partitioning, or copying devices
statement: Users must identify the actual device name on their own system before running storage commands rather than copying example device names.

condition: when detaching a filesystem from the tree
statement: The umount command unmounts a mounted filesystem.

condition: when manually mounting a filesystem
statement: A mount point is an ordinary directory where a filesystem is attached.

condition: when using a non-empty directory as a mount point
statement: Mounting over a non-empty directory hides the directory's previous contents until the mounted device is unmounted.

condition: when manually mounting a filesystem whose type is supplied
statement: The mount -t option specifies the filesystem type for a manual mount.

condition: when umount reports the device is busy
statement: A filesystem cannot be unmounted while it is in use by a user or process.

condition: when the shell is located inside the mount point
statement: Leaving a mounted filesystem as the current working directory can make it busy and prevent unmounting.

condition: when umount fails because the current shell is in the mounted filesystem
statement: Changing the working directory away from a mount point can resolve a busy unmount caused by the shell itself.

condition: when preparing removable storage for removal
statement: Unmounting a storage device flushes remaining buffered data to the device so it can be removed safely.

condition: when using removable storage
statement: Removing a storage device without unmounting can lose unwritten data and corrupt filesystem metadata.

condition: when interpreting storage device names
statement: Modern Linux names most disk-like devices with /dev/sd* paths, with trailing digits identifying partitions.

condition: when automatic mounting does not reveal a device name
statement: Following syslog with tail -f or following the systemd journal with journalctl -f can reveal device names as removable devices are attached.

condition: when identifying disks and partitions
statement: The lsblk command lists attached block devices whether or not they are mounted.

condition: when relying on an observed device name
statement: A newly attached block device name remains stable while it stays physically attached and the computer is not rebooted.

condition: when preparing a disk with new partitions and filesystems
statement: Creating new filesystems on a drive requires a partition layout step and a filesystem-creation step.

condition: when practicing parted or mkfs operations
statement: Partitioning and formatting examples should be performed only on drives whose contents can be erased.

condition: when invoking parted
statement: parted operates on an entire disk device rather than on an individual partition device.

condition: when manipulating partitions on a mounted device
statement: A device partition should be unmounted before editing its partition table with parted.

condition: when checking an existing partition layout
statement: The parted print command displays the current partition table for the selected device.

condition: when removing an existing partition in parted
statement: The parted rm command deletes a partition by partition number.

condition: when creating partitions interactively with parted
statement: The parted mkpart command creates a partition using a partition type, filesystem type hint, and start and end positions.

condition: when confirming a partitioning operation
statement: After partitioning, lsblk should be used to verify that the expected partitions exist.

condition: when formatting a partition
statement: mkfs creates a filesystem on a specified device or partition.

condition: when creating named filesystems
statement: mkfs -t selects the filesystem type, and -L assigns a volume label where supported.

condition: when using mkfs for NTFS with --quick
statement: The NTFS quick format option skips bad-block checking and is faster than a full check.

condition: when formatting with a specific filesystem type
statement: Different filesystem types support different mkfs options, so the mkfs manual should be consulted for details.

condition: when automatically mounting labeled removable partitions
statement: Removable-storage volume labels can be used by the desktop to create mount-point names under /media.

condition: when boot-time filesystem checks are configured
statement: fsck checks filesystem integrity during boot according to the order specified in /etc/fstab.

condition: when interpreting fstab fsck order
statement: fstab entries with a final check-order value of zero are not routinely checked by fsck at boot.

condition: when attempting filesystem repair
statement: fsck can repair corrupted filesystems with success depending on damage severity.

condition: when checking or repairing a partition with fsck
statement: A filesystem should be unmounted before running fsck on it.

condition: when fsck recovers damaged file contents
statement: Recovered fragments from Unix-like filesystem repair are placed in the filesystem's lost+found directory.

condition: when using dd
statement: The dd command copies raw blocks of data from an input file or device to an output file or device.

condition: when using dd with disks or image files
statement: dd input and output specifications must be double-checked because reversing or mistyping them can destroy data.

condition: when exact block-level copies are needed
statement: dd can clone one device to another device of the same size or save a device image into an ordinary file.

condition: when imaging data optical media
statement: dd can create an ISO image from a data CD or DVD by copying the optical device to a file.

condition: when the source media is an audio CD
statement: dd is not suitable for imaging audio CDs because audio CDs do not use a filesystem for storage.

condition: when building optical-media image content from files
statement: genisoimage creates an ISO image from a prepared directory tree.

condition: when creating ISO images for Unix-like metadata preservation
statement: The genisoimage -R option adds Rock Ridge metadata for long filenames and POSIX-style permissions.

condition: when creating ISO images intended for Windows compatibility
statement: The genisoimage -J option adds Joliet extensions for Windows long-filename support.

condition: when inspecting an ISO image before writing it to optical media
statement: An ISO image can be mounted directly with mount using iso9660 type and the loop option.

condition: when finished inspecting a mounted ISO image
statement: A loop-mounted ISO image should be unmounted when it is no longer needed.

condition: when reusing CD-RW optical media
statement: Rewritable CD-RW media must be blanked before reuse, and wodim can perform fast blanking.

condition: when burning an optical image
statement: wodim writes an ISO image to optical media when given the writer device and image file.

condition: when preparing optical media for commercial reproduction
statement: wodim disc-at-once mode should be used for discs intended for commercial reproduction.

condition: when validating large downloaded files such as installation images
statement: sha256sum can verify that a downloaded image file is complete and uncorrupted.

condition: when reasoning about checksum integrity checks
statement: A checksum changes significantly if the checked file differs by even one bit.

condition: when manually comparing a binary download to a published checksum
statement: sha256sum -b computes a checksum for a binary file.

condition: when verifying one file from a multi-file checksum list
statement: sha256sum -c checks downloaded files against a checksum file, and --ignore-missing suppresses complaints about listed files not present locally.

condition: when following the book's networking examples
statement: Some networking commands may need additional packages or superuser privileges depending on the distribution.

condition: when checking network connectivity
statement: ping verifies basic reachability by sending ICMP echo requests to a host and observing replies.

condition: when interpreting failed ping results
statement: A host or firewall can be configured to ignore or block ICMP echo traffic, so failed ping output does not always prove the host is down.

condition: when running ping interactively
statement: ping continues sending packets until interrupted and then prints packet-loss and timing statistics.

condition: when using ping as a first connectivity check
statement: A healthy ping test generally shows zero packet loss and indicates that interface, cabling, routing, and gateway elements are working broadly.

condition: when interpreting ping response hostnames
statement: The host that replies to ping can differ in name from the requested site because one machine can host multiple site names.

condition: when tracing network paths
statement: traceroute lists the network hops between the local system and a destination host.

condition: when interpreting traceroute output
statement: Asterisks in traceroute output indicate hops that did not provide identifying information, often because of configuration, congestion, or filtering.

condition: when default traceroute output is blocked or incomplete
statement: traceroute options such as -T or -I may help when ordinary routing information is blocked.

condition: on modern Linux systems
statement: The ip command is the modern Linux network configuration and inspection tool replacing deprecated ifconfig usage.

condition: when diagnosing basic network interface state
statement: For casual interface diagnostics with ip address show, check that the interface is UP and has a valid inet address.

condition: when the interface obtains addresses via DHCP
statement: On DHCP-configured systems, a valid inet address in ip output indicates that DHCP is working.

condition: when inspecting routing configuration
statement: ip route show displays routes including direct local networks and the default gateway.

condition: when seeing a 169.254 route or address
statement: Automatic Private IP Addressing can assign a 169.254.0.0-range address when DHCP is unavailable.

condition: when shortening ip commands such as ip address show or ip route show
statement: The ip command accepts object and command abbreviations as long as they are unambiguous, and show is the default command.

condition: when considering FTP for authenticated transfer
statement: Original FTP transmits usernames and passwords in cleartext and is therefore insecure on untrusted networks.

condition: when using legacy FTP servers for public downloads
statement: Anonymous FTP reduces credential exposure by using a public anonymous login rather than a real account password.

condition: when choosing a command-line FTP-style client
statement: The lftp client adds conveniences over traditional ftp, including multi-protocol support, retries, background processes, and tab completion.

condition: when using curl without an output option
statement: curl transfers data from URLs and writes to standard output by default.

condition: when selecting curl options for a transfer
statement: curl supports many protocols and options for naming output files, suppressing output, authenticating, and showing verbose transfer details.

condition: when downloading content from web or FTP sites without an interactive session
statement: wget is useful for non-interactive downloads of single files, multiple files, or entire sites.

condition: when using wget options for long or interrupted downloads
statement: wget can continue partial downloads and run downloads in the background.

condition: when choosing a remote-login method on modern networks
statement: rlogin and telnet are inappropriate for Internet-age remote login because they transmit communications, including credentials, in cleartext.

condition: when using SSH for remote access
statement: SSH provides secure remote communication by authenticating the remote host and encrypting traffic between local and remote systems.

condition: under the default SSH server configuration described by the book
statement: An SSH server listens for incoming connections on TCP port 22 by default.

condition: when enabling remote SSH logins
statement: A system must have the OpenSSH server installed, configured, running, and reachable through any firewall to receive SSH connections.

condition: when no separate remote system is available for SSH examples
statement: localhost can be used as the remote host for SSH practice when an SSH server is installed on the same machine.

condition: when connecting to a new SSH host
statement: The first SSH connection to a host prompts the user to accept the host credentials because the client has not seen that host before.

condition: when using ssh for an interactive remote shell
statement: An SSH session remains connected until exit is run in the remote shell, after which the local shell resumes.

condition: when the remote account name is different
statement: ssh user@host connects to a remote account whose username differs from the local username.

condition: when SSH rejects a changed host key
statement: An SSH host-identification-changed warning may indicate either a man-in-the-middle attack or a benign remote host reinstallation or key change.

condition: when SSH reports remote host identification has changed
statement: A changed SSH host key warning should be checked with the remote system administrator before the known-hosts entry is changed.

condition: when resolving a verified benign host-key change
statement: After a changed SSH host key is confirmed benign, the obsolete known_hosts entry can be removed with ssh-keygen -R or by deleting the indicated line.

condition: when a remote shell session is not needed
statement: ssh can execute one command on a remote host and display the command output locally.

condition: when a remote command contains wildcards or shell syntax
statement: Remote ssh commands should be quoted when expansions must happen on the remote host rather than on the local shell.

condition: when redirecting output from an ssh remote command
statement: Redirection outside the remote ssh command quotes affects the local machine, while redirection inside the quotes affects the remote machine.

condition: when an SSH connection is established
statement: SSH creates an encrypted tunnel that can carry commands, results, and many other types of network traffic.

condition: when the local system runs an X server and SSH X forwarding is enabled
statement: SSH X forwarding can run an X client on a remote host while displaying its window locally.

condition: when ssh -X does not enable the needed X forwarding behavior
statement: Some systems require ssh -Y rather than ssh -X for graphical X forwarding.

condition: when copying files over SSH
statement: scp copies files through an SSH-encrypted tunnel using cp-like source and destination syntax.

condition: when copying between local and remote systems with scp
statement: scp remote paths can be prefixed with host or user@host followed by a colon.

condition: when using interactive secure file transfer
statement: sftp provides an FTP-like interface over an SSH encrypted tunnel.

condition: when choosing secure FTP-like transfer to an SSH-capable host
statement: sftp requires only an SSH server on the remote host rather than a separate FTP server.

condition: when the file manager supports SFTP locations
statement: Graphical Linux file managers can often access remote SSH files through sftp:// URIs.

condition: when finding files by name with locate
statement: The locate command performs a fast database search of pathnames by substring.

condition: when locate substring matching is too broad
statement: locate output can be combined with tools such as grep for more selective pathname searches.

condition: when relying on locate options such as regular expressions or wildcards
statement: Different locate implementations support different option sets, so the installed locate man page should be checked.

condition: when explaining locate freshness
statement: The locate database is built by updatedb, commonly through a scheduled cron job.

condition: when locate misses a newly created file
statement: Very recent files may not appear in locate results because the locate database is not updated continuously.

condition: when locate needs to see newly created pathnames immediately
statement: Running updatedb manually as superuser refreshes the locate database.

condition: when locating files by more than name substring
statement: The find command searches specified directories and subdirectories for files matching attributes.

condition: when counting or processing find results
statement: find writes its result list to standard output, so it can be piped to tools such as wc.

condition: when building find commands
statement: find uses options, tests, and actions to identify and process matching files.

condition: when searching only for a specific filesystem object type
statement: The find -type test restricts matches to file types such as directories, regular files, symbolic links, and device files.

condition: when using find -name with wildcard patterns
statement: A wildcard passed to find -name should be quoted so the shell does not expand it before find receives it.

condition: when searching by size with find
statement: The find -size test uses plus for larger than, minus for smaller than, and no sign for exactly the specified size.

condition: when writing find -size arguments
statement: find size suffixes specify units such as bytes, kilobytes, megabytes, and gigabytes.

condition: when choosing find predicates
statement: find tests can match modification times, ownership, permissions, inode identity, emptiness, invalid users or groups, and filenames.

condition: when identifying files changed since the last backup marker
statement: find -newer is useful for backup scripts because it can find files changed since a marker file was updated.

condition: when auditing filesystem ownership
statement: find -nouser and -nogroup can help detect files from deleted accounts or suspicious activity.

condition: when building compound find expressions
statement: find combines tests with logical operators, with -and implied when no operator is supplied.

condition: when grouping find predicates on a shell command line
statement: Parentheses in find expressions group tests but must be escaped or quoted for the shell and separated from surrounding words with spaces.

condition: when combining find tests and actions
statement: find uses short-circuit AND/OR evaluation, so the left expression can determine whether the right expression is evaluated.

condition: when running find without explicit actions
statement: find performs the -print action by default when no other action is specified.

condition: when deleting files from find results
statement: The find -delete action deletes matching files and should be used with extreme caution.

condition: when preparing a destructive find command
statement: Before using find -delete, substitute -print first to verify the exact matches that would be deleted.

condition: when combining find predicates and actions
statement: The order of find tests and actions matters because actions participate in the expression logic.

condition: when applying a command to each find match
statement: The find -exec action runs an arbitrary command with the current pathname substituted for braces.

condition: when writing find -exec on a shell command line
statement: The braces and semicolon used by find -exec must be quoted or escaped so the shell passes them to find.

condition: when each matched-file action should be confirmed interactively
statement: The find -ok action prompts before executing each user-defined action.

condition: when using traditional find -exec termination
statement: find -exec with a semicolon launches the command once per matching file.

condition: when reducing command-launch overhead for find results
statement: find -exec with a trailing plus batches matching pathnames into a single command invocation when possible.

condition: when piping pathnames or items into a command
statement: xargs converts standard input into an argument list for another command.

condition: when standard input produces too many arguments for one command line
statement: xargs splits overly long argument lists into multiple command invocations when system command-line length limits would be exceeded.

condition: when investigating xargs batching limits
statement: xargs --show-limits reports the system command-line size limits used by xargs.

condition: when pathnames are passed through xargs without null separation
statement: Filenames containing spaces or newlines can break whitespace-delimited xargs pipelines.

condition: when piping arbitrary pathnames from find to xargs
statement: Use find -print0 with xargs --null or -0 to handle filenames containing embedded whitespace safely.

condition: when creating nested directory structures
statement: mkdir -p creates missing parent directories along a specified path.

condition: when generating a predictable test or work tree
statement: Brace expansion combined with mkdir or touch can create large structured sets of directories and files concisely.

condition: when using touch on pathnames
statement: touch updates file access, change, and modification times and creates an empty file if the named file does not exist.

condition: when interpreting find output order
statement: find result order is determined by filesystem layout rather than sorted like ls output.

condition: when inspecting timestamps, ownership, mode, inode, or size details
statement: The stat command displays detailed file or filesystem attributes known to the system.

condition: when finding files changed after a marker file
statement: The find -newer test can identify files modified after a reference file timestamp.

condition: when applying separate permission rules to files and directories
statement: find can combine type, permission, and action expressions to repair different file and directory permissions in one traversal.

condition: when a compound find command becomes hard to read
statement: For everyday work, separate simpler find commands may be easier than one large compound expression.

condition: when constraining find traversal
statement: find options such as maxdepth, mindepth, mount, depth, and noleaf control the scope or traversal behavior of a search.

condition: when choosing file-search tools to master
statement: locate is simpler than find, but find is more expressive and worth learning for filesystem operations.

condition: when administering or protecting system data
statement: Timely backups are a primary way to keep system data secure.

condition: when handling collections of files
statement: Archiving and backup tools are useful even for non-administrators who need to copy or move large file collections.

condition: when compressing files
statement: Data compression reduces redundant data to store or transmit information in less space.

condition: when comparing compression methods
statement: Lossless compression restores exactly the original data, while lossy compression restores only an approximation.

condition: when compressing ordinary files for storage or backup
statement: General computer data should use lossless compression because most data cannot tolerate loss.

condition: when running gzip on file arguments
statement: gzip compresses files by replacing each original with a .gz compressed version.

condition: when decompressing gzip files
statement: gunzip restores gzip-compressed files and replaces the compressed version with the uncompressed original.

condition: when compressing and decompressing with gzip as demonstrated
statement: gzip and gunzip preserve file permissions and timestamps in the basic workflow shown.

condition: when compressed output should be redirected or piped without replacing the source
statement: gzip -c writes compressed output to standard output and keeps the original file.

condition: when verifying gzip compressed files
statement: gzip -t tests compressed-file integrity, and -v shows verbose messages.

condition: when choosing gzip compression level options
statement: gzip compression levels range from fastest and least compression to slowest and most compression, with a default middle setting.

condition: when inspecting compressed text
statement: zcat and zless allow gzip-compressed text files to be viewed without explicitly decompressing them to ordinary files.

condition: when choosing between gzip and bzip2
statement: bzip2 works similarly to gzip but usually achieves higher compression at the cost of speed.

condition: when handling bzip2-compressed files
statement: bzip2 uses the .bz2 extension and has bunzip2 and bzcat companion commands.

condition: when a bzip2-compressed file is damaged
statement: bzip2recover can attempt to recover damaged .bz2 files.

condition: when considering compression of files such as JPEG images
statement: Compressing an already effectively compressed file usually wastes time and may make the file larger.

condition: when archiving files on Linux or Unix-like systems
statement: tar is the classic Unix-like tool for bundling files and directory hierarchies into archives.

condition: when interpreting archive filenames
statement: .tar commonly denotes a plain tar archive and .tgz denotes a gzip-compressed tar archive.

condition: when choosing tar operation mode
statement: tar modes include create, extract, append, and list.

condition: when forming tar command options
statement: The tar mode must be specified before tar options such as f.

condition: when reading or writing a tar archive file
statement: The tar f option supplies the archive filename.

condition: when extracting an archive
statement: tar extracts files relative to the current working directory.

condition: when restoring tar archives
statement: Files extracted from tar archives are owned by the extracting user unless extraction is performed as superuser.

condition: when archiving absolute paths with tar
statement: tar strips leading slashes from archived absolute pathnames, making extraction relative rather than forced to original root paths.

condition: when restoring a root filesystem tree from a tar archive
statement: When restoring a tar archive that should recreate root-relative paths, first change to the root directory before extraction.

condition: when extracting selected files from a tar archive
statement: tar can selectively extract specific pathnames, but the pathname must match the full relative pathname stored in the archive.

condition: when archiving selected find results
statement: find can feed tar append mode to build archives from files matching search criteria.

condition: when designing simple incremental backups
statement: find with a timestamp marker can feed tar to create incremental archives of files newer than the last archive.

condition: when piping tar archives
statement: tar uses a dash filename convention to read from standard input or write to standard output.

condition: when supplying many archive members from find output
statement: tar --files-from or -T reads the list of archived pathnames from a file or standard input.

condition: when creating compressed tar archives directly
statement: GNU tar can apply gzip compression with z and bzip2 compression with j.

condition: when both systems have tar and ssh available
statement: tar output can be piped through ssh and extracted on another system to transfer directory trees over an encrypted connection.

condition: when exchanging archives with Windows systems
statement: zip is both an archiver and a compression tool using the .zip format familiar to Windows users.

condition: when zipping a directory tree
statement: zip requires -r to archive a directory's contents recursively.

condition: when adding files to an existing zip archive
statement: If zip targets an existing archive, it updates that archive rather than replacing it wholesale.

condition: when extracting a zip archive into a directory with existing files
statement: unzip extracts zip archives and prompts before replacing conflicting existing files.

condition: when inspecting a zip archive
statement: unzip -l lists archive contents without extracting them.

condition: when the extraction target should not be the current directory
statement: unzip -d extracts a zip archive into a specified destination directory.

condition: when comparing zip with tar for streaming transfers
statement: unzip does not accept standard input for archive extraction, which limits zip/unzip for tar-style network copying pipelines.

condition: when choosing an archive format on Linux
statement: On Linux, tar with gzip is generally preferred for archiving, while zip is mainly useful for Windows interoperability.

condition: when keeping directories synchronized
statement: rsync synchronizes local or remote files and directories by transferring only the differences needed to make destinations match sources.

condition: when repeating backups or deployments
statement: rsync is faster and more economical than ordinary copy programs for repeated synchronization because it detects unchanged files.

condition: when forming rsync commands
statement: rsync source and destination operands may be local paths, SSH-style remote paths, or rsync-server URIs.

condition: when planning rsync transfer topology
statement: rsync does not support remote-to-remote copying because either source or destination must be local.

condition: when mirroring directory trees with rsync
statement: rsync -a enables archive behavior including recursion and preservation of file attributes.

condition: when specifying rsync source directories
statement: A trailing slash on an rsync source directory copies the directory contents rather than the directory itself.

condition: when comparing rsync source/ with shell globbing
statement: Using a trailing slash with rsync copies hidden files too, unlike a simple shell source/* pattern.

condition: when maintaining a true synchronized backup copy
statement: rsync --delete removes destination files that no longer exist in the source, making later backups mirror deletions as well as additions.

condition: when synchronizing to a remote host
statement: rsync can use ssh as its remote shell for encrypted network synchronization, and modern systems commonly make ssh the default.

condition: when synchronizing from a public or configured rsync server
statement: An rsync daemon can serve repositories over rsync:// URIs for efficient mirroring.

condition: when searching or manipulating text
statement: Regular expressions are symbolic notations for matching patterns in text and are more expressive than shell wildcard matching.

condition: when applying regex knowledge across tools
statement: Regular expression dialects vary among tools and languages, so POSIX regular expressions are the book's command-line baseline.

condition: when using grep with a regex
statement: grep searches files for lines matching a regular expression and writes matching lines to standard output.

condition: when selecting grep output behavior
statement: grep options can ignore case, invert matches, count matches, list files with or without matches, show line numbers, suppress filenames, or run quietly for scripts.

condition: when passing regex patterns through a shell
statement: Regular expressions containing metacharacters should be quoted on the command line to prevent shell expansion before grep sees them.

condition: when using POSIX-style regular expressions
statement: The dot metacharacter in a regular expression matches any single character in that position.

condition: when using line-oriented regular expressions
statement: In regular expressions, caret anchors a match to the beginning of a line and dollar sign anchors it to the end of a line.

condition: when searching for empty lines
statement: The regular expression consisting of beginning and ending anchors with nothing between them matches blank lines.

condition: when using regex character sets
statement: Bracket expressions match one character from a specified set.

condition: inside bracket expressions
statement: Most regex metacharacters lose their special meaning inside bracket expressions.

condition: when using negated bracket expressions
statement: A caret as the first character in a bracket expression negates the set and requires a character not in that set.

condition: when caret is not the first bracket-expression character
statement: A caret outside first position in a bracket expression is treated as an ordinary character.

condition: when using bracket ranges
statement: A dash expresses a character range inside a bracket expression unless positioned where it is interpreted literally.

condition: when matching dash as a character inside a bracket expression
statement: Placing a dash first in a bracket expression is a way to include a literal dash in the set.

condition: when locale collation is not traditional ASCII order
statement: Traditional ranges such as A-Z can behave unexpectedly under locale collation rules.

condition: when matching broad character categories portably
statement: POSIX character classes provide safer named character sets such as upper, lower, digit, alpha, alnum, space, and xdigit.

condition: when writing bracket expressions for regex or glob contexts
statement: POSIX character classes can be used in both regular expressions and shell pathname expansion.

condition: when considering traditional range behavior by setting LANG=POSIX
statement: Changing LANG to POSIX restores traditional ASCII collation behavior but also changes locale behavior to U.S. English ASCII.

condition: when choosing BRE versus ERE syntax
statement: POSIX basic regular expressions recognize a smaller metacharacter set than POSIX extended regular expressions.

condition: when using GNU grep as described by the book
statement: grep uses basic regular expressions by default and extended regular expressions when invoked with -E.

condition: when using extended regular expressions
statement: In ERE, alternation with the vertical bar matches one expression from a set of alternatives.

condition: when passing ERE alternation through a shell
statement: Extended regular expressions containing alternation should be quoted so the shell does not treat the vertical bar as a pipeline operator.

condition: when combining alternation with anchors or other elements
statement: Parentheses group alternatives with surrounding regex elements; omitting them can change the scope of alternation.

condition: when using the ? quantifier
statement: In ERE, the question mark makes the preceding element optional by matching it zero or one time.

condition: when using the * quantifier
statement: In ERE, the asterisk matches the preceding element zero or more times.

condition: when using the + quantifier
statement: In ERE, the plus sign requires the preceding element to occur one or more times.

condition: when using {n}, {n,m}, {n,}, or {,m}
statement: In ERE, braces express exact, bounded, lower-bounded, or upper-bounded repetition counts.

condition: when a punctuation character should be matched literally
statement: Escaping regex metacharacters makes them match as literal characters in the relevant regex dialect.

condition: when validating entire records such as phone-number lines
statement: A grep validation expression should anchor both ends when the whole line must match the required format.

condition: when finding invalid lines in a list
statement: grep -v can invert a validation regex to report records that do not match the required format.

condition: when using regular expressions with find
statement: find -regex requires the entire pathname to match the regular expression, unlike grep which can match a substring of a line.

condition: when searching find pathnames for unacceptable characters
statement: A find regex that should match a substring anywhere in the pathname needs leading and trailing wildcards such as dot-star.

condition: when auditing filenames for spaces or other unwanted characters
statement: find with a negated bracket expression can locate pathnames containing characters outside an acceptable filename set.

condition: when using locate implementations described by the book
statement: locate supports regular-expression searches through options for basic or extended regex matching.

condition: when searching within less or vim
statement: less and vim both use slash followed by a regex to search text.

condition: when porting ERE patterns to vim search
statement: vim search uses basic regular expression syntax, so some metacharacters that are special in ERE must be escaped to act as metacharacters.

condition: when matches are not highlighted by default
statement: vim search highlighting can be enabled with :hlsearch when the installed vim supports it.

condition: when searching compressed man pages or other gzip-compressed text
statement: zgrep applies grep-style searching to compressed files.

condition: when investing effort in text-processing skills
statement: Regular expressions appear across many command-line programs, so learning them has broad practical value.

condition: when working with Unix-like systems
statement: Unix-like systems rely heavily on text files for data storage, which is why they include many text-manipulation tools.

condition: when authoring documents in formats such as Markdown or other markup languages
statement: Plain text plus markup can represent large formatted documents while preserving text-based editability.

condition: when treating web content as text data
statement: Web pages are text documents described with markup languages such as HTML or XML.

condition: when inspecting raw email messages
statement: Email is fundamentally text-based, with headers describing message source and transit before the body content.

condition: when understanding email transport
statement: Non-text email attachments are converted into text representations for transmission.

condition: when printing text or graphical pages
statement: Unix-like printer workflows send plain text or text-based page description data such as PostScript to the printing system.

condition: when working with Unix-like command-line tools
statement: Program source code is text, which makes text-processing tools important for software development and system administration.

condition: when inspecting hidden characters in text
statement: cat -A reveals nonprinting characters such as tabs, carriage returns, and end-of-line positions.

condition: when diagnosing whitespace at line ends
statement: cat -A can expose trailing spaces because the displayed line-end marker appears after the true end of the text.

condition: when diagnosing cross-platform text-file line endings
statement: Unix text lines end with linefeed, while DOS and Windows text lines traditionally end with carriage-return plus linefeed.

condition: when dos2unix is unavailable or when understanding the conversion
statement: DOS-format text can be converted to Unix format by removing carriage-return characters.

condition: when using cat to modify displayed text
statement: cat -n numbers lines and cat -s suppresses repeated blank lines.

condition: when sorting text streams or files
statement: sort reads standard input or named files, sorts lines, and writes the result to standard output.

condition: when combining several text files into a sorted list
statement: sort can merge multiple input files into one sorted output stream.

condition: when sorting numbers embedded at the sort key
statement: sort -n sorts by numeric value rather than lexical character order.

condition: when reverse ordering is needed
statement: sort -r reverses sort order, producing descending rather than ascending output.

condition: when sorting tabular text by a specific column
statement: sort -k selects one or more key fields instead of sorting by the entire line.

condition: when all input files are already sorted
statement: sort -m merges presorted input files without performing a new full sort.

condition: when saving sorted results directly
statement: sort -o writes sorted output to a named file rather than standard output.

condition: when sorting delimiter-separated data such as colon-separated records
statement: sort -t defines a field separator character other than the default whitespace behavior.

condition: when interpreting default sort field behavior
statement: By default, sort treats whitespace as field separators and includes delimiters as part of fields during sorting.

condition: when one field alone is not enough to order records correctly
statement: Multiple sort -k options can define multi-key sorts such as alphabetic primary key and numeric secondary key.

condition: when using sort key ranges
statement: A sort key range such as first-field to first-field limits the key to exactly that field.

condition: when applying per-key sort behavior
statement: Sort key modifiers such as n, r, and b can be attached to individual key specifications.

condition: when sorting dates or other structured fields stored inside one field
statement: sort key offsets can select characters within a field, enabling sorting by pieces of a field such as year, month, and day.

condition: when choosing date formats for machine sorting
statement: ISO-style year-month-day date formats are easier to sort chronologically than month-day-year formats.

condition: when sorting fields separated by characters such as colons
statement: With non-whitespace delimiters, sort treats each delimiter occurrence individually rather than coalescing runs as it does for whitespace.

condition: when removing duplicates with uniq
statement: uniq removes only adjacent duplicate lines, so input normally must be sorted first.

condition: when using GNU sort
statement: GNU sort -u can remove duplicates while sorting, overlapping a common sort-plus-uniq workflow.

condition: when counting duplicate lines
statement: uniq -c prefixes each output line with the number of adjacent occurrences.

condition: when tailoring uniq comparisons or output
statement: uniq options can report only repeated lines, only unique lines, ignore case, or skip leading fields or characters.

condition: when slicing columns from text
statement: cut extracts selected character positions or fields from each input line and writes them to standard output.

condition: when choosing cut for extraction
statement: cut is best suited to clean machine-generated text rather than irregular human-typed text.

condition: when extracting tab-delimited fields with cut
statement: cut -f extracts fields, with tabs as the default field delimiter.

condition: when extracting fields from non-tab-delimited data
statement: cut -d changes the field delimiter used with cut -f.

condition: when selecting fixed character positions
statement: cut -c extracts character ranges, which works best when line positions are stable.

condition: when using cut -c on tabbed text
statement: The expand command converts tabs to the corresponding spaces so character-position operations become more predictable.

condition: when reversing space expansion where appropriate
statement: The unexpand command can substitute tabs for spaces.

condition: when recombining columns of text
statement: paste combines columns from multiple input files into one output stream in the order the files are given.

condition: when merging related tabular text from separate files
statement: join combines rows from two files using a shared key field, similar to a relational database join.

condition: when preparing files for join
statement: Input files must be sorted on the join key for join to work properly.

condition: when reading default join output
statement: join uses whitespace as the default input delimiter and a single space as the default output delimiter unless options change this behavior.

condition: when reversing the order of records or log lines
statement: tac concatenates file content in reverse line order.

condition: when inspecting chronological logs from the end backward
statement: tac can place the most recent log entries at the top when logs are normally newest at the bottom.

condition: when transforming line text characterwise
statement: rev reverses the characters within each input line.

condition: when fixed character positions from the line start are easier to cut
statement: rev can be paired with cut to remove a suffix from variable-length lines by temporarily moving the suffix to the front.

condition: when administering systems or developing software
statement: Comparing text versions is important for diagnosing configuration changes and reviewing source-code changes.

condition: when comparing two sorted text lists
statement: comm compares two text files and reports lines unique to the first file, unique to the second file, and common to both.

condition: when filtering comm comparison output
statement: comm column-suppression options can select only common lines or only lines unique to one side.

condition: when comparing text files or source trees
statement: diff detects differences between files and supports formats suitable for human review and patch generation.

condition: when comparing source trees
statement: diff can recursively examine directories of source code.

condition: when choosing a diff format for review or patching
statement: Unified diff format is more concise than context format because it avoids duplicating context lines.

condition: when reading unified diffs
statement: In unified diff output, blank lines are shared context, minus lines are removed from the first file, and plus lines are added in the second file.

condition: when applying patches to text files or source trees
statement: patch applies changes described by diff output to convert older text into newer text.

condition: when sharing or reviewing source changes
statement: diff and patch are useful because a patch file is much smaller than a whole source tree and makes changes easier to review.

condition: when preparing a diff file for patch
statement: GNU documentation recommends diff -Naur old new > diff_file as a practical form for patch input.

condition: when applying a properly formed unified diff
statement: patch can infer target filenames from a unified diff header, so a separate target filename is not always needed.

condition: when performing character-level conversions
statement: tr transliterates characters from standard input to standard output using corresponding source and target character sets.

condition: when specifying tr conversion sets
statement: tr character sets can be enumerated lists, ranges, or POSIX character classes.

condition: when using character ranges with tr
statement: tr ranges can be affected by locale collation and should be used with caution where that matters.

condition: when collapsing several characters into one output character
statement: tr can map multiple source characters to one target character when the first set is larger than the second.

condition: when deleting unwanted characters from text
statement: tr -d can delete characters from a stream, such as removing carriage returns to convert DOS text to Unix line endings.

condition: when collapsing repeated neighboring characters
statement: tr -s squeezes adjacent repeated instances of specified characters into single instances.

condition: when interpreting tr -s results
statement: tr squeezing has no effect on repeated characters that are not adjacent.

condition: when evaluating ROT13 for secrecy
statement: ROT13 performed with tr is text obfuscation rather than strong encryption.

condition: when applying scripted text edits
statement: sed edits a stream of text from standard input or files non-interactively.

condition: when choosing how to supply sed instructions
statement: sed can receive a single editing command on the command line or a script file containing multiple commands.

condition: when writing sed substitutions
statement: The sed substitution command has the form s delimiter pattern delimiter replacement delimiter, with the delimiter chosen by the character after s.

condition: when sed patterns contain slash characters
statement: Choosing an alternate sed delimiter can make substitution commands more readable when the pattern or replacement contains slashes.

condition: when no sed address precedes the command
statement: A sed command without an address applies to every line in the input stream.

condition: when limiting sed edits to selected input lines
statement: sed addresses can target a line number, the last line, a regex match, a range, stepped lines, relative following lines, or all lines except a match.

condition: when using sed p as a filter
statement: sed prints every input line by default, so sed -n is needed with p when only selected lines should be printed.

condition: when negating sed address selection
statement: A sed address followed by ! applies the command to lines that do not match the address.

condition: when selecting sed command letters
statement: sed basic commands include printing line numbers, appending, deleting, inserting, printing, quitting, substituting, and transliterating.

condition: when using matched text in sed replacements
statement: In sed substitutions, ampersand in the replacement expands to the text matched by the regex.

condition: when rearranging matched text in sed replacements
statement: In sed substitutions, back references  through \9 refer to captured subexpressions from the regex.

condition: when writing sed regexes without extended-regex options
statement: sed uses basic regular expressions by default, so grouping and repetition syntax often need backslash escaping.

condition: when every occurrence on each line should change
statement: The sed substitution g flag replaces all matches on a line rather than only the first match.

condition: when sed edits become too complex for one command line
statement: sed -f runs editing commands from a script file.

condition: when maintaining sed scripts
statement: sed script comments begin with # and blank lines can improve script readability.

condition: when writing multi-line sed commands such as insert, append, or change
statement: A sed line-continuation character is a backslash immediately followed by a newline, with no intervening spaces.

condition: when choosing between sed y and tr
statement: sed y transliteration requires source and target sets of the same length and does not support ranges or POSIX classes as tr does.
sed is best reserved for simple stream-editing tasks, while larger or more language-like text processing work is better handled by tools such as awk or perl.
condition: when a text task grows beyond simple one-line editing or small scripts

statement: awk is especially suited to manipulating tabular data because it processes text line by line with address-like patterns and actions.
condition: when the input is structured as rows and fields

statement: Perl can replace shell scripts for many system administration tasks because it is a full programming language rather than a narrow text filter.
condition: when administration logic outgrows simple shell pipelines

statement: The command-line spell checker aspell can be used directly on prose files with check mode to interactively inspect and correct suspected misspellings.
condition: when a text file contains ordinary prose

statement: Aspell is not guaranteed to be installed by default, so scripts or procedures that depend on it should account for package availability.
condition: when using aspell on a distribution or host not yet checked for the package
